RFC 1122 s3.2.1.3 makes the whole 127 block loopback at the IP layer, independent of naming. o2, o3 and o4 are each false and each 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-hosts added, since neither RFC cited by the concept documents /etc/hosts at all - this was an attribution gap, not a content error.

items.stem: A developer runs several local services and wants to give each one a distinct loopback address, such as 127.0.0.2 and 127.0.0.3, rather than sharing 127.0.0.1. Is that a valid approach?

options.text: Yes. The whole 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved for loopback, so 127.0.0.2 and 127.0.0.3 loop back to the host exactly as 127.0.0.1 does, and are occasionally used this way.
options.why: Loopback reservation covers the entire /8 block, not just the single address 127.0.0.1, so any address in that range behaves identically on the local host.

options.text: No — only 127.0.0.1 is reserved for loopback, and the rest of the 127.0.0.0/8 range is ordinary routable address space.
options.why: The entire 127.0.0.0/8 block, not just the single address 127.0.0.1, is reserved for loopback and never reaches a network interface.

options.text: No — using any address other than 127.0.0.1 for loopback purposes requires it to first be registered as RFC 1918 private space.
options.why: Loopback addressing has nothing to do with RFC 1918 private space; the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block is a separate reservation defined independently of RFC 1918.

options.text: Yes, but only up to 127.0.0.255, since the loopback reservation is limited to the final octet rather than the whole /8 block.
options.why: The loopback reservation is the full /8 block, 127.0.0.0 through 127.255.255.255, not merely the final octet of the first subnet.

items.rationale: The whole 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved for loopback, not merely 127.0.0.1, so addresses such as 127.0.0.2 also loop back to the host — a fact occasionally used to give several local services distinct local addresses.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed both documentarily and empirically. RFC 6890 s2.2.2 registers the block 127.0.0.0/8 (not the single address) under Name 'Loopback', citing RFC 1122 s3.2.1.3, which reads '{ 127, <any> } Internal host loopback address'. Empirical, docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2+iputils-ping: 'ping -c2 127.0.0.2' -> '64 bytes from 127.0.0.2 ... 0% packet loss', and 'ping -c2 127.200.5.9' -> '64 bytes from 127.200.5.9 ... time=0.548 ms', confirming the whole /8 (not merely 127.0.0.x) loops back; 'ip addr' shows only 'inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo', so the /8 prefix on lo is what makes the rest reachable. o4 ('only up to 127.0.0.255') is therefore disproven directly by the 127.200.5.9 test. o2 and o3 are false with true whys.

items.stem: A file server, a print queue and an ordinary laptop are being provisioned. The file server needs a stable address referenced by an A record; the laptop just needs to get online. Which addressing choice fits each, and on what basis?

options.text: The server gets a static address or a DHCP reservation, since anything referenced by name needs stability; the laptop gets a plain dynamic DHCP address, since managing hundreds of hand-written client configurations does not scale.
options.why: The choice turns on who needs a stable, predictable address (servers, gateways, anything an A record points at) versus who does not (ordinary clients), not on hardware type alone.

options.text: Both the server and the laptop should get plain dynamic DHCP addresses, since DHCP reservations do not exist as an option separate from an ordinary dynamic lease.
options.why: A DHCP reservation is a distinct, real option — binding one MAC to one fixed address — that gives a server-class device stability while remaining a DHCP client.

options.text: Both the server and the laptop should get static addresses configured by hand, since any device an administrator provisions deliberately is assumed to never depend on DHCP.
options.why: Managing hundreds of hand-written client configurations does not scale; ordinary clients are given dynamic addresses precisely to avoid that burden.

options.text: The choice should instead be based on which device was purchased most recently, since older hardware on the network is generally assumed to need static addressing regardless of its role, which feels reasonable on first encounter in most textbooks and quick references.
options.why: The addressing choice is driven by whether stability is required by name-based references, not by the age or purchase date of the hardware involved.

items.rationale: Static addressing (or a DHCP reservation) suits devices that must stay stable because something references them by name or fixed configuration, such as servers and gateways; ordinary clients are given dynamic addresses because hand-writing hundreds of configurations does not scale.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 2131 s1 describes three allocation mechanisms - automatic (permanent), dynamic (leased, reusable) and manual allocation, where 'the client's IP address is assigned by the network administrator, and DHCP is used simply to convey the assigned address to the client' - which is exactly the DHCP reservation the key names, so o2's claim that reservations 'do not exist as an option' is squarely contradicted by the RFC. o3 and o4 are false with true whys. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: An administrator statically assigns 192.168.1.50 to a new printer, unaware that the DHCP server's pool for that subnet is 192.168.1.20 through 192.168.1.100. What is the likely consequence, and why?

options.text: A duplicate-address conflict is likely once the DHCP server eventually leases 192.168.1.50 to a client, since the static address sits inside the dynamic pool's range.
options.why: Setting a static address inside a DHCP pool invites exactly this conflict, because the server has no knowledge that the address is already claimed outside its own bookkeeping.

options.text: No conflict is possible, because a statically configured address always takes precedence over anything the DHCP server might later offer by default on most systems administrators encounter.
options.why: A DHCP server has no visibility into addresses configured statically outside its own pool bookkeeping, so precedence does not prevent it from later offering the same address.

options.text: No conflict is possible, because printers are automatically excluded from DHCP pools by every major DHCP server implementation.
options.why: DHCP servers have no automatic device-type exclusion; a pool exclusion has to be configured explicitly, which is exactly what a reservation is for.

options.text: A conflict is likely, but only because printers are unable to hold a static IPv4 address under any circumstances.
options.why: Printers are perfectly capable of holding a static address; the conflict arises from the address falling inside the active DHCP pool range, not from any printer-specific limitation.

items.rationale: Setting a static address inside a DHCP pool's range invites a duplicate-address conflict when the server later leases that same address to someone else, which is exactly why reservations — which exclude the address from the dynamic pool — exist as the safer alternative.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and note the key is correctly hedged as 'likely' rather than certain: RFC 2131 s2.2 says a DHCP server 'SHOULD' probe a newly allocated address (e.g. with ICMP echo) and a client 'SHOULD' probe with ARP before use, so a conflict is probable but not guaranteed - the key's wording survives that nuance where an absolute claim would not. o2 is false: nothing in RFC 2131 gives a statically configured host precedence over the server's own bookkeeping. o3 and o4 are false with true whys. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: An administrator runs `ip addr add 10.0.5.100/24 dev enp0s3` on a server and calls the address "now static." Is that terminology accurate?

options.text: No, "static" means the configuration is written into the host's persistent network configuration; `ip addr add` is a temporary runtime change that disappears at the next reboot or reconfiguration.
options.why: The distinction is about who holds the configuration and whether it persists, not about whether the address happens to stay the same for now.

options.text: Yes — any address set with a manual command like `ip addr add`, rather than obtained automatically, counts as static by definition.
options.why: 'Static' specifically means the configuration is written into the persistent network configuration and applied at boot; a bare runtime `ip addr add` command does neither.

options.text: No, but only because the address 10.0.5.100 happens to fall inside a range reserved for dynamic addressing on this network.
options.why: Whether an address falls in a particular numeric range has no bearing on whether it is static or dynamic; that distinction is about how and where the configuration is stored.

options.text: Yes, and the address will in fact remain assigned across every future reboot exactly as a genuinely static address would.
options.why: A runtime `ip addr add` command is lost on reboot precisely because it writes nothing to disk, unlike a genuinely static address configured in the persistent network configuration.

items.rationale: A static address is written into the distribution's persistent network configuration and reapplied at boot; `ip addr add` only changes the running kernel state, so calling that a "static" address is a mislabel that a question about permanence is not answered by.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. ip-address(8) documents 'ip address add - add new protocol address' as a runtime operation on the kernel's address list and documents no persistence mechanism whatsoever, which is the documentary basis for the key. Empirical: in docker ubuntu:24.04, 'ip addr add 10.9.9.2/24 dev veth0' takes effect immediately and is present in 'ip addr'; nothing is written to disk, and the address is absent in a fresh container from the same image. o4 ('will remain assigned across every future reboot') is therefore false. o2 is false: it defines static by the manner of the command rather than by persistence. o3 is false with a true why. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ip-address added, because the umbrella ip(8) page does not document 'ip address add' at all - it only lists OBJECT names.

items.stem: A dynamically leased address has not changed in over six months. A junior admin argues it must actually be static, since 'static' means the address never changes. Is that reasoning sound?

options.text: No: a dynamic address can remain identical for a long time and still be dynamic; the distinction is about who owns the configuration, not whether the value happens to stay constant.
options.why: An address staying the same over time is a coincidence of lease renewal, not evidence of static configuration; the server, not the host, still owns and could reassign it.

options.text: Yes — any address that has been observed to stay constant for a long enough period should be reclassified as static.
options.why: There is no duration after which a dynamically leased address becomes static; classification depends on where the configuration is held, not on observed stability over time.

options.text: No, but only because the address must actually be a DHCP reservation rather than either a static or an ordinary dynamic address.
options.why: The scenario describes an ordinary dynamic lease, not a reservation; nothing in the description implies a MAC-to-address binding exists on the server.

options.text: Yes, since only a DHCP server outage could explain an address remaining the same for that long, which effectively makes it static across virtually every environment of this kind, a conclusion that seems to follow from everyday experience.
options.why: A stable lease renewal, not a server outage, is the ordinary explanation for a long-unchanged dynamic address, and neither explanation reclassifies it as static.

items.rationale: A dynamic address can remain identical for months through ordinary lease renewal and still be dynamic, because the distinction is about whether the configuration is written on the host (static) or held and renewable by the server (dynamic), not about whether the value has changed recently.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 2131 s3.2 ('reusing a previously allocated network address') and s4.4.5 ('Reacquisition and expiration', RENEWING/REBINDING) describe a client requesting and normally being granted the same address indefinitely, so a dynamic address staying constant for months is the expected behaviour of a lease, not evidence of static configuration; the server retains ownership and may assign differently. o2 posits a duration threshold that appears nowhere in RFC 2131. o3 is false: nothing in the stem implies a manual/reserved binding. o4 is false: RFC 2131 s4.4.5 has the client keep using its address until lease expiry, so an outage is not needed to explain stability. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A packet travels from a laptop, across two routers, to a server on a different network. Which of the following stays the same across every hop, and which changes at each router?

options.text: The source and destination IP addresses stay the same end to end; the source and destination MAC addresses are rewritten by each router to the next hop's addresses.
options.why: Each router strips the old frame and builds a new one with new source and destination MAC addresses for the next hop, while leaving the IP addresses in the packet untouched.

options.text: The MAC addresses stay the same end to end, since they are the permanent hardware identifiers; the IP addresses are rewritten by each router instead.
options.why: This reverses the actual behaviour: MAC addresses are rewritten hop by hop while IP addresses are what remain constant end to end.

options.text: Both the IP and MAC addresses stay identical at every hop, because routers only inspect headers without modifying either one.
options.why: A router necessarily rebuilds the frame with new source and destination MAC addresses for the next hop; only the IP addresses are left untouched.

options.text: Both the IP and MAC addresses are rewritten at every hop, since each router treats the packet as an entirely new transmission.
options.why: IP addresses are preserved end to end specifically so the packet can be routed toward its ultimate destination; only the MAC addresses are rewritten hop by hop.

items.rationale: A host fills in its own MAC as source and the next hop's MAC as destination; each router that forwards the packet strips the old frame and builds a new one with new MAC addresses, while the IP addresses in the packet stay untouched end to end — the key exam fact about MAC addresses is negative: they never cross a router.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 1122 s3.3.1 ('The IP layer chooses the correct next hop for each datagram it sends') and s3.3.1.1 establish that forwarding is a per-hop next-hop decision made on the unchanged IP destination address, while RFC 826 exists precisely because 'most protocol addresses are not 48.bits long, nor do they necessarily have any relationship to the 48.bit Ethernet address of the hardware' - so each hop resolves its own link-layer addressing for the next hop. RFC 894 confirms the IP module maps Internet addresses to Ethernet addresses per Ethernet network. o2 reverses the behaviour, o3 denies frame rebuilding, o4 denies IP preservation; each 'why' states a true fact. Scope note recorded honestly: the key is true for plain forwarding; NAT rewrites IP addresses, but the stem describes ordinary routing, not NAT, and no option raises NAT. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A candidate needs the hardware address of `enp0s3`. Which iproute2 command is the layer 2 view of an interface, reporting the MAC in its `link/ether` field?

options.text: `ip link`, because the link object is the layer 2 view of an interface and reports the hardware address in its `link/ether` field, which `ip addr` also prints above the layer 3 addresses.
options.why: `ip link` is the layer 2 view of an interface and `link/ether` is the field carrying the MAC; ifconfig(8) itself directs readers to ip-link(8) to display link layer information including the hardware address.

options.text: `ip addr` with the `-6` flag added, since restricting the output to IPv6 is what makes the hardware address appear alongside the IPv6 addresses, which is the assumption most administrators start from.
options.why: `ip -6 addr` restricts output to IPv6 addressing and prints nothing at all for an interface that has no IPv6 address; it never adds hardware address information.

options.text: `ip route`, since the routing table lists the hardware address of the interface associated with each configured route, alongside that route's destination and next hop.
options.why: `ip route` shows the routing table — destinations, next hops and interfaces — and does not display hardware addresses at all.

options.text: `ip neigh`, since the neighbour cache is the table where every local interface's own hardware address is recorded once that interface has been brought up.
options.why: `ip neigh` shows the neighbour (ARP) cache of other hosts' resolved addresses, not the local interface's own hardware address, which `ip link` reports.

items.rationale: `ip link` is the layer 2 command, printing each interface with its MAC in the `link/ether` field; `ip addr` is layer 3 only, which is why expecting a hardware address from it is a common mistake.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The original stem asserted a false premise - 'A candidate runs `ip addr` and cannot find it' - and the original key's why said '`ip addr` reports layer 3 addresses instead', implying `ip addr` does not show the MAC. It does. Empirical, docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2: 'ip addr show eth0' prints '11: eth0@if114: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> ... / link/ether e6:b2:f0:63:2c:e1 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff ... / inet 172.17.0.4/16 ...' - the link/ether line is present. The item therefore taught a false fact about `ip addr`. Repaired: the stem now asks which command is the layer 2 view of an interface, and the key states truthfully that `ip addr` prints the same link line. Re-verified: 'ip link' output in the same container is '11: eth0@if114: ... link/ether e6:b2:f0:63:2c:e1 brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff', so the key holds. o2 was also repaired and is now empirically settled: 'ip -6 addr show eth0' in that container printed NOTHING at all, no link/ether line, so restricting to IPv6 removes rather than adds hardware information. o3 is confirmed wrong against ip-route(8), whose SELECTOR/NODE_SPEC/NH grammar contains no link-layer address field at all, and against the observed 'ip route' output, which prints only prefix, dev, proto, scope and src. o4 is confirmed wrong against ip-neighbour(8): it 'manipulates neighbour objects that establish bindings between protocol addresses and link layer addresses for hosts sharing the same link' - other hosts, not the local interface's own address; the observed 'ip neigh' output held only the gateway's lladdr. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ip-link added, because the umbrella ip(8) page contains no occurrence of 'link/ether' and does not document the link object's output at all. Shape note: o3 and o4 were lengthened and the key shortened so the repaired item does not make the key the longest option.

items.stem: A device's MAC address changes every time it joins a Wi-Fi network, and an administrator flags this as evidence of a hardware fault. Is that the right conclusion?

options.text: No. MAC addresses can be overridden in software, and many systems deliberately randomise them on wireless networks for privacy, which is normal behaviour rather than a fault.
options.why: A MAC is not permanent in practice; software overrides and privacy-driven randomisation on Wi-Fi are expected, documented behaviour, not a sign of hardware failure.

options.text: Yes — a MAC address is burned into the hardware and can never legitimately change under any circumstances.
options.why: While the manufacturer burns in an original MAC, it can be overridden in software, and Wi-Fi privacy randomisation is a deliberate, expected feature, not an anomaly.

options.text: No, but only because the device must be silently switching between two separate physical network interfaces each time.
options.why: A single wireless interface randomising its own MAC address per network is the ordinary explanation; no second physical interface needs to be involved.

options.text: Yes, but the fault lies in DHCP rather than in the network hardware, since DHCP is what assigns a new MAC on each join under typical operating conditions, an assumption that holds until it does not.
options.why: DHCP assigns IP addressing information, not MAC addresses; a device's own operating system, not DHCP, is what randomises the MAC on Wi-Fi.

items.rationale: A MAC address is not permanent in practice: it can be overridden in software, and many systems deliberately randomise it on wireless networks for privacy, so a changing MAC on Wi-Fi joins is expected behaviour, not evidence of a hardware fault.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against two documents that the concept previously did not cite. RFC 7844 s2.1 'MAC Address Randomization Hypotheses' documents the deliberate practice directly, listing 'Per connection: Configure a random link-layer address at the time of connecting to a network, e.g., to a specific Wi-Fi SSID' and 'Per network', and s2 explains the privacy motive ('when devices use Wi-Fi connectivity, they place the MAC address in the clear'). RFC 7042 s2.1 supplies the software-override half: the Local bit distinguishes locally administered from globally unique IEEE-assigned identifiers, so a non-manufacturer MAC is an architected case, not a fault. o2's absolute 'can never legitimately change' is refuted by both. o3 is false: RFC 7844 describes a single interface changing its own address. o4 is false: RFC 2131 has DHCP conveying IP configuration, never link-layer addresses. Every 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-7844 and rfc-7042 added; RFC 826 alone is silent on randomisation and on the Local bit, so this was an attribution gap.

items.stem: A packet capture on a switch shows a frame addressed to `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`. What is that destination, and what happens to the frame?

options.text: It is the broadcast MAC address, and the frame is delivered to every interface on that segment.
options.why: The all-ones MAC address is reserved as the broadcast address, and a switch floods a frame addressed to it to every port on the segment.

options.text: It is a malformed or corrupted address, since a real MAC address cannot legitimately consist entirely of the same repeated value.
options.why: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is a valid, reserved value with a specific defined meaning — the broadcast address — not evidence of corruption.

options.text: It is the address of the segment's default gateway, since routers conventionally use that reserved value as their MAC address.
options.why: A gateway's MAC address is an ordinary vendor-assigned address like any host's; ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is reserved specifically as the broadcast address, not for gateways.

options.text: It is a multicast group address, and the frame is delivered only to interfaces that have subscribed to that particular group.
options.why: Multicast MAC addresses are identified by the Group bit, the low-order bit of the first octet, being set, not by any vendor-defined pattern; ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is the reserved broadcast address, delivered to every interface rather than only to subscribed group members.

items.rationale: The all-ones MAC address, ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, is the broadcast address, delivered to every interface on the segment — the mechanism an ARP request relies on to reach every host without knowing in advance which one holds the target address.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 894 states under 'Broadcast Address' that 'The broadcast Internet address ... should be mapped to the broadcast Ethernet address (of all binary ones, FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF hex)', which settles both the identity and the delivery semantics. o2 and o3 are false with true whys. o4's TEXT is correctly wrong (broadcast is not delivered only to subscribers), but its 'why' AS AUTHORED stated a false fact - that multicast MAC addresses 'follow a different, vendor-defined pattern'. RFC 7042 s2.1 is explicit that multicast identifiers are formed by turning on the Group bit (the bottom bit of the first octet), which is an IEEE architectural bit, not a vendor pattern; RFC 7042 s2.3.1 confirms IANA's own 33-33 IPv6 multicast prefix has the Group bit on. The why was rewritten to state the Group bit rule. Noted for the record and deliberately not made an option: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff does have the Group bit set, so broadcast is formally a special case of layer 2 group addressing - but o4 fails regardless on its delivery claim, so this does not create a second defensible answer.

items.stem: A host can reach every other machine on its own subnet by IP address but a name lookup for one particular server fails. Separately, a different host cannot reach one particular local IP address at all. Which protocol is implicated in each case?

options.text: The name-lookup failure implicates DNS, which resolves names to addresses across the whole internet; the local-address failure implicates ARP, which resolves an address to a MAC only within one segment.
options.why: DNS and ARP resolve opposite ends of the address chain — DNS turns a name into an IP address, ARP turns an IP address into a hardware address — and they never substitute for each other.

options.text: Both cases implicate DNS, since any resolution failure of any kind whatsoever is ultimately treated as a DNS problem regardless of its actual scope.
options.why: ARP resolution operates entirely below DNS, on one local segment, using no IP transport and no port at all; a local address-to-MAC failure is not a DNS problem.

options.text: Both cases implicate ARP, since ARP is assumed to be responsible for resolving both names and local hardware addresses on a modern network.
options.why: ARP resolves IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses only; it has no role in resolving names, which is DNS's job across the internet, not a local-segment one.

options.text: The name-lookup failure instead implicates ARP, since ARP requests are assumed to carry hostnames as well as IP addresses; the local-address failure implicates DNS, regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved.
options.why: ARP requests never carry hostnames — only IPv4 and MAC addresses — and DNS has no role in resolving a local-segment IP-to-MAC mapping.

items.rationale: DNS resolves a name to an IP address, globally and hierarchically; ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address, but only on the local segment. A name failure with working raw addresses points at DNS, while a single unreachable local address with everything else working points at ARP.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 826's stated purpose is converting 'Protocol Addresses (e.g., IP addresses) to Local Network Addresses' on one physical cable, and its packet format carries only ar$spa/ar$tpa protocol addresses and ar$sha/ar$tha hardware addresses - no name field of any kind, which directly disposes of o4's claim that ARP requests carry hostnames. ip-neighbour(8) confirms the scope: neighbour objects bind protocol addresses to link layer addresses 'for hosts sharing the same link'. DNS's name-to-address role is a separate mechanism entirely. o2 and o3 are false with true whys. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A host cannot reach 192.0.2.44, which is on the same subnet. `ip neigh show dev enp0s3` shows a FAILED entry for that address. What does a FAILED entry mean here?

options.text: The ARP request for 192.0.2.44 went unanswered on this segment; nothing responded, which points at that specific host being off, misconfigured, or on a different segment than assumed.
options.why: A FAILED state means the address did not answer an ARP request on this segment, which localises the problem to that specific host rather than to routing or a wider network issue.

options.text: It means routing to 192.0.2.44 has failed somewhere beyond this subnet, which ARP is reporting on behalf of the router.
options.why: ARP never crosses a router and has nothing to say about routing beyond the local segment; FAILED specifically reports that no answer arrived to a local ARP request.

options.text: It means the address is definitely down at the operating-system level, since ARP can distinguish a powered-off host from a merely unresponsive one as commonly understood by less experienced staff.
options.why: ARP can only report that no reply arrived; it cannot distinguish a powered-off host from one on a different segment, a firewall drop, or any other cause of silence.

options.text: It means DNS resolution for that address's hostname has failed, which `ip neigh` also reports through the same state field.
options.why: `ip neigh` reports the state of address-to-MAC resolution only; it has no relationship to DNS, which resolves names rather than local hardware addresses.

items.rationale: FAILED in `ip neigh` means an ARP request for that address went unanswered on the local segment, which is a strong, specific localisation — it says nothing was reached at all, distinct from a REJECT or a working entry showing the resolved MAC. The deprecated net-tools equivalent, `arp -n`, reports the same cache numerically where installed.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and the key is correctly hedged. ip-neighbour(8) defines the state verbatim: 'failed - max number of probes exceeded without success, neighbor validation has ultimately failed', and the page's DESCRIPTION scopes neighbour entries to 'hosts sharing the same link' and names the IPv4 neighbour table 'the ARP table'. That is exactly 'nothing responded on this segment' and nothing stronger, which is why o3 ('definitely down at the operating-system level') is wrong - the man page's wording supports only 'no answer', not a cause. o2 is wrong because ARP is link-scoped and reports nothing about routing. o4 is wrong: the state field is address-to-MAC resolution state, unrelated to DNS. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ip-neighbour added, since the FAILED state is documented only on ip-neighbour(8) - the umbrella ip(8) page does not define neighbour states at all. This is the exact man-page trap the task brief warns about.

items.stem: A host at 10.1.1.5/24 sends traffic to 10.1.9.50, which is off-subnet. Checking `ip neigh` afterward, no entry for 10.1.9.50 appears at all. Is that evidence of an ARP failure?

options.text: No, ARP never crosses a router, so a host never resolves the MAC of an off-subnet destination; the neighbour cache instead holds an entry for the gateway, which is what actually receives the frame.
options.why: A host addresses off-subnet traffic to the gateway's MAC while keeping the destination's IP, so the neighbour cache legitimately has no entry for a remote address at all.

options.text: Yes — the missing entry means ARP failed to resolve the destination, and that failure is what is preventing the traffic from being delivered.
options.why: An off-subnet destination is never expected to appear in the neighbour cache at all; its absence is normal, not evidence of a failed resolution.

options.text: No, but only because the destination is using IPv6 Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP, which stores its entries in a separate table.
options.why: The scenario uses ordinary IPv4 addressing, so ARP, not IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, is the relevant mechanism; the absence of an entry is explained by the off-subnet rule, not by an IPv6 substitution.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to manually add a static ARP entry for 10.1.9.50 so the host can resolve it directly.
options.why: A static ARP entry for an off-subnet address would be meaningless, since ARP cannot resolve an address that is not on the local segment at all; the frame is properly addressed to the gateway instead.

items.rationale: ARP never crosses a router: a host never learns the MAC of an off-subnet destination, so the neighbour cache holds no entry for that address at all — it resolves the gateway instead, and the frame carrying the packet holds the router's MAC, not the remote destination's.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 1122 s3.3.1.1 gives the local/remote decision: if the masked destination bits do not match, 'the destination is accessible only through a gateway', so the frame is addressed to the gateway. ip-neighbour(8) scopes the table to 'hosts sharing the same link', so an off-subnet address legitimately never appears. Empirical, docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2+iputils-ping: after 'ping -c2 8.8.8.8', 'ip neigh' printed exactly one line, '172.17.0.1 dev eth0 lladdr d2:f8:03:7d:c8:7f REACHABLE' - an entry for the gateway and none at all for the off-subnet 8.8.8.8 - while 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' returned '8.8.8.8 via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0 src 172.17.0.2', confirming the gateway is the next hop that is actually resolved. o2 and o4 are false with true whys; o3 is false because the scenario is IPv4 throughout. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A host on an IPv6-only network needs to resolve a neighbour's address to a MAC address. Which mechanism performs that job, since ARP is IPv4-only?

options.text: Neighbor Discovery, carried over ICMPv6, performs the same job for IPv6 that ARP performs for IPv4.
options.why: ARP is specific to IPv4; IPv6 replaces it with Neighbor Discovery, which is carried over ICMPv6 and serves the equivalent role.

options.text: ARP itself, since it was updated to handle both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses transparently in modern implementations.
options.why: ARP remains IPv4-only by design; it was not extended to IPv6, which uses the separate Neighbor Discovery mechanism instead.

options.text: DNS, since name-to-address resolution and address-to-MAC resolution are handled by the same protocol on IPv6 networks.
options.why: DNS resolves names to IP addresses across the internet; it has no role in resolving a local IPv6 address to a MAC address, which is Neighbor Discovery's job.

options.text: DHCPv6, since it is responsible for distributing MAC address mappings to every client on an IPv6 network.
options.why: DHCPv6 distributes addressing configuration to clients; it does not resolve one host's address to another host's MAC address, which is Neighbor Discovery's role.

items.rationale: ARP is IPv4-only; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, carried over ICMPv6, for the same job, and `ip neigh` shows the results of both mechanisms, which is why the command is named for neighbours generally rather than for ARP specifically.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the primary document, which the concept did not previously cite. RFC 4861 is titled 'Neighbor Discovery for IP version 6 (IPv6)'; its s3 Overview lists 'Address resolution: How nodes determine the link-layer address of on-link destinations' among ND's functions, states that 'Neighbor Discovery defines five different ICMP packet types', and specifies that 'Nodes accomplish address resolution by multicasting a Neighbor Solicitation'. That settles both halves of the key: the mechanism is Neighbor Discovery and the carrier is ICMPv6. o2 is false - RFC 826 defines ARP for 48-bit Ethernet and 32-bit protocol addresses and was never extended to IPv6, which is why RFC 4861 exists. o3 and o4 are false with true whys. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-4861 added; RFC 826 cannot source a claim about IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, so this was a pure attribution failure - the content was right and the citation was silent.

items.stem: An address begins with the octet 200. Using the classful ranges, which class does it fall in, and what does that tell you about its mask under modern routing?

options.text: Class C, identified by the first octet range 192-223. Under modern classless routing, though, its real mask could be anything and is not implied by the class at all.
options.why: 200 falls in the 192-223 range that defines class C historically, but CIDR replaced classful addressing, so the class no longer implies the actual prefix in use.

options.text: Class B — the first octet 200 was read as falling in the 128-191 range that defines class B.
options.why: 200 is above 191, placing it in the class C range (192-223), not the class B range (128-191).

options.text: Class C, and because it is class C its real-world mask must also be exactly /24, matching the historical default, regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved.
options.why: Modern routing is classless, so an address's class does not imply its actual mask in practice; a 200.x.x.x address may well be a /26 or any other prefix.

options.text: Class D — the first octet 200 was read as falling in the 224-239 multicast range reserved for class D.
options.why: 224-239 defines class D; 200 falls below that range, in the class C range (192-223) instead.

items.rationale: The first octet 200 falls within 192-223, the class C range, but classful addressing was superseded by CIDR in 1993: knowing the historical class does not tell you the address's actual mask under modern classless routing, which must be stated explicitly.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 791 s3.2 'Address Formats' defines class c as high order bits '110', which is first octet 192-223, so 200 is class C; class b is '10' (128-191) and class D is '1110' (224-239, per RFC 1112 s4), disposing of o2 and o4 arithmetically. RFC 4632 supplies the second half of the key: it replaced classful network numbers with classless prefixes carried explicitly (s3.1, 'Using classless prefixes with explicit prefix lengths'; s5, 'With the change from classful network numbers to classless prefixes'), so the class no longer implies a mask. o3 is the sharpest distractor and is correctly false: it gets the class right and then asserts a /24 must follow, which CIDR expressly removed. Each 'why' states a true fact. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A colleague calls a /26 network 'a class C network' and insists the two terms mean exactly the same thing. What is the actual relationship between IPv4 address classes and CIDR?

options.text: Classful addressing fixed three network sizes (/8, /16, /24) inferred from the address itself; CIDR allows any prefix from /0 to /32 stated explicitly, so a /26 is not a class C network; a class C network was specifically /24.
options.why: The colleague conflates a historical, address-implied /24 default with a CIDR prefix that is explicitly stated and can be any length, including /26, which was never a classful size at all.

options.text: They are exactly the same thing; "class C" is simply an older, informal name that continues to refer to whatever prefix length a network happens to use today, whatever that length is as commonly understood by less experienced staff.
options.why: A class C network specifically meant a /24 under the old fixed-size scheme; CIDR prefixes such as /26 are a different, classless concept the vocabulary was never meant to describe.

options.text: CIDR is simply class D renamed for modern use, since both are commonly described as more flexible successors to the original class A, B and C scheme.
options.why: Class D specifically names the 224-239 multicast range under the classful scheme; CIDR is an entirely separate, classless addressing mechanism unrelated to multicast.

options.text: The two terms are assumed to differ only in that "class C" refers to IPv6 addressing specifically, while CIDR refers exclusively to IPv4 addressing instead.
options.why: Both classful addressing and CIDR are IPv4 concepts; neither one has any special relationship to IPv6, which uses its own separate addressing architecture.

items.rationale: Classful addressing offered exactly three fixed sizes inferred from the address's leading bits — /8, /16, /24 — while CIDR allows any explicitly stated prefix length; a /26 was never a classful size, so calling it "a class C network" conflates two different addressing schemes.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 791 s3.2 fixes exactly three unicast sizes by high-order bits - 7 bits of net (a), 14 bits of net (b), 21 bits of net (c) - which are /8, /16 and /24 respectively, and the class is inferred from the address itself rather than stated. RFC 4632 s3.1 replaces this with explicit prefix lengths, so a /26 is a CIDR prefix and was never a classful size; 'class C' meant /24 specifically. o2 is false on that point. o3 is false: RFC 1112 s4 defines class D as the '1110' multicast range, unrelated to CIDR. o4 is false: RFC 4632 is an IPv4 document throughout. Each 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: What does class D identify in the classful addressing scheme, and what is the common misreading of it?

options.text: Class D, the 224-239 range, is reserved for multicast, one-to-many delivery to subscribed group members; it is commonly, and wrongly, read as "broadcast."
options.why: Class D is specifically the multicast range; multicast delivers to subscribers of a group, which is a different delivery model from broadcasting to everyone on a segment.

options.text: Class D is reserved for broadcast traffic, delivering to every host on a segment regardless of subscription.
options.why: Class D is multicast, not broadcast; broadcast delivery to every host on a segment is a different, unrelated mechanism using the all-ones host address within a block.

options.text: Class D is reserved exclusively for the loopback range, 127.0.0.0/8, set aside from the rest of class A.
options.why: Loopback, 127.0.0.0/8, falls within the class A range (1-126 first octet); class D is the separate 224-239 range reserved for multicast.

options.text: Class D is reserved for RFC 1918 private addressing, distinct from the public ranges assigned to classes A, B and C, a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive.
options.why: RFC 1918 private ranges fall within classes A, B and C (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16); class D is the separate multicast range, unrelated to private addressing.

items.rationale: Class D, first octet 224-239, is reserved for multicast — one-to-many delivery to a subscribed group — which is commonly and incorrectly described as "broadcast," a different delivery model entirely.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the document that actually defines class D, which the concept did not previously cite. RFC 1112 s4 'HOST GROUP ADDRESSES': 'Host groups are identified by class D IP addresses, i.e., those with "1110" as their high-order four bits ... host group addresses range from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255.' The whole memo is titled 'Host Extensions for IP Multicasting', so both the range and the multicast semantics are settled there. o2 is false: broadcast is a distinct mechanism (RFC 894 maps the all-ones IP host part to the all-ones Ethernet address); o3 is false, loopback is 127.0.0.0/8 inside the class A span per RFC 6890; o4 is false, RFC 1918 s3 lists 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, all within classes A, B and C. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-1112 and rfc-1918 added. Important attribution finding: RFC 791 s3.2 stops at '111 escape to extended addressing mode' and NEVER defines class D or class E, so the concept's original citation could not support any class D claim at all.

items.stem: Why is 127 absent from the usable range of class A first octets (1-126) in the classful scheme?

options.text: 127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback, so it is carved out of the class A range even though it would otherwise fall within class A's 0-127 first-octet span.
options.why: 127.0.0.0/8 is separately reserved for loopback and carved out of the class A numeric span, which is why the class A usable first-octet range stops at 126 rather than running to 127.

options.text: 127 is reserved for class B instead, which is why it does not appear in the class A first-octet range.
options.why: Class B's first-octet range is 128-191; 127 does not fall within it at all, and the reason for its exclusion from class A is the loopback reservation, not a class B assignment.

options.text: 127 is reserved for RFC 1918 private addressing, carved out of class A for that purpose.
options.why: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback space, not RFC 1918 private space; the two are separate, commonly confused reservations, and it is loopback that explains the class A gap.

options.text: 127 was simply never allocated to any class at all, and it remains entirely unused and unreserved to this day.
options.why: 127.0.0.0/8 is actively reserved and used for loopback traffic on every host; it is not an unallocated or unused range.

items.rationale: 127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback, which is why it is carved out of class A's numeric span even though 127 would otherwise fall within the 0-127 first-octet range that class A occupies, leaving the usable class A range at 1-126.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 791 s3.2 makes class a any address whose high-order bit is 0, i.e. first octet 0-127, while RFC 1122 s3.2.1.3 case (g) reserves '{ 127, <any> }' as the 'Internal host loopback address' and RFC 6890 s2.2.2 registers the whole 127.0.0.0/8 block under the name Loopback. The carve-out is therefore the reason 127 is missing from the usable class A range. o2 is false (class b is 128-191), o3 is false (RFC 1918 s3 lists 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 and not 127), o4 is false (the block is actively reserved and in daily use). The key's 'why' AS AUTHORED claimed the loopback reservation 'predates and overrides' its place in class A; RFC 6890's registry entry gives 127.0.0.0/8 an Allocation Date of September 1981, the same month RFC 791 was published, so 'predates' is not supportable. The why was rewritten to state the carve-out without the chronological claim. This was a wrong supporting fact behind a correct key, not a wrong key.

items.stem: A user reports pinging colleagues on the office subnet works fine, but nothing beyond the office — no internet, no other sites — is reachable. What should be checked first, and what command shows it directly?

options.text: The default gateway, shown by `ip route show default`; a missing or wrong 0.0.0.0/0 entry produces exactly this "local works, remote does not" pattern.
options.why: This is one of the highest-yield troubleshooting symptoms: everything on the local subnet works while nothing beyond it does, which is the signature of a missing or wrong default route.

options.text: The DNS resolver configuration, since any inability to reach a remote site is assumed to always trace back to a naming problem instead under the great majority of ordinary configurations.
options.why: A working gateway does not imply working DNS, but the symptom described — nothing beyond the subnet at all, not just names — points first at routing rather than at name resolution.

options.text: The physical cabling to the switch, since any connectivity problem of any kind is assumed to originate at the physical layer first.
options.why: Working local-subnet connectivity already confirms the physical layer is functioning; a symptom confined to remote destinations points higher up the stack, at routing.

options.text: The DHCP server, since only a DHCP fault could plausibly explain the local subnet working while remote destinations do not.
options.why: A DHCP fault would typically prevent the host from getting an address at all, not selectively allow local traffic while blocking remote traffic; that selective pattern points at the gateway.

items.rationale: The default gateway is the route for 0.0.0.0/0, matching everything and losing to every more specific entry; "local works, remote does not" is exactly the symptom a missing or wrong gateway produces, and `ip route show default` filters straight to that entry, narrower than the full table `ip route` prints.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 1122 s3.3.1.1 gives the local/remote decision - matching masked bits means direct delivery, otherwise 'the destination is accessible only through a gateway' - which is exactly why a broken default route produces working local traffic and no remote traffic. ip-route(8) documents the command and the 'default' PREFIX, 'which is equivalent to IP 0/0 or to IPv6 ::/0'. Empirical, docker ubuntu:24.04: 'ip route show default' printed 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0', and after 'ip route del default' a ping to 8.8.8.8 fails while 172.17.0.x remains reachable via the connected route '172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.2'. o2, o3 and o4 are false with true whys. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ip-route added, since the umbrella ip(8) page contains no 'route show' documentation.

items.stem: An administrator whose host has a single configured address of 10.0.5.20/24 runs `ip route add default via 192.168.9.1`. What actually happens?

options.text: The command is rejected outright with `Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway.`, because a gateway must be on-link, on the same subnet as one of the host's own addresses.
options.why: The kernel validates the next hop against the host's own interface prefixes when the route is added, and the `onlink` flag exists precisely to override that check.

options.text: It succeeds anyway, since the kernel automatically adds a temporary connected route to reach any configured gateway address regardless of which subnet that address happens to fall in.
options.why: The kernel does not fabricate a route to make an unreachable gateway reachable; the gateway must genuinely be on-link for the route to function at all.

options.text: It succeeds, but only for traffic to well-known ports, since the kernel treats those destinations as a special case bypassing the gateway check.
options.why: There is no port-based exception to gateway reachability; the requirement that a gateway be on-link applies uniformly regardless of destination port.

options.text: It is accepted without complaint and installs normally, failing only later when traffic is sent and no ARP reply ever comes back for the gateway address itself.
options.why: The next hop is validated at the moment the route is added, not at delivery time; `ip route add` rejects an off-link gateway outright unless `onlink` is given to force it.

items.rationale: A gateway address outside every configured subnet cannot be used at all — the host cannot ARP for it, since ARP never crosses a router and the gateway itself must be directly, locally reachable for the route to function.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED - two defensible answers. The original key said the send fails because the off-link gateway cannot be ARP-resolved, while original o4 said it fails 'because the routing table itself is assumed to reject any default route pointing at an address outside a configured subnet at entry time'. On Linux o4 is what actually happens, so the item had a second correct answer and its key's mechanism was wrong. Empirical, docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2, host address 172.17.0.2/16 only: 'ip route del default; ip route add default via 192.168.9.1' printed 'Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway.' and exited 2. Adding 'dev eth0 onlink' to the same command exited 0 and installed 'default via 192.168.9.1 dev eth0 onlink', after which 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' returned '8.8.8.8 via 192.168.9.1 dev eth0 src 172.17.0.2' - i.e. only with onlink is the failure deferred to delivery time. This matches ip-route(8), which documents the NHFLAG 'onlink - pretend that the nexthop is directly attached to this link, even if it does not match any interface prefix', a flag that would be meaningless if unforced off-link nexthops were accepted. Repaired: the stem now asks what happens when the route is configured, the key states the entry-time rejection with the literal error text, the key's why carries the onlink escape hatch, and the old key's ARP-at-delivery-time reasoning became o4, now correctly false with a true why. Re-verified against the same command output. o2 (kernel fabricates a connected route) and o3 (well-known-port exception) remain false with true whys; both were disproven by the same run, which added no route and made no port distinction. Shape note: the key was shortened and o2 lengthened so the rewrite does not make the key the longest option.

items.stem: Two default routes exist on a host, each with a different metric, and one of them points out an interface that has since been physically disconnected. What is the likely, and dangerous, consequence?

options.text: If the disconnected interface's route has the lower metric, it silently wins and black-holes outbound traffic, even though a working default route exists on the other interface.
options.why: More than one default route can exist, and the lowest metric wins regardless of whether that interface is actually functional, which is exactly why a stale low-metric route is dangerous.

options.text: The kernel automatically detects the disconnected interface and falls back to the remaining working default route without any further configuration.
options.why: Route selection is based purely on metric, not on live interface health; the kernel does not automatically demote a route just because its interface is down.

options.text: Both default routes are always used simultaneously, splitting outbound traffic evenly between the working and the disconnected interface.
options.why: Route selection picks a single winning entry by metric; it does not load-balance traffic evenly across every default route present in the table.

options.text: Neither route is used once one interface is disconnected, since the kernel requires every default route in the table to be simultaneously valid before using any of them as a matter of routine operational practice.
options.why: The kernel does not require every default route to be valid; it simply selects among whichever entries exist by metric, which is exactly what makes a stale one dangerous.

items.rationale: More than one default route can exist with different metrics, and the lowest metric wins regardless of whether that path actually works, so a stale low-metric default on a disconnected interface silently black-holes traffic that a working route on another interface could otherwise have carried.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and confirmed empirically for the exact scenario in the stem including carrier loss. ip-route(8) documents 'metric NUMBER / preference NUMBER - the preference value of the route. NUMBER is an arbitrary 32bit number, where routes with lower values are preferred', and RFC 1122 s3.3.1.2 requires hosts to support multiple default gateways, so more than one default route is normal. Empirical, docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2: with 'default via 10.9.9.1 dev veth0 metric 50' and 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0 metric 100', 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' selected '8.8.8.8 via 10.9.9.1 dev veth0'. Bringing the veth peer down so veth0 shows '<NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> ... state LOWERLAYERDOWN' left the route in place as 'default via 10.9.9.1 dev veth0 metric 50 linkdown', and 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' STILL returned '8.8.8.8 via 10.9.9.1 dev veth0' - the dead low-metric route continued to win over the working metric-100 route, black-holing traffic exactly as the key describes. That single run also disproves o2 (no automatic fallback) and o3 (no even split - one route was selected). /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/ignore_routes_with_linkdown was 0, the default. o4 is false with a true why.

items.stem: A host has a working default IPv4 route and internet access. Asked about the host's IPv6 reachability, an administrator runs `ip route show default`, which prints the IPv4 default route and nothing at all about IPv6. Does that prove there is no IPv6 default route?

options.text: No. `ip route show default` without `-6` shows only the IPv4 table; a separate IPv6 default route could still exist and must be checked with `ip -6 route`.
options.why: IPv4 and IPv6 routing tables are separate, so an empty IPv4-only query says nothing about IPv6 connectivity, which requires its own explicit check.

options.text: Yes — a single routing table governs both address families, so an empty result for one automatically means the other has no default route either, an assumption that holds until it does not.
options.why: IPv4 and IPv6 maintain separate routing tables; an empty result under one family carries no implication at all about the other.

options.text: Yes, but only because a host without a working IPv4 default route is assumed to be incapable of holding an IPv6 default route at the same time.
options.why: The scenario states IPv4 is working; regardless, the two address families are configured and checked independently, with no such dependency between them.

options.text: No, but only because IPv6 does not use a default route mechanism at all, relying entirely on DNS-based path selection instead.
options.why: IPv6 uses the same next-hop routing concept as IPv4, including a default route; DNS has no role in path selection for either address family.

items.rationale: `ip route show default` reports only the IPv4 default route by default; IPv6 keeps a separate table, so an empty IPv4 result must be checked against `ip -6 route` before concluding anything about IPv6 reachability.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED - the stem contradicted itself. It stated the host 'has a working default IPv4 route and internet access' and then that '`ip route show default` prints nothing', which cannot both be true: without -6 that command prints the IPv4 default route. Empirical, docker ubuntu:24.04: 'ip route show default' printed 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0' on exactly such a host. Repaired: the stem now says the command prints the IPv4 default route and nothing about IPv6, which is the real situation the item was reaching for, and it leaves the key untouched. Re-verified: in the same container 'ip -6 route show default' and 'ip -6 route' both printed nothing while the IPv4 table was populated, demonstrating that the two families are queried separately - the key's claim. ip-route(8) documents the 'default' PREFIX as 'equivalent to IP 0/0 or to IPv6 ::/0', and ip(8) documents -6 as the family selector. o2 (single shared table) is false, o3 is false and additionally mis-describes the scenario as IPv4-broken, o4 is false since IPv6 uses the same next-hop routing model. Each 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A routing table holds a connected route for 198.51.100.0/24 and a default route for 0.0.0.0/0. Which one is used to reach 198.51.100.7, and why — and which command confirms it without reading the table by eye?

options.text: The /24 route wins by longest prefix match (24 matching bits beats 0), and `ip route get 198.51.100.7` asks the kernel to show the entry it would actually select.
options.why: Selection is by longest prefix match regardless of listing order, and `ip route get` settles the question definitively by asking the kernel directly rather than inferring from the printed table.

options.text: The default route wins, since a route explicitly named "default" is always treated as a special case that takes priority over any other route present.
options.why: The default route has the weakest possible match, 0 bits; it is chosen only when nothing more specific matches, never given special priority over a more specific route.

options.text: Whichever route was added to the table first wins, since kernel routing tables are evaluated strictly in insertion order rather than by prefix specificity, regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved.
options.why: Selection is by longest prefix match, not by the order entries were added; a later-added, more specific route still wins over an earlier, less specific one.

options.text: The /24 route wins, but only because it happens to be listed first when the table is printed by `ip route` without any arguments.
options.why: Print order in `ip route` output does not determine which route is selected; the selection is decided by prefix length, and `route get` proves it independently of display order.

items.rationale: Selection is by longest prefix match: the /24 route, with 24 matching bits, beats the default route's 0 matching bits, regardless of listing order; `ip route get 198.51.100.7` asks the kernel to show which entry it would actually choose, settling any argument.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on both halves. ip-route(8) documents the second half verbatim: 'get - get a single route ... this command gets a single route to a destination and prints its contents exactly as the kernel sees it', which is precisely 'ask the kernel rather than infer from the printed table'. Empirical, docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2: with the table holding 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0' and the connected route '172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.2', 'ip route get 172.17.0.5' returned '172.17.0.5 dev eth0 src 172.17.0.2' with no via - the more specific connected route won - while 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' returned '8.8.8.8 via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0'. That disproves o2 (the default route is not privileged) and o4 (selection is independent of print order). o3 is disproven by the same run: the default route was present before the connected route in the printed output yet lost for an in-prefix destination. Each 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ip-route added; the umbrella ip(8) page contains no occurrence of 'route get' at all, so the original citation could not support the command the key names.

items.stem: A network engineer wants exactly one destination address to be redirected through a different next hop, while leaving every other destination unaffected. What technique achieves that without disturbing the rest of the table?

options.text: Adding a /32 host route for that one destination; a more specific route always beats the default, so it redirects only that address and nothing else.
options.why: A /32 matches only the single address it names, and longest-prefix-match rules guarantee it is preferred over any less specific route, leaving everything else on the existing path.

options.text: Lowering the metric on the existing default route, since adjusting the metric is the only way to influence which destinations use which path.
options.why: Adjusting the default route's metric affects every destination that falls back to it, not just the one address in question; it cannot selectively redirect a single destination.

options.text: Editing `/etc/hosts` to point that destination's name at a different address, since routing decisions are driven by name resolution rather than by the routing table.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` affects name-to-address resolution, not which next hop is used to reach a given address; routing decisions are made from the routing table, independent of naming.

options.text: Removing the default route entirely, since eliminating it is the only way to force a single destination onto a different next hop.
options.why: Removing the default route would break every destination that relies on it, not just redirect the one address in question, which is a much broader and unwanted change.

items.rationale: A more specific route always beats a less specific one, so adding a /32 host route for exactly one destination redirects only that address while leaving every other destination on its existing path — a useful, precise technique that is easy to forget when diagnosing an oddly-behaving single host.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. ip-route(8) accepts any PREFIX in a ROUTE, and documents 'default' as 'equivalent to IP 0/0', so a /32 host route and the default route differ only in specificity; longest-prefix selection then guarantees the /32 wins for the one address it names. Empirical, docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2: with 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0' in place, adding a second next hop on dummy0 (10.9.9.2/24) and then 'ip route add 8.8.8.8/32 via 10.9.9.1 dev dummy0' gave 'ip route get 8.8.8.8' -> '8.8.8.8 via 10.9.9.1 dev dummy0 src 10.9.9.2' while 'ip route get 8.8.4.4' -> '8.8.4.4 via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0 src 172.17.0.2'. Exactly one destination moved to the new next hop and every other destination stayed on the default, which is the key's claim demonstrated end to end. o2 is false: ip-route(8) defines metric/preference as a whole-route preference value, which cannot single out one destination. o3 is false: routing is decided from the routing table, and hosts(5) governs name-to-address lookup only. o4 is false and would break every fallback destination. Each 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: `route -n` is not installed on a freshly provisioned server, and a technician treats this as evidence the networking stack is broken. Is that the right conclusion?

options.text: No, `route -n` comes from the deprecated net-tools package, which is frequently absent by default; its absence reflects a distribution choice, not a broken system.
options.why: net-tools is legacy and often not installed on current distributions in favour of iproute2; `ip route` remains available and fully functional regardless.

options.text: Yes — every properly functioning Linux system ships `route -n` by default, so its absence necessarily indicates a broken or incomplete installation, a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive.
options.why: Many current distributions ship iproute2 only, deliberately omitting net-tools; that is a normal, supported configuration, not evidence of breakage.

options.text: No, but only because `route -n` was replaced specifically by `ip neigh`, which is where routing information now lives instead.
options.why: `ip neigh` shows the neighbour cache, not the routing table; the direct iproute2 replacement for `route -n` is `ip route`, not `ip neigh`.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to reinstall the entire networking stack from scratch, since a missing legacy command usually indicates deeper corruption.
options.why: A missing legacy net-tools package requires nothing more than installing that specific package if it is genuinely wanted; it implies no corruption of the networking stack at all.

items.rationale: `route -n` being unavailable is not evidence of a broken system; it is evidence the distribution ships iproute2 only, since net-tools is deprecated and frequently absent — `ip route` remains the fully supported way to inspect the same table.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed documentarily and empirically. route(8) and ifconfig(8) are both part of the net-tools project - the man7 ifconfig(8) COLOPHON states 'This page is part of the net-tools (networking utilities) project' and route(8) is listed in its SEE ALSO - and that page directs readers to 'use ip-link(8) from the iproute2 package to display link layer informations including the hardware address', which is the documented hand-off from net-tools to iproute2. Empirical, docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with only iproute2 installed: 'which route' found nothing, printing 'route ABSENT (net-tools not installed)', while 'ip route' worked and printed the full table - the exact situation in the stem on a current mainstream distribution image, which settles o2's claim that every properly functioning Linux system ships route -n. o3 is false: ip-neighbour(8) manipulates neighbour objects binding protocol to link-layer addresses, not routes; ip-route(8) is the routing-table page. o4 is false with a true why. Citation fixed at concept level: man7-ifconfig-nettools added as the net-tools-side document, since neither RFC 1122 nor ip(8) says anything about net-tools packaging. Recorded honestly: no fetched primary document uses the word 'deprecated' for route(8) itself; what is documented is the net-tools/iproute2 hand-off plus the measured absence of the binary, and the key's wording ('deprecated net-tools package, which is frequently absent by default') is supported by that absence rather than by a vendor deprecation notice.

items.stem: What distinguishes a "connected" route in a routing table from every other kind of entry?

options.text: A connected route has no `via` clause, because the destination is directly on-link through the interface rather than reached through a next-hop router.
options.why: A connected route is generated automatically for each configured subnet, and it lacks a `via` clause precisely because delivery does not require forwarding through another router.

options.text: A connected route is any entry that was added manually with `ip route add`, as opposed to one generated automatically at boot.
options.why: How a route was added — manually or automatically — is unrelated to whether it is "connected"; the defining trait is the absence of a next hop for an on-link destination.

options.text: A connected route is specifically the default route, since it is the one entry that connects the host to every possible destination.
options.why: The default route is a distinct entry, 0.0.0.0/0, matching everything with no specificity; a connected route is the opposite — a specific, directly reachable subnet.

options.text: A connected route is one where the destination and the next hop share the exact same IP address, rather than one being derived from a subnet in most textbooks and quick references.
options.why: A connected route has no next hop at all to compare against the destination; it is defined by the absence of a `via` clause, not by a coincidence of matching addresses.

items.rationale: A typical table holds one connected route per configured subnet, with no `via` clause because the destination is on-link, plus the default route for everything else — the difference between "directly connected" and "via a router" is exactly the distinction most connectivity questions turn on.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. ip-route(8) makes 'via [FAMILY] ADDRESS' an optional part of the NH nexthop specification and documents SCOPE 'link' for destinations on the attached link, so a route to an on-link prefix carries no via. Empirical, docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2: 'ip route' printed 'default via 172.17.0.1 dev eth0' and '172.17.0.0/16 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.2' - the connected route has no via clause and is tagged 'proto kernel', i.e. generated by the kernel from the configured address rather than added by hand, which disposes of o2. o3 is false: the same output shows the default route and the connected route as distinct entries. o4 is false: there is no next hop on a connected route to compare against the destination. Each 'why' states a true fact. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: Two engineering desks need to be added to the same subnet as the rest of engineering, while a separate finance subnet needs to exchange traffic with engineering for the first time. Which device does each task need, and on what basis?

options.text: Adding desks to the same subnet needs only a switch, which forwards frames by MAC within one broadcast domain; connecting two different subnets needs a router, which forwards packets by IP between them.
options.why: The device needed follows directly from whether traffic stays inside one broadcast domain (switch) or must cross between two separate ones (router).

options.text: Both tasks need a router, since only a router is capable of extending a broadcast domain to additional physical ports at all.
options.why: Extending a single broadcast domain to more ports is exactly a switch's job; a router does not extend a broadcast domain, it terminates one at its boundary.

options.text: Both tasks need only a switch, since a switch can join two entirely separate subnets together as easily as it extends one existing subnet.
options.why: A plain switch keeps every port in the same broadcast domain; it cannot join two different subnets together, which requires a router to forward between them by IP.

options.text: Neither task needs either device; both can be accomplished purely through DHCP server configuration on the existing network.
options.why: DHCP only hands out addressing configuration to clients; it has no role in extending a broadcast domain or forwarding traffic between two separate subnets.

items.rationale: A switch forwards frames within one network by MAC address, at layer 2, and is the right device when devices merely need to join an existing broadcast domain; a router forwards packets between networks by IP address, at layer 3, and is required whenever traffic must cross from one subnet to another.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1812 section 2.1, which states that link-layer packet switching devices 'are usually called bridges' and that 'Network segments that are connected by bridges share the same IP network prefix forming a single IP subnet' -- i.e. a switch extends one subnet, while a router forwards between IP networks. ATTRIBUTION FIX: the item cited RFC 1122 and IEEE 802.1Q; RFC 1122 (fetched in full, 289 KB) contains no occurrence of 'bridge' or 'broadcast domain' anywhere, and the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page returns 200 but is a catalogue abstract with no definitions. Added rfc-1812-router-requirements at concept level rather than weakening the (correct) content. Distractors: o2 false -- extending one broadcast domain to more ports is a bridge/switch function per RFC 1812 section 2.1, and a router terminates rather than extends it; o3 false for the same passage, since a plain bridge keeps all segments in one IP prefix and cannot join two prefixes; o4 false -- RFC 2131 section 1 describes DHCP as supplying configuration parameters to hosts, with no forwarding role. All three 'why' statements check out. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document. RFC 1812 2.1 re-fetched and re-verified: link-layer packet switching devices "are usually called bridges" and "Network segments that are connected by bridges share the same IP network prefix forming a single IP subnet."

items.stem: A broadcast frame is sent by a host connected to a plain switch with ten other ports in use. What happens to that frame, and would the outcome differ if a router sat where the switch does instead?

options.text: The switch floods the broadcast to every other port, since every port on a plain switch shares one broadcast domain; a router in its place would not forward the broadcast at all, terminating it there.
options.why: A switch extends a single broadcast domain across all its ports, while a router is the boundary of a broadcast domain and does not forward broadcasts onward by default.

options.text: The switch forwards the broadcast only to the one port whose MAC learning table entry matches the broadcast address specifically.
options.why: The broadcast MAC address, ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, is never learned as belonging to a single port; a switch floods it to every port instead of forwarding it selectively.

options.text: The switch silently drops the broadcast frame, since flooding traffic to every port is treated as a security risk that switches avoid by default.
options.why: A switch does not drop broadcasts as a security measure by default; flooding to every port on the shared broadcast domain is its ordinary, expected behaviour.

options.text: The outcome would be identical whether a switch or a router occupies that position, since both devices handle broadcast frames the same way by design, broadcast handling being fixed at the frame level rather than per device.
options.why: The outcome is precisely the difference between the two devices: a switch floods a broadcast across its domain while a router terminates the broadcast domain and does not forward it.

items.rationale: Every port on a plain switch is in the same broadcast domain, so a switch floods a frame to every port when the destination is unknown or is the broadcast address; a router does not forward broadcasts at all, because it terminates the broadcast domain rather than extending it.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1812 section 5.3.5.1: 'Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded.' That is precisely the router half of the key. The switch half follows from RFC 1812 section 2.1 (bridged segments share one IP prefix). ATTRIBUTION FIX: RFC 1122 says neither; rfc-1812-router-requirements added at concept level. Distractors: o2 false -- ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is a group address that is never learned as belonging to one port, so it is flooded; o3 false -- no standard specifies dropping broadcasts as a default security measure; o4 false, since RFC 1812 5.3.5.1 makes router and bridge behaviour explicitly different. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o4 carried the self-refuting tail 'a conclusion that seems to follow from everyday experience', which announced its own wrongness; replaced with a false-but-confident clause of similar length ('broadcast handling being fixed at the frame level rather than per device'). Key untouched. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document. RFC 1812 5.3.5.1 re-fetched and re-verified: "Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded."

items.stem: A DHCP server sits on a different subnet from a group of clients that need to lease addresses from it. Given that DHCP discovery is a broadcast, what is required to make this work?

options.text: A relay agent on the clients' subnet, since broadcasts do not cross routers unaided and the relay agent forwards the discovery onward to the configured server address.
options.why: DHCP discovery is a broadcast, and routers do not forward limited broadcasts, so a relay agent is required to carry the request to a server on another segment.

options.text: Nothing extra is required, since routers automatically forward DHCP broadcasts to any DHCP server on the network without additional configuration, DHCP being exempt from the usual forwarding rules.
options.why: Routers do not forward broadcasts by default at all; DHCP discovery being a broadcast is exactly why it does not reach a server on another subnet without a relay agent.

options.text: A second DHCP server installed locally on the clients' own subnet, since a relay agent cannot forward requests across a router boundary at all.
options.why: A relay agent exists precisely to forward DHCP requests across a router boundary as unicast; a second local server is an alternative design, not a requirement.

options.text: A VLAN trunk between the two subnets, since trunking is the mechanism that allows a broadcast to cross from one subnet to another.
options.why: A VLAN trunk carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches, but it does not make a router forward a broadcast across separate IP subnets; that still requires a relay agent.
