items.rationale: Because DHCP discovery and ARP requests are broadcasts, neither crosses a router unaided — DHCP needs a relay agent to serve a subnet whose server sits elsewhere, converting the broadcast into a unicast message the remote server can receive and reply to.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED (overstatement in the key) and repaired. RFC 2131 section 1 states 'Using BOOTP relay agents eliminates the necessity of having a DHCP server on each physical network segment', and RFC 1812 section 5.3.5.1 states 'Limited broadcasts MUST NOT be forwarded' -- together these settle the key's mechanism. However the key as authored asserted the relay agent 'forwards the discovery as unicast'. RFC 1542 section 4.1.1 says the relaying destination 'MUST be configurable' and that the network manager 'may wish the relaying destination to be an IP unicast, multicast, broadcast, or some combination'. Unicast is therefore common but not specified, so 'as unicast to the remote server' was rewritten to 'onward to the configured server address', and the key's why was aligned. Re-checked after the rewrite: key now matches RFC 1542 exactly. Distractors: o2 false per RFC 1812 5.3.5.1; o3 false -- relaying across a router boundary is exactly what RFC 1542 section 4.1.1 specifies; o4 false -- an 802.1Q trunk carries tagged frames between bridges and does not make a router forward a limited broadcast. REPAIRED: o2 carried the hedge tail 'under the great majority of ordinary configurations'; replaced with a false clause of similar length. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document.

items.stem: A vendor markets a "layer 3 switch." What does that device actually do, and what should not be concluded from the name?

options.text: It performs layer 2 switching in hardware alongside layer 3 routing in the same box; the name should not be read as evidence that switching itself is a layer 3 function.
options.why: A layer 3 switch genuinely does both jobs, routing in hardware for speed, but combining two functions in one device does not redefine which layer either function belongs to.

options.text: It performs routing only, and the word "switch" in its name is understood to be a purely historical artefact with no functional meaning today.
options.why: A layer 3 switch genuinely performs layer 2 switching as well as layer 3 routing; the name is not a meaningless historical artefact but describes real dual functionality.

options.text: It performs switching only, with "layer 3" describing merely the number of physical ports the device happens to provide.
options.why: "Layer 3" refers to the OSI network layer at which the device also routes, not to a port count; the device genuinely adds routing capability, not just extra ports.

options.text: It performs neither switching nor routing, functioning instead purely as a firewall that happens to be named after both functions for marketing purposes.
options.why: A layer 3 switch genuinely switches and routes; it is not a firewall by function, even though the marketing name references both switching and a layer number.

items.rationale: A "layer 3 switch" is a marketing name for a device that both switches at layer 2 and routes at layer 3; performing routing in hardware inside a switch-shaped box does not make switching itself a layer 3 function, since the two remain distinct operations happening in one device.

verification.reasoning: The two halves the key turns on are each sourced: RFC 1812 section 2.1 separates layer-3 forwarding (routers) from link-layer packet switching devices 'usually called bridges', and notes bridged segments share one IP prefix. A device doing both therefore does layer 2 switching plus layer 3 routing, and the layer at which each function sits is not changed by co-locating them. LIMIT RECORDED: 'layer 3 switch' is vendor marketing terminology and is not defined in any primary standard I could reach -- RFC 1812, RFC 1122 and RFC 5517 do not use the phrase, and the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page is a catalogue abstract only. The key's claim about what the *name* should not be read to imply is therefore reasoned from the sourced layer definitions rather than quoted; that is recorded here as a limit rather than asserted as sourced. Distractors: o2 false (the device does switch), o3 false ('layer 3' names an OSI layer, not a port count -- RFC 1812 section 2.1 uses the layered model), o4 false (a firewall is a filtering function, distinct from either). All three 'why' statements are true. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document. LIMIT UNCHANGED AND REAFFIRMED: "layer 3 switch" is vendor marketing terminology that no reachable primary standard defines; the item rests on RFC 1812 2.1 separating link-layer bridging from IP forwarding, and nothing was substituted in to cover the phrase itself.

items.stem: A company's internal hosts, all on private addresses, can browse the internet without issue, but an external partner cannot connect to an internal web server without a separately configured rule. What explains the asymmetry?

options.text: NAT's translation table is built by outbound traffic; an unsolicited inbound packet has no matching entry and is dropped, so reaching the internal server requires an explicit destination-NAT (port forwarding) rule.
options.why: Outbound connections create the mapping that allows return traffic back in, but nothing creates a mapping for a connection that originates from outside, which is why inbound needs an explicit rule.

options.text: NAT is configured to allow outbound traffic only as a deliberate security policy decision, actively blocking every inbound connection attempt by design.
options.why: NAT itself applies no policy at all; it drops unmatched inbound packets purely as a side effect of having no translation entry, not because it makes a security decision.

options.text: The internal web server is unreachable because its private address is inherently invalid for any inbound connection, regardless of what NAT rules exist.
options.why: A private address is a perfectly valid address on its own network; it becomes reachable from outside once an appropriate NAT and forwarding rule exists, which is exactly the missing piece here.

options.text: The asymmetry is caused by DNS, since the partner's resolver has not yet been updated with the internal server's address.
options.why: The scenario describes a connection failure after a rule is configured, which is about reachability through NAT, not about whether a name resolves to an address.

items.rationale: NAT is the reason outbound connections from a private network 'just work' while inbound connections do not: the translation table is built by outbound traffic, so an unsolicited inbound packet has no entry to match and is dropped until an explicit destination-NAT rule creates one.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 3022 section 2: 'In a traditional NAT, sessions are uni-directional, outbound from the private network. Sessions in the opposite direction may be allowed on an exceptional basis using static address maps for pre-selected hosts', and section 2.2: 'All inbound sessions ... are assumed to be directed to the NAT router as the end node, unless the target service port is statically mapped to a different node in the local network.' That is exactly destination-NAT / port forwarding. Distractors: o2 false -- RFC 3022 describes translation state, not policy, and section 6.1 frames the effect as privacy arising from the mechanism; o3 false -- RFC 1918 section 3 states private addresses are usable within an enterprise and RFC 3022 shows them reachable through static maps; o4 false -- the scenario is about reachability of an unsolicited inbound session, not name resolution. All 'why' statements true. No distractor is defensible as also-correct.

items.stem: A network with heavy NAT translation in place is described by a manager as "secure, since NAT hides our internal addressing." Is NAT itself a security control?

options.text: No. NAT blocks unsolicited inbound traffic as a side effect of having no mapping, not as a policy decision, and it inspects nothing; a network can run NAT with no filtering rules at all.
options.why: NAT performs address and port rewriting only; any security benefit is incidental to that mechanism, not the result of NAT applying or enforcing any policy of its own.

options.text: Yes — NAT actively inspects every packet's payload and applies a deny-by-default policy to anything that looks suspicious before translating it.
options.why: NAT inspects nothing about a packet's payload and applies no policy; it only rewrites addresses and ports and forwards based on whether a mapping exists.

options.text: Yes, but only in its capacity as the mechanism that also enforces TLS encryption on every translated connection passing through it.
options.why: NAT has no relationship to TLS or encryption at all; it operates purely on addresses and ports, leaving the payload, encrypted or not, untouched.

options.text: No, but only because a firewall is what actually performs NAT's address translation, with NAT itself being a purely cosmetic label.
options.why: NAT is a real, distinct translation mechanism in its own right, commonly co-located with a firewall on the same device but not identical to or dependent on it.

items.rationale: NAT is not a firewall: it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic only as a side effect of having no translation mapping, not as a policy decision, and it inspects nothing about the packet — a network can run NAT with no filtering rules configured at all.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 3022 section 6.1: 'Traditional NAT can be viewed as providing a privacy mechanism as sessions are uni-directional from private hosts and the actual addresses of the private hosts are not visible to external hosts' -- a property of the mechanism, not an enforced policy. RFC 4864 (added at concept level) states in its abstract that beyond address amplification 'there is a perception that other benefits exist, such as a variety of management and security attributes', and the document exists to show those are obtainable without translation. Distractors: o2 false -- RFC 3022 section 1 makes payload inspection the job of a separate ALG, not of NAT itself; o3 false -- NAT operates on addresses and transport identifiers only (RFC 3022 sections 2.1-2.2) and RFC 3022 section 1 notes IPsec-protected payloads defeat ALGs, so it plainly does not terminate encryption; o4 false -- RFC 3022 specifies NAT as a distinct function of a router. All 'why' statements true.

items.stem: A web server behind a heavily used NAT gateway logs every visitor's IP address for an access-control list based on client location. What problem does this design run into?

options.text: The server sees the NAT device's translated address as the source for every client, so logs and access-control decisions based on 'client IP' actually reflect the gateway, not the real visitor.
options.why: NAT breaks the end-to-end assumption some protocols and logging schemes make: the server never sees the original client address once it has been rewritten by the translation.

options.text: NAT preserves the original client address unchanged all the way to the server, so the access-control list works exactly as intended without any modification, since translation touches only the destination address on the return path.
options.why: NAT specifically rewrites the source address as part of its normal operation; the server does not see the original client address unless a forwarded header is added separately.

options.text: The access-control list fails only because NAT blocks all logging traffic outright, preventing the server from recording any address at all.
options.why: NAT does not block logging traffic; the server logs an address just fine, it is simply the gateway's translated address rather than the original client's.

options.text: The problem is unrelated to NAT and is instead caused by DNS caching returning a stale address for each visitor's hostname.
options.why: The scenario concerns the source IP address seen on incoming connections, which is a NAT translation effect, not a DNS caching or name-resolution issue.

items.rationale: NAT breaks the end-to-end assumption some protocols and logging schemes make: a server behind NAT sees the translated source address, so logs and access-control lists based on client IP see the NAT device's address rather than the real client's, which is why forwarded headers exist to recover it.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 3022 section 3: the modification 'includes IP address (source IP address for outbound packets and destination IP address for inbound packets)', and section 1: NAT has 'the disadvantage of taking away the end-to-end significance of an IP address'. Section 6.1 adds that the actual addresses of private hosts 'are not visible to external hosts' and that this makes tracing an abusing host harder -- precisely the logging failure the key describes. Distractors: o2 false by RFC 3022 section 3 (the source address of outbound packets is rewritten); o3 false -- nothing in RFC 3022 blocks a server from writing its own logs; o4 false -- the observed source address of an inbound connection is not produced by DNS caching. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o2 ended 'which is why the assumption spreads so easily', a self-refuting tail that told the reader the option is the popular misconception; replaced with a confident false clause of similar length.

items.stem: Why is IPv6 generally said to make NAT unnecessary, rather than to standardise it?

options.text: IPv6's address space is vast enough that every device can hold a globally unique, routable address, removing the address-scarcity problem that made NAT necessary for IPv4.
options.why: NAT exists in IPv4 primarily because there are not enough public addresses for every device; IPv6 was designed with enough address space to give every device its own, eliminating that specific pressure.

options.text: IPv6 was specifically designed to standardise and formalise NAT as a mandatory part of every network's addressing architecture.
options.why: IPv6 was designed in the opposite direction: to remove the address scarcity that made NAT necessary in IPv4, not to make NAT a mandatory, standardised feature.

options.text: IPv6 makes NAT unnecessary because it eliminates private addressing entirely, so every IPv6 address is inherently public and requires no local addressing scheme at all, the private ranges having been dropped in the redesign.
options.why: IPv6 retains its own private-style addressing concepts, such as unique local addresses; the reason NAT becomes unnecessary is abundant address space, not the absence of any private addressing.

options.text: IPv6 makes NAT unnecessary because routers under IPv6 forward every packet regardless of its source address, bypassing the need for translation entirely.
options.why: Router forwarding behaviour under IPv6 is not what removes the need for NAT; it is the sheer size of the address space, which removes the scarcity that motivated NAT in IPv4.

items.rationale: IPv6 was designed with an address space vast enough that every device can hold its own globally unique, routable address, removing the address-scarcity problem that made NAT necessary for IPv4 — IPv6 was designed to make NAT unnecessary, not to standardise it.

verification.reasoning: ATTRIBUTION FIX. The item cited only RFC 3022 and RFC 1918, and neither mentions IPv6 at all, so the key was true but unsourced. Settled by RFC 4864, abstract: NAT's 'primary benefit of "amplifying" available address space is not needed in IPv6' and 'IPv6 was designed with the intention of making NAT unnecessary'; section 4 adds that 'Due to the large IPv6 address space available, there is plenty of' room for global addressing. rfc-4864-local-network-protection-ipv6 registered and wired into the concept. Distractors: o2 is the direct negation of the RFC 4864 abstract; o3 is false because RFC 4864 section 3.2 documents Unique Local Addresses, set aside for local communications, so IPv6 does retain a private-style addressing concept -- which is exactly what o3's why says; o4 false, since router forwarding behaviour is not what removes the motivation for NAT. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o3 ended in the hedge 'in every configuration seen in practice'; replaced with a false clause of similar length. Key untouched.

items.stem: Two hosts sit on the same physical switch but are configured in different VLANs. Can they communicate directly through the switch alone?

options.text: No; separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains, exactly as if the hosts were on physically distinct switches, so a router or a layer 3 switch is required to forward between them.
options.why: A VLAN divides a single physical switch into what behave as separate networks; hosts in different VLANs cannot reach each other without a device that forwards between broadcast domains.

options.text: Yes — since they share the same physical hardware, VLAN membership has no effect on whether two hosts can reach each other directly.
options.why: VLAN membership is exactly what determines broadcast-domain boundaries on a switch; sharing physical hardware does not override that separation.

options.text: Yes, but only if both VLANs happen to use IP addresses from the same subnet, in which case the switch bridges them automatically.
options.why: VLANs remain separate broadcast domains regardless of whether their addressing happens to overlap; a switch does not automatically bridge VLANs based on address similarity.

options.text: No, but only because 802.1Q tagging actively blocks all traffic between any two ports on the same physical switch by default.
options.why: 802.1Q tagging identifies which VLAN a frame belongs to on trunk links; it does not blanket-block traffic between ports, and access ports carry no tag at all.

items.rationale: VLANs are separate broadcast domains independent of physical location, so hosts in different VLANs cannot reach each other without a router or a layer 3 switch to forward between them, exactly as if they were on physically distinct switches — a broadcast-based protocol such as ARP or DHCP discovery stays inside its own VLAN.

verification.reasoning: SOURCE SUBSTITUTION. The only citation was ieee-802-1q at https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/802.1Q/10323/. Fetched: HTTP 200, 360 KB, but the extracted text is a catalogue listing of abstracts (about 15,000 words of amendment blurbs) and contains no definition of a VLAN, of tagging, or of port roles -- exactly the '200 OK and no content' failure mode. The standard itself is licence-gated (the page points at the IEEE GET programme for the PDF), so the item must not turn on it. Substituted RFC 5517, freely readable, section 1: 'In an Ethernet switch, a VLAN is a broadcast domain in which hosts can establish direct communication with one another at Layer 2', and section 3: 'A regular VLAN is a single broadcast domain.' That settles the key: separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains, so crossing between them needs a device that forwards between broadcast domains (RFC 1812 section 2.1 for the router half). Distractors: o2 false -- shared hardware does not merge broadcast domains; o3 false -- RFC 5517 ties the boundary to VLAN membership, not to address ranges; o4 false -- the tag identifies VLAN membership on trunk links, it is not a blanket block, and access ports carry untagged frames (RFC 5517 section 4 on access versus hybrid/trunk ports). All 'why' statements true. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document. RFC 5517 1 re-fetched and re-verified: "In an Ethernet switch, a VLAN is a broadcast domain in which hosts can establish direct communication with one another at Layer 2."

items.stem: What is the difference between an access port and a trunk port in 802.1Q VLAN configuration?

options.text: An access port carries untagged traffic for a single VLAN; a trunk port carries traffic for several VLANs at once, with an 802.1Q tag inserted into each frame identifying which VLAN it belongs to.
options.why: This is the defining functional split: access ports serve one VLAN without tags, while trunk ports multiplex several VLANs across one physical link using the tag.

options.text: An access port carries every VLAN untagged simultaneously; a trunk port is restricted to exactly one VLAN at a time, because an 802.1Q tag can only ever name a single VLAN membership for the whole of a physical link.
options.why: This reverses the actual roles: an access port is restricted to one VLAN, while a trunk port is the one that carries multiple VLANs, distinguished by tags.

options.text: An access port and a trunk port are simply two names for the same configuration, differing only in which vendor's equipment uses which term.
options.why: Access and trunk describe genuinely different port behaviours defined by the 802.1Q standard, not two vendor-specific names for identical configuration.

options.text: An access port requires a router directly attached to it, while a trunk port can only ever connect to an end-user host device.
options.why: Neither port type requires a router to be directly attached; access ports typically connect to end-host devices and trunk ports typically connect switches to each other.

items.rationale: Ports are configured as access ports, carrying untagged traffic for a single VLAN, or as trunk ports, carrying traffic for several VLANs with an 802.1Q tag inserted into each frame — a switch strips the tag before delivering a frame to an access port, so end hosts normally never see tags at all.

verification.reasoning: SOURCE SUBSTITUTION, as for vlan.01: the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page is a catalogue abstract with no port-role definitions, and the standard is licence-gated. RFC 5517 section 4 settles both the roles and o3's why: ports 'can either be access ports or hybrid/trunk ports (according to the terminology presented in Annex D of the IEEE 802.1Q specification, up to its 2004 revision)' -- so access and trunk are genuinely distinct roles with standard provenance, not two vendors' names for one configuration. RFC 5517 section 5 confirms that traffic on these VLANs is 'tagged according to the IEEE 802.1Q standard ... with at most a single standard VLAN tag'. Distractors: o2 exactly reverses the roles; o3 false per RFC 5517 section 4; o4 false -- neither role requires a directly attached router. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o2 ended 'the opposite of the usual arrangement in the overwhelming majority of real deployments', which announced its own wrongness in the option text; replaced with a confident false clause, and sized so the option stays longer than the key rather than exposing a length cue the padding had been masking. the standards.ieee.org 802.1Q page (ieee-802-1q) returns 200 over 360 KB but contains 0 occurrences of "broadcast domain" -- amendment abstracts only, with the normative PDF licence-gated. Dropped so no item turns on a licence-gated document. RFC 5517 4 re-fetched and re-verified: ports "can either be access ports or hybrid/trunk ports (according to the terminology presented in Annex D of the IEEE 802.1Q specification, up to its 2004 revision)."

items.stem: A "the network is down" report turns out to have raw IP addresses working perfectly while every name-based connection fails. Which service is implicated, and how does that differ from a DHCP failure?

options.text: DNS is implicated: it translates names to addresses, and its failure signature is addresses working while names do not; DHCP failure instead shows up as no address at all, or a 169.254 link-local one.
options.why: DNS and DHCP are the two automatic-sounding services most often conflated, but their failure signatures are opposite and distinct: one affects naming, the other affects getting an address in the first place.

options.text: DHCP is implicated, since a report described broadly as "the network is down" traces back to an addressing failure before any other service is affected.
options.why: A host with working raw IP connectivity already has a working address; the symptom described — names failing while addresses work — is specifically DNS, not DHCP.

options.text: ARP is implicated, since ARP is the step that maps a hostname onto the MAC address a frame has to carry before it can leave the host.
options.why: ARP resolves addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment only; a host with working raw IP connectivity to remote addresses has already succeeded past any ARP step involved.

options.text: NAT is implicated, since NAT rewrites the hostname carried inside each packet alongside the addresses in its headers.
options.why: NAT rewrites addresses in transit and has no role in name resolution at all; a NAT failure would not selectively break names while leaving raw address connectivity intact.

items.rationale: A very large share of "the network is down" reports are DNS failures, with a distinct signature — raw IP addresses work while names do not — separate from DHCP failure, whose signature is no address at all or a 169.254 link-local self-assignment.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed in two halves. DNS half: RFC 1034 section 2.1 gives the domain system the job of mapping names to resources, so a DNS failure leaves numeric addressing untouched. DHCP half: RFC 3927 section 1 defines the 169.254/16 link-local prefix a host configures when 'no other configuration mechanism' such as DHCP is available -- which is the '169.254 or no address at all' signature the key names. ATTRIBUTION FIX: neither RFC 1034 nor RFC 1035 mentions 169.254 or DHCP; rfc-3927-ipv4-link-local registered and wired into the concept. Distractors: o2 false -- a host with working raw IP connectivity already holds a usable address; o3 false -- ARP resolves IP addresses to link-layer addresses and never sees a hostname; o4 false -- NAT rewrites headers only (RFC 3022 section 3) and has no name-resolution role. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: all three distractors carried self-refuting 'is assumed to' / 'are described as' framings that told the reader they were the wrong answer ('since any report ... is assumed to always trace back', 'since ARP failures are assumed to explain any situation', 'since NAT translation failures are described as producing exactly this pattern'). Each was rewritten as a plain confident false assertion of similar length; the 'why' texts, which were already true, are unchanged. Key untouched.

items.stem: Three DNS query tools are available: `dig`, `nslookup` and `host`. A script needs the fewest lines of output to parse programmatically, while a full investigation needs every section and flag visible. Which tool suits each need?

options.text: `host` gives the terse output the script wants; `dig` gives the full response detail (sections, flags, TTLs) that a full investigation needs.
options.why: `host` is deliberately terse and easy to parse, while `dig` shows the complete response structure that a thorough diagnosis needs and the others hide.

options.text: `nslookup` gives the terse script-friendly output, while `host` gives the full response detail a deep investigation requires, including section headers, flags and per-record TTLs.
options.why: `nslookup` is the older interactive tool with moderate detail, not the terse option; `host` is the terse one, and `dig` is the tool with full response detail, not `host`.

options.text: `dig` gives the terse script-friendly output by default, while `host` gives the full response detail with sections and flags.
options.why: This reverses the actual defaults: `dig` prints the full response by default, and `host` is the terse tool, not the other way around.

options.text: All three tools produce identical output by default, differing only in the command name used to invoke them.
options.why: The three tools have genuinely different default verbosity and output formats; they are not interchangeable wrappers around identical output.

items.rationale: `dig` is the detailed query tool showing sections, flags and TTLs; `nslookup` is the older interactive tool with moderate detail; `host` is the terse one, best suited to scripts that just need the answer without parsing extra structure.

verification.reasoning: ATTRIBUTION FIX, and the reason this item needed one: it cited only RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, which describe the protocol and say nothing about dig, host or nslookup. Fetched the three BIND 9 manual pages. host(1): 'host is a simple utility for performing DNS lookups. It is normally used to convert names to IP addresses and vice versa.' dig(1): 'dig is a flexible tool for interrogating DNS name servers ... because of its flexibility, ease of use, and clarity of output. Other lookup tools tend to have less functionality than dig', and it documents +short precisely as the non-default terse mode, confirming that dig is verbose by default. nslookup(1): 'nslookup is a program to query Internet domain name servers. nslookup has two modes: interactive and non-interactive' -- the middling interactive tool, not the terse one. Key confirmed; man-dig-1, man-host-1 and man-nslookup-1 wired into the concept. Distractors: o2 and o3 each swap two of the three roles and are contradicted by the above; o4 false -- the three manual pages describe visibly different default output. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o2 ended in the hedge 'under the great majority of ordinary configurations'; replaced with a concrete false detail of similar length.

items.stem: A resolver is reachable and answers queries quickly, but every lookup for a particular internal zone returns NXDOMAIN. Is this a connectivity problem?

options.text: No: a resolver being reachable does not mean it will answer for that zone; NXDOMAIN from a working resolver is a data problem, not a connectivity problem.
options.why: DNS assigns nothing and configures nothing; it only answers questions, and a working, reachable resolver returning NXDOMAIN is reporting that the name does not exist in that zone as far as it knows.

options.text: Yes — any resolver returning an error response of any kind is, by definition, evidence that the resolver itself is unreachable or malfunctioning.
options.why: NXDOMAIN is a valid, well-formed answer from a functioning, reachable resolver stating the name does not exist; it is not evidence of unreachability or malfunction.

options.text: No, but only because the internal zone in question must actually be hosted on a completely different port than the standard DNS port 53.
options.why: DNS conventionally uses port 53 regardless of which zone is being queried; nothing about an internal zone implies a nonstandard port is involved here.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is always to restart the resolver process, since a reachable resolver returning errors indicates its cache has become corrupted.
options.why: A cache is not implicated by an NXDOMAIN answer for a name that genuinely does not exist in the zone; restarting the resolver addresses a different class of problem entirely.

items.rationale: DNS assigns nothing and configures nothing; it only answers questions, so a reachable, functioning resolver returning NXDOMAIN is reporting a data problem — the name genuinely is not present in that zone as far as the resolver can determine — not a connectivity failure.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 4.1.1, which defines RCODE 3, 'Name Error', as 'meaningful only for responses from an authoritative name server, this code signifies that the domain name referenced in the query does not exist' -- a well-formed answer, carried in a normal response header, not a transport failure. RFC 1034 section 4.3.4, negative response caching, likewise treats a name error as an ordinary cacheable answer rather than a fault. So a reachable resolver returning NXDOMAIN is reporting data, exactly as the key says. Distractors: o2 false -- an RCODE is part of a successfully delivered response, so it is evidence the resolver is reachable, not that it is not; o3 false -- RFC 1035 section 4.2 assigns port 53 for all DNS messages regardless of zone; o4 false -- NXDOMAIN for a name that genuinely does not exist is not a cache-corruption symptom. All 'why' statements true. No distractor is defensible as also-correct.

items.stem: Over which transport protocol, and on which port, does DNS operate?

options.text: Both UDP and TCP, on port 53. Ordinary queries usually travel over UDP, while TCP is used when a response is too large for UDP or for zone transfers.
options.why: DNS is defined to use both transports on the same port number, with UDP as the common case and TCP reserved for larger responses and zone transfers specifically.

options.text: UDP only, on port 53, since DNS was designed without ever needing a reliable, ordered transport for any of its operations.
options.why: TCP port 53 is used when a response is too large for UDP, or for zone transfers, so DNS is not UDP-only despite UDP handling the common case.

options.text: TCP only, on port 53, since name resolution is treated as requiring the same connection-oriented reliability guarantees a file transfer needs, so UDP was never assigned a DNS port.
options.why: Ordinary DNS queries travel over UDP for speed and low overhead; TCP is the exception for large responses and zone transfers, not the default transport.

options.text: Both UDP and TCP, but on two different port numbers, 53 for UDP and 853 for TCP, matching the split used by DNS over TLS.
options.why: Both UDP and TCP DNS use the same port, 53; port 853 is instead associated with DNS over TLS, an unrelated, separately encrypted protocol.

items.rationale: DNS queries usually travel over UDP port 53 for speed; TCP port 53 is used when a response is too large for the UDP path or for zone transfers — both transports share the same port number.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against RFC 1035 section 4.2: 'The Internet supports name server access using TCP [RFC-793] on server port 53 (decimal) as well as datagram access using UDP [RFC-768] on UDP port 53 (decimal).' Section 4.2.1: 'Messages carried by UDP are restricted to 512 bytes (not counting the IP or UDP headers)' and 'UDP is not acceptable for zone transfers, but is the recommended method for standard queries' -- both halves of the key's UDP-usual, TCP-for-large-and-zone-transfer split. Distractors: o2 false by the same passage (TCP is explicitly supported); o3 false by the same passage (UDP is explicitly assigned port 53 and is the recommended method); o4 false -- both transports use 53, and 853 is DNS over TLS, assigned separately. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o3 ended 'as a matter of routine operational practice', a hedge that flagged it as the wrong answer; replaced with a definite false claim of similar length.

items.stem: A stale `/etc/hosts` entry sends every application on a host to the wrong server, but `dig` for the same name returns the correct address. Which command reproduces what the applications actually see, and why does `dig` disagree?

options.text: `getent hosts` reproduces the application's view, because it walks the same name service switch applications use, including `/etc/hosts`; `dig` bypasses the switch entirely and queries a nameserver directly.
options.why: `dig` builds a DNS query and sends it straight to a nameserver, never consulting `/etc/hosts` or nsswitch, which is exactly why it can disagree with what applications resolve.

options.text: `dig` reproduces the application's view correctly, and the disagreement means `/etc/hosts` is being silently ignored by the operating system entirely.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` is not being ignored; it is consulted by the name service switch that applications use, which `dig` specifically bypasses, explaining the disagreement.

options.text: `nslookup` reproduces the application's view, since it is the one DNS tool that is defined to consult `/etc/hosts` before querying a nameserver.
options.why: `nslookup`, like `dig`, queries DNS directly and does not consult `/etc/hosts` or the name service switch at all.

options.text: `host` reproduces the application's view, since its terse output format is specifically designed to reflect the nsswitch resolution order.
options.why: `host`, like `dig` and `nslookup`, queries a nameserver directly; its terse output format has no relationship to whether it consults the name service switch.

items.rationale: `getent hosts` performs a lookup through the same name service switch an application uses, including `/etc/hosts` and any resolver plugin named on the `hosts:` line, while `dig`, `nslookup` and `host` build a DNS query and send it straight to a nameserver, bypassing the switch entirely.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed by source and by experiment. getent(1): 'getent - get entries from Name Service Switch libraries ... which are configured in /etc/nsswitch.conf' -- so getent walks the same switch applications use. dig(1): dig 'tries each of the servers listed in /etc/resolv.conf', i.e. it builds a DNS query and sends it to a nameserver; nothing in dig(1) routes it through NSS. ATTRIBUTION FIX: the item cited only nsswitch.conf(5) and hosts(5), neither of which documents getent or dig; man7-getent-1 and man-dig-1 wired into the concept. EMPIRICAL: docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04, printf '\n192.0.2.99 example.com\n' >> /etc/hosts with hosts: files dns -> `getent ahosts example.com` returned '192.0.2.99 STREAM example.com', while `dig +short example.com` returned 104.20.23.154, `host example.com` returned 'example.com has address 104.20.23.154' and `nslookup example.com` returned 104.20.23.154. All three DNS tools bypassed the hosts file; getent did not. That also settles o3 and o4 directly. Distractors: o2 false (the empirical run shows /etc/hosts is honoured, not ignored); o3 false (nslookup returned the DNS answer, not the hosts entry); o4 false (host returned the DNS answer). NUANCE RECORDED, not a defect: on a host where systemd-resolved owns /etc/resolv.conf, dig aimed at the 127.0.0.53 stub can still see /etc/hosts, because nss-resolve(8) notes systemd-resolved 'supports /etc/hosts internally'. The stem's scenario has dig disagreeing, so it describes the ordinary upstream-nameserver case and remains correct as written.

items.stem: What does the conventional `hosts:` value `files dns` in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` actually determine?

options.text: It determines the order name resolution sources are consulted: `/etc/hosts` is read first, and a nameserver is queried only if no entry there matches.
options.why: The `hosts:` line lists sources in priority order, and `files dns` specifically means the local hosts file wins first, with DNS consulted only as a fallback.

options.text: It determines which DNS record types a resolver is permitted to request, restricting queries to the record types both listed sources are able to supply.
options.why: The `hosts:` line governs which sources are consulted and in what order, not which record types may be requested from a nameserver once one is queried.

options.text: It determines the TTL applied to cached answers, with `files` and `dns` each specifying a separate caching duration.
options.why: TTL governs how long a resolver caches an answer and is set per DNS record, not derived from the `hosts:` line, which is only about source order.

options.text: It determines whether `/etc/resolv.conf` is regenerated automatically at boot, based on which of the two keywords appears first.
options.why: Regeneration of `/etc/resolv.conf` is managed separately by NetworkManager, a DHCP client, or systemd-resolved; the `hosts:` line has no role in that process.

items.rationale: The `hosts:` line in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` sets the order in which name-resolution sources are consulted; `files dns`, the conventional value, means `/etc/hosts` is read first and a nameserver is queried only if no entry there matches, which explains why a stale hosts entry can silently override a correct DNS record.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against nsswitch.conf(5): the columns after the database name 'describe the order of sources to query', and 'The order of the services on the line determines the order in which those services will be queried, in turn, until a result is found.' EMPIRICAL: docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with '192.0.2.99 example.com' in /etc/hosts. With 'hosts: files dns', getent ahosts example.com returned 192.0.2.99. After sed to 'hosts: dns files', the same command returned 104.20.23.154. Source order, and only source order, changed the winner. Distractors: o2 false -- nsswitch.conf(5) documents databases and source order, never record types; o3 false -- no TTL semantics appear anywhere in nsswitch.conf(5), and TTLs are carried in DNS records; o4 false -- resolv.conf(5) and systemd-resolved.service(8) show that file being generated by a network manager or resolved, with no input from the hosts: line. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o2 ended 'in every configuration seen in practice', a hedge tail marking it as wrong; replaced with a false clause of similar length.

items.stem: A host running systemd-resolved has `resolve` included on its `hosts:` line, and `getent hosts` returns an answer that seems to come from neither `/etc/hosts` nor the nameserver in `/etc/resolv.conf` directly. What explains this?

options.text: The `resolve` entry hands the lookup to systemd-resolved over its own IPC socket, so the answer can come from resolved cache, from its internal `/etc/hosts` handling, or from a synthesized record.
options.why: The `resolve` source is the nss-resolve module, which talks to systemd-resolved directly over `/run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve`, and resolved answers from its own cache, its own reading of `/etc/hosts`, or a synthetic record.

options.text: The `resolve` entry means the query went to the 127.0.0.53 stub listener named in `/etc/resolv.conf`, which is the only route by which systemd-resolved is ever able to answer a lookup.
options.why: The 127.0.0.53 stub serves clients that go through the glibc DNS path or a tool such as `dig`; the `resolve` nsswitch module reaches systemd-resolved over a separate IPC socket, so the stub is not the only route.

options.text: The `resolve` entry means the nsswitch order has been silently reversed to `dns files`, so DNS is now consulted ahead of `/etc/hosts` for every lookup this host performs.
options.why: `resolve` names a distinct nsswitch source served by systemd-resolved, not evidence that the files-versus-dns order has been reversed on the `hosts:` line.

options.text: The `resolve` entry means the answer must have come from a DHCP-supplied static name mapping handed out with the lease, rather than from any resolver at all.
options.why: DHCP supplies addressing configuration such as nameserver addresses, not static name-to-address mappings; the answer's source here is systemd-resolved, reached through the `resolve` module.

items.rationale: On systems running systemd-resolved the `hosts:` line commonly includes `resolve`, which answers from systemd-resolved over the `/run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve` socket rather than through the 127.0.0.53 stub that the separate glibc DNS path uses — either way the answer need not come from the nameserver a naive reading of `/etc/resolv.conf` suggests, which is exactly the kind of source `getent hosts` reveals and `dig` does not.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED: the key was factually wrong. It claimed that 'the `resolve` entry routes lookups through systemd-resolved's local stub, commonly at 127.0.0.53'. nss-resolve(8) says otherwise: 'Communication between nss-resolve and systemd-resolved.service takes place via the /run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve' socket. The 127.0.0.53 stub is a separate compatibility path -- systemd-resolved.service(8) describes it as 'a local DNS stub listener on the IP addresses 127.0.0.53 and 127.0.0.54' provided for programs that go through /etc/resolv.conf and the glibc DNS path. The item therefore conflated the NSS route with the DNS-stub route, the precise confusion the topic exists to dispel, and it did so while citing only nsswitch.conf(5) and hosts(5), neither of which documents the resolve module at all. REWRITTEN: the key now names the IPC route and the three real sources of a resolved answer, all from nss-resolve(8): systemd-resolved 'supports /etc/hosts internally, but with caching', and 'systemd-resolved will synthesize DNS resource records'. Distractor o2 was replaced with the 127.0.0.53 misconception itself, so the item now teaches the distinction that the original key got wrong; o3 and o4 kept, with their why texts tightened to stop implying the stub. RE-VERIFIED after the rewrite against nss-resolve(8) and systemd-resolved.service(8): key correct, no distractor also-correct, every why true. CITATION FIX at concept level: man7-nss-resolve-8, systemd-resolved-service, man7-getent-1 and man-dig-1 added to sysadmin.networking.dns-resolution-order. FINAL REVIEW (lens 2, 2026-08-19): the RATIONALE still said lookups "may be served by a local stub at 127.0.0.53" via the `resolve` module, which is the very misconception o2 is scored false for. nss-resolve(8): "Communication between nss-resolve and systemd-resolved.service takes place via the /run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve AF_UNIX socket"; that page has 0 occurrences of 127.0.0.53. Rationale corrected; key and all options unchanged. The same error was found and fixed in the guide at study-guide/02-system-administration/networking.md.

items.stem: Is reversing the nsswitch `hosts:` line to `dns files`, so DNS is consulted before the local hosts file, a legal configuration?

options.text: Yes, the order is configurable, and reversing it to `dns files` is legal and changes which source wins when both have an entry for the same name.
options.why: The `hosts:` line is a configuration choice, not a fixed rule; swapping the order to `dns files` is a legitimate configuration that changes precedence.

options.text: No — `files` must always precede `dns` on the `hosts:` line, since the order is fixed by the nsswitch specification and cannot be changed.
options.why: The order on the `hosts:` line is configurable, not fixed; `files dns` is simply the conventional value, not an enforced requirement.

options.text: Yes, but only on systems that do not run systemd, since the reversed order is unsupported wherever systemd-resolved is present.
options.why: Reversing the `hosts:` order is a general nsswitch configuration option, not one restricted by whether systemd-resolved happens to be running.

options.text: No, changing the order requires editing `/etc/hosts` itself rather than `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, since that is where source order is actually configured.
options.why: Source order is configured on the `hosts:` line of `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, not inside `/etc/hosts`, which holds name-to-address mappings rather than resolution order.

items.rationale: Reversing the switch order to `dns files` is legal and changes which source wins for a name present in both; the conventional `files dns` value is a common default, not a fixed rule, so predicting the winning source always requires reading the actual `hosts:` line in force.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against nsswitch.conf(5), which prints 'hosts: dns [!UNAVAIL=return] files' as one of its own worked examples -- the reversed order is not merely legal, it is a documented example -- and states that 'The order of the services on the line determines the order in which those services will be queried.' EMPIRICAL: docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 with '192.0.2.99 example.com' in /etc/hosts; sed the line to 'hosts: dns files' and getent ahosts example.com switched from 192.0.2.99 to 104.20.23.154, with no error or warning. Distractors: o2 false, directly contradicted by the manual's own example; o3 false -- nss-resolve(8) recommends placing 'resolve' before 'files' and imposes no constraint on the relative order of dns and files, so nothing about systemd makes the reversal unsupported; o4 false -- hosts(5) defines /etc/hosts as a table of address, canonical name and aliases, with no ordering syntax. All 'why' statements true.

items.stem: A migration test needs one specific hostname to resolve to a new server on a single test machine, without touching DNS or affecting any other host. An engineer edits `/etc/resolv.conf` to add a line for the new server. Was that the right file?

options.text: No. `/etc/hosts` holds name-to-address mappings directly and takes effect immediately with no restart; `/etc/resolv.conf` only lists which nameservers to ask and contains no name-to-address data at all.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` is the fastest way to override name resolution on one host for exactly this kind of testing, while `/etc/resolv.conf` cannot express a name-to-address mapping in the first place.

options.text: Yes — `/etc/resolv.conf` is where individual name-to-address overrides belong, since it is the file most commonly edited by hand for testing purposes.
options.why: `/etc/resolv.conf` lists nameservers to query and search domains; it has no syntax for mapping a specific name to a specific address, which is `/etc/hosts`'s job.

options.text: No, but only because the correct approach is instead to lower the target record's TTL and wait for the change to propagate through DNS.
options.why: Lowering a TTL is preparation for a DNS change everywhere, not a way to test on a single machine without touching DNS at all, which is what the scenario specifically asks for.

options.text: No, but only because the correct fix is to add a static ARP entry binding the hostname to the new server's MAC address.
options.why: ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses on the local segment; it has no mechanism for resolving a hostname at all, which is a completely different layer of the problem.

items.rationale: `/etc/hosts` is the fastest way to override name resolution on one host — for testing a migration before changing DNS — and because the file is read on each lookup, changes take effect immediately with no restart, unlike `/etc/resolv.conf`, which only names servers to ask and holds no name data of its own.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against both cited pages. hosts(5) gives the line format 'IP_address canonical_hostname [aliases...]' -- a direct name-to-address mapping, a plain text file with no reload step. resolv.conf(5) enumerates every directive the file accepts (nameserver, search, sortlist, domain, options) and none of them maps a name to an address; the file only says which servers to ask. So editing resolv.conf cannot express the override the scenario needs. Distractors: o2 false by that enumeration; o3 false -- lowering a TTL is a preparation for changing DNS globally, and the scenario forbids touching DNS; o4 false -- ARP resolves IP to link-layer addresses and never handles a hostname. All 'why' statements true. No distractor is defensible as also-correct. EMPIRICAL support: in ubuntu:24.04 an appended /etc/hosts line took effect on the very next getent call with no service restart.

items.stem: An engineer wants `/etc/hosts` to alias `web01.example.com` and also create an MX record pointing mail at a different host. Which of these can `/etc/hosts` actually express?

options.text: Only the name-to-address alias; `/etc/hosts` can map a name (and aliases) to an address, but it has no record types at all and cannot express an MX record or anything beyond a literal mapping.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` lines are address, canonical hostname, then optional aliases — nothing more; it has no wildcards, no record types, and no TTL, so an MX-style entry is simply not expressible.

options.text: Both — `/etc/hosts` supports the full range of DNS record types, including MX, provided each entry is written on its own line.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` has no record-type syntax whatsoever; every line is a plain address-to-name mapping, with no way to express an MX record or any other typed record.

options.text: Neither — `/etc/hosts` can only be used for the special name `localhost` and cannot hold any custom name-to-address mapping at all.
options.why: Every system ships a `127.0.0.1 localhost` entry, but `/etc/hosts` is fully capable of holding arbitrary additional custom mappings beyond that default line.

options.text: Only the MX-style mail routing entry — `/etc/hosts` was designed specifically for mail routing, and general name-to-address mapping was only added to its line format much later, during the BSD era.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` predates DNS as a general name-to-address table; it was never designed around mail routing specifically, and it has no MX-record capability at all.

items.rationale: `/etc/hosts` lines contain an address, a canonical hostname, and optional aliases, and nothing else — it has no wildcards, no record types, and no TTL, so it can only ever map a literal name to a literal address, never an MX record or anything else DNS can express.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against hosts(5): the whole syntax is 'IP_address canonical_hostname [aliases...]', with 'Optional aliases provide for name changes, alternate spellings, shorter hostnames'. There is no record-type field, no TTL field and no wildcard anywhere in the page, so an MX entry is not expressible -- exactly the key's claim, and it establishes the alias half at the same time. Distractors: o2 false by the same syntax line; o3 false -- hosts(5) shows 127.0.0.1 localhost as a default entry but nothing restricts the file to it, and its history section describes the file as the general host table 'for resolving hostnames on the fledgling Internet'; o4 false, and the same history passage disproves the mail-routing origin. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o4 ended 'a conclusion that seems to follow from everyday experience', a self-refuting tail; replaced with a definite false historical claim, sized so the option stays longer than the key rather than exposing a length cue the padding had been masking. Key untouched.

items.stem: A departing contractor left a line in `/etc/hosts` on a production server pointing an internal hostname at a decommissioned test box. How long will this override persist, and who is affected?

options.text: Because an override in `/etc/hosts` is per host, it persists indefinitely until someone edits the file and affects only this one host, changing nothing for anyone else on the network.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` has no expiry mechanism of its own, and because it is per host, the stale entry silently affects only whichever host holds the file until someone notices and removes it.

options.text: It persists until the entry's TTL expires, after which it is automatically removed the same way a DNS record's cache entry would be.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` has no TTL concept at all; unlike a cached DNS answer, an entry here has no expiry and remains until someone edits the file by hand.

options.text: It affects every host on the network that queries this server for DNS, since `/etc/hosts` entries are automatically propagated out to the other resolvers by the local name service switch.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` is strictly local to the host that holds it; nothing propagates its entries to other hosts or resolvers on the network.

options.text: It persists only until the next reboot, at which point the operating system automatically resets `/etc/hosts` to its default contents.
options.why: The operating system does not automatically reset `/etc/hosts` on reboot; a hand-edited entry survives across reboots exactly like any other line in the file.

items.rationale: It is per host: an override added on one server changes nothing for anyone else, so a stale `/etc/hosts` entry is a testing tool, not a deployment mechanism, and it persists indefinitely — with no TTL or automatic reset — until someone edits it away.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against hosts(5), which describes the file as a static table of address, canonical hostname and aliases held on the local machine. The page documents no expiry field, no TTL and no propagation mechanism of any kind; its history section explains that the file predates DNS as the mechanism 'for resolving hostnames on the fledgling Internet', a per-host table. Absence here is decisive rather than merely unmentioned, because the page enumerates the complete line syntax. Distractors: o2 false -- there is no TTL concept in the file format; o3 false -- nothing in hosts(5) or nsswitch.conf(5) shares entries with other hosts, and nsswitch.conf(5) describes the switch as consulting local sources for this host's own lookups; o4 false -- the file is ordinary persistent configuration and is not regenerated at boot. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o3 ended 'under the great majority of ordinary configurations', a hedge that signalled its own wrongness; replaced with a definite false mechanism, sized so the option stays longer than the key rather than exposing a length cue the padding had been masking. Key untouched.

items.stem: Every system ships a default entry in `/etc/hosts` mapping `127.0.0.1` to a name. What is that name, and what is the IPv6-aware equivalent line?

options.text: The loopback address mapped to the conventional name for the local host: `127.0.0.1 localhost`, and on IPv6-aware systems also `::1 localhost`.
options.why: Every system ships this default pairing so that the name `localhost` resolves to the loopback address on both address families where IPv6 is present.

options.text: `127.0.0.1 gateway`, since the loopback address is conventionally named after the default route it represents on a fresh installation.
options.why: `localhost`, not `gateway`, is the conventional name for the loopback address; a gateway is an entirely separate concept referring to the route off the local subnet.

options.text: `0.0.0.0 localhost`, since the wildcard bind address is what every system maps to the name `localhost` by default.
options.why: `127.0.0.1`, not `0.0.0.0`, is the loopback address mapped to `localhost`; `0.0.0.0` is a wildcard bind address, a different concept entirely.

options.text: `127.0.0.1 hostname`, where `hostname` is a literal keyword rather than the actual configured hostname of the machine.
options.why: The default entry uses the literal name `localhost`, not a placeholder keyword called `hostname`; the machine's actual hostname is a separate, distinct name.

items.rationale: Every system ships with `127.0.0.1 localhost` and, on IPv6-aware systems, `::1 localhost`, giving the conventional loopback name a mapping on both address families by default.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against the EXAMPLES section of hosts(5), which prints '127.0.0.1       localhost' and '::1             localhost ip6-localhost ip6-loopback'. Both halves of the key -- the IPv4 default entry and the IPv6-aware ::1 line -- are the manual's own example lines. Distractors: o2 false, 'gateway' appears nowhere as the loopback name; o3 false, hosts(5) shows 127.0.0.1 and not 0.0.0.0; o4 false, the example uses the literal name localhost, not a placeholder keyword. All 'why' statements true. No distractor is defensible as also-correct. EMPIRICAL: cat /etc/hosts in a plain ubuntu:24.04 container shows both the 127.0.0.1 localhost line and the ::1 ip6-localhost lines.

items.stem: An administrator hand-edits `/etc/resolv.conf` to fix a wrong nameserver, and the fix works — until the next DHCP lease renewal silently reverts it. What went wrong, and where does the durable fix belong?

options.text: On a modern system the file is commonly generated by NetworkManager, a DHCP client, or systemd-resolved, so a hand edit is overwritten at the next renewal; the durable change belongs in that generating tool's configuration.
options.why: A hand edit to a generated file is overwritten at the next lease renewal, reboot, or network reconfiguration — the durable change belongs in NetworkManager, Netplan or systemd-resolved configuration instead.

options.text: The hand edit failed because `/etc/resolv.conf` is read-only by design and never actually accepted the change in the first place.
options.why: The scenario states the fix worked initially, so the file was writable and the edit took effect; it was later overwritten by regeneration, not rejected outright.

options.text: The DHCP lease renewal reverted the change because `/etc/resolv.conf` entries are considered part of the IP address lease itself and expire along with the address when the lease is renewed.
options.why: The nameserver lines are regenerated by whichever tool manages the file, not because they are literally part of the address lease; the mechanism is regeneration, not lease expiry of the file's content.

options.text: The durable fix belongs in `/etc/hosts` instead, since that is the file that persists correctly across DHCP renewals on a modern system.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` holds name-to-address mappings, not nameserver addresses; it has no bearing on which nameservers are queried, which is what `/etc/resolv.conf` governs.

items.rationale: On modern systems the file is generated — by NetworkManager, a DHCP client, or as a symlink into systemd-resolved's runtime directory — so a hand edit to a generated file is overwritten at the next lease renewal, reboot or network reconfiguration; the durable change belongs in that tool's own configuration.

verification.reasoning: ATTRIBUTION FIX. The item cited only resolv.conf(5), and that page describes the file's syntax and the resolver routines that read it -- it says nothing about the file being generated, overwritten or managed by anything. The claim is nonetheless true and is settled by systemd-resolved.service(8), whose /ETC/RESOLV.CONF section sets out four modes of handling the file, including symlinks to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf, /usr/lib/systemd/resolv.conf and /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf, all of which it 'is always kept up-to-date', and states that 'Alternatively, /etc/resolv.conf may be managed by other packages'. Per the standing precedent, the citation was fixed rather than the correct content weakened: systemd-resolved-service wired into the concept. Distractors: o2 false and self-contradicting with the stem, which states the fix worked; o3 false -- the nameserver lines are rewritten by whichever tool owns the file, and resolv.conf(5) gives them no lease semantics whatever; o4 false -- resolv.conf(5) shows the file lists nameservers, while hosts(5) holds mappings, so /etc/hosts cannot express a nameserver choice. All 'why' statements true.

items.stem: An `/etc/resolv.conf` lists five `nameserver` lines, hoping for extra resilience. How many will actually be used?

options.text: Up to MAXNS, currently 3; further lines beyond the third are simply ignored, so listing five does not add any resilience.
options.why: MAXNS caps the number of nameserver lines the resolver will use at 3; entries beyond that limit are present in the file but never consulted.

options.text: All five will be queried in parallel on every lookup, since the resolver is designed to race every listed nameserver simultaneously for speed.
options.why: The resolver does not race every listed nameserver in parallel; it uses up to MAXNS (3) in order, and lines beyond that cap are ignored entirely.

options.text: Only the first one will ever be used, with the remaining four serving no purpose at all under any circumstances.
options.why: Up to three nameserver lines are used, not just one; the resolver falls back to subsequent listed servers, up to the MAXNS limit, if the first is unavailable.

options.text: All five will be used, but only in round-robin fashion across successive independent DNS queries rather than in a fixed priority order.
options.why: Only up to MAXNS (3) nameserver lines are used at all; the remaining two beyond that cap are never consulted, round-robin or otherwise.

items.rationale: `nameserver` lines list the resolvers to query in order, but up to MAXNS (currently 3) are used and further lines are ignored, so listing more than three nameservers does not add resilience — entries beyond the cap are simply never consulted.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against resolv.conf(5): 'Up to MAXNS (currently 3, see <resolv.h>) name servers may be listed, one per keyword. If there are multiple servers, the resolver library queries them in the order listed', with the algorithm being to try a name server, and on timeout try the next. EMPIRICAL, which is what settles the distractors: docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04, resolv.conf written as 'options timeout:1 attempts:1' plus nameserver 192.0.2.1, 192.0.2.2, 192.0.2.3 and the real resolver in fourth position -> getent hosts example.com FAILED, proving the fourth line is never consulted. Rewriting the same file with the real resolver in third position -> getent hosts example.com returned the address. MAXNS is 3 in practice, not merely in the header. Distractors: o2 false -- the run shows serial fallback with timeouts, not a parallel race; o3 false -- the second run succeeded on the third listed server, so more than the first is used; o4 false -- the fourth server was never used in any round. All 'why' statements true.

items.stem: A host running systemd-resolved shows only `nameserver 127.0.0.53` in `/etc/resolv.conf`. A junior admin flags this as broken, since it points at the host itself rather than a real upstream server. Is that the right read?

options.text: No, this is normal on a systemd-resolved system, where the file names the local stub resolver at 127.0.0.53 rather than the actual upstream nameserver directly.
options.why: Seeing only `nameserver 127.0.0.53` is normal on a systemd-resolved system and does not mean DNS is misconfigured; the stub itself forwards to the real upstream servers.

options.text: Yes — a `nameserver` line pointing at any address on 127.0.0.0/8 always indicates a broken or incomplete DNS configuration.
options.why: 127.0.0.53 specifically is the conventional systemd-resolved stub address and is an expected, working configuration, not evidence of a broken setup.

options.text: Yes, but only because a correctly configured host must list at least two nameserver lines rather than a single stub address.
options.why: A single `nameserver` line is a valid, complete configuration when it points to a working resolver, stub or otherwise; the count of lines alone does not determine correctness.

options.text: No, but only because the file must actually be a symlink into `/etc/hosts` rather than a genuine `/etc/resolv.conf` file at all, as is required wherever a stub listener is in use.
options.why: On a systemd-resolved system the file is typically a symlink into systemd-resolved's own runtime directory, not into `/etc/hosts`, which serves a completely different purpose.

items.rationale: On modern systems the file is often a symlink into systemd-resolved's runtime directory, in which case it names the local stub, commonly 127.0.0.53, rather than any real upstream server — seeing only that address is normal and does not indicate misconfiguration.

verification.reasoning: ATTRIBUTION FIX, and this is the hazard the task called out by name: the item cited resolv.conf(5) alone, and resolv.conf(5) documents neither systemd-resolved nor 127.0.0.53 -- I fetched the whole page and the string 127.0.0.53 does not occur in it; systemd-resolved appears only in SEE ALSO. The material lives in systemd-resolved.service(8), which states that resolved 'provides a local DNS stub listener on the IP addresses 127.0.0.53 and 127.0.0.54 on the local loopback interface', that 'The DNS stub resolver on 127.0.0.53 provides the full feature set of the local resolver', and that /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf 'lists the 127.0.0.53 DNS stub as the only DNS server' and 'may be symlinked from /etc/resolv.conf in order to connect all local clients' to resolved. Key confirmed on that page; systemd-resolved-service wired into the concept. Distractors: o2 false -- 127.0.0.53 is the documented, expected value on such a system; o3 false -- resolv.conf(5) sets no minimum count, only the MAXNS ceiling of 3; o4 false -- the symlink target is resolved's own runtime directory, never /etc/hosts, which systemd-resolved.service(8) makes explicit. All 'why' statements true. REPAIRED AS AUTHORED: o4 ended 'a conclusion that seems to follow from everyday experience', a self-refuting tail; replaced with a definite false requirement of similar length.

items.stem: What does the `search` directive in `/etc/resolv.conf` do, and how does `options ndots:N` interact with it?

options.text: `search` supplies domain suffixes appended to unqualified names; `options ndots:N` controls how many dots a name must already contain before it is tried as absolute rather than run through the search list first.
options.why: These two directives work together: `search` provides candidate suffixes, and `ndots` decides whether a given name is qualified enough to skip that suffix-appending process.

options.text: `search` lists which record types may be queried, while `ndots` sets the maximum number of nameservers the resolver may contact per query.
options.why: Neither directive does this; `search` supplies domain suffixes for unqualified names, and `ndots` governs whether the search list is applied, not record types or nameserver counts.

options.text: `search` sets the TTL used for cached negative answers, while `ndots` sets the TTL used for cached positive answers.
options.why: TTL values come from the DNS records themselves and the zone's SOA parameters, not from `search` or `ndots`, which govern suffix-appending behaviour instead.

options.text: `search` lists nameservers to fall back to if the primary one in `nameserver` fails, while `ndots` counts how many of those fallbacks may be used.
options.why: Fallback nameservers are listed with additional `nameserver` lines up to MAXNS, not with `search`, which is unrelated and governs suffix appending for unqualified names.

items.rationale: `search <domain> ...` supplies suffixes appended to names that are not fully qualified, and `options ndots:N` controls how many dots a name must contain before it is tried as absolute rather than being run through the search list first — together they determine what an unqualified name actually resolves to.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against resolv.conf(5). search: 'Resolver queries having fewer than ndots dots (default is 1) in them will be attempted using each component of the search path in turn until a match is found.' options ndots:n: 'Sets a threshold for the number of dots which must appear in a name given to res_query(3) before an initial absolute query will be made. The default for n is 1, meaning that if there are any dots in a name, the name will be tried first as an absolute name before any search list elements are appended to it.' That is precisely the key's account of the two directives and their interaction. Distractors: o2 false -- the page's directive list contains nothing about record types, and the nameserver ceiling is MAXNS, not ndots; o3 false -- no TTL semantics appear anywhere in resolv.conf(5); o4 false -- fallback servers are additional nameserver lines, and search takes domain names, not server addresses. All 'why' statements true. No distractor is defensible as also-correct.

items.stem: A team needs to alias `www.example.com` to `example.com` and also needs `example.com` itself, the zone apex, to carry its own delegation and administrative records. A junior engineer proposes a CNAME at the apex to simplify things. Why won't that work?

options.text: A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, and the apex must carry NS and SOA records, so a CNAME cannot be placed there at all.
options.why: This is a structural rule of the DNS record system: any name with a CNAME can have no other records at that name, which directly conflicts with the NS and SOA records every zone apex must carry.

options.text: A CNAME can be placed at the apex without issue; the restriction only ever applies to subdomains, never to the zone apex itself.
options.why: The restriction applies universally to any name carrying a CNAME, including the apex; the apex is in fact the clearest example of why the rule matters, since it must carry NS and SOA.

options.text: A CNAME cannot be placed at the apex because CNAME records are restricted to IPv6-only zones, and this zone uses IPv4 addressing, a pattern that holds across most deployments encountered.
options.why: CNAME restriction has nothing to do with address family; it applies equally in IPv4 and IPv6 zones, and the actual reason is the coexistence rule with other record types.

options.text: A CNAME cannot be placed at the apex because the apex name is reserved exclusively for A and AAAA records by the DNS protocol.
options.why: The apex is not restricted to only A and AAAA records; it also carries NS and SOA, among others — the actual restriction is that a CNAME cannot coexist with any other record at its name.

items.rationale: A CNAME cannot coexist with other record types at the same name, which is why a CNAME cannot be placed at a zone apex — the apex must carry NS and SOA records, and a CNAME there would conflict with both.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1034 section 3.6.2, read verbatim: "If a CNAME RR is present at a node, no other data should be present". RFC 1034 section 4.2.1 states that the RRs describing the top node of a zone "are of two types: name server RRs that list, one per RR, all of the servers for the zone, and a single SOA RR", so the apex necessarily carries other data and therefore cannot carry a CNAME. RFC 2181 section 10.1 makes the rule exhaustive (an alias may carry only SIG, NXT and KEY alongside the CNAME), which does not rescue an apex needing NS and SOA. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the same coexistence rule; o3's address-family claim appears nowhere in RFC 1034, 1035 or 2181 and CNAME is address-family agnostic because it aliases names rather than addresses; o4 is refuted by RFC 1034 section 4.2.1, which puts NS and SOA at the apex. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-2181-dns-clarifications added to sysadmin.networking.dns-record-types, since RFC 1034 says only "should" while RFC 2181 section 10.1 is the enumeration that settles it.

items.stem: A website resolves correctly but the same domain's email keeps bouncing. Given `dig A example.com` returns a good answer, what should be checked next, and with which query?

options.text: The mail exchanger records, checked with `dig MX example.com`, since a working A record says nothing about whether mail-directing MX records exist or point anywhere valid.
options.why: A working forward lookup implies nothing about mail delivery; MX records are a completely separate entry that directs where mail for the domain should go.

options.text: The same A record again, since `dig A` also reports mail-routing status as part of its output when a domain has email configured.
options.why: `dig A` reports only the IPv4 address record; it carries no information about mail routing, which lives in a separate MX record entirely.

options.text: The PTR record for the web server's address, since reverse lookups are what mail servers use to decide whether to accept a website's traffic.
options.why: PTR records support reverse lookups for the mail server's own sending address in anti-spam checks, not the website's own forward A record, and are not the first thing to check for bouncing mail on this domain.

options.text: The TTL on the A record, since a low TTL is what commonly causes email delivery to fail for a domain with an otherwise working website.
options.why: TTL governs cache lifetime for a record and has no direct bearing on whether mail delivery succeeds; the missing piece here is the MX record, a distinct entry entirely.

items.rationale: A working forward lookup implies nothing about reverse or mail-routing records: MX names the mail exchangers for a domain, a separate entry from A, so bouncing mail on an otherwise working domain points straight at checking `dig MX` next.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 3.3.9 (MX is a distinct RR type carrying a mail exchanger for the owner name) and verified empirically. Ran in a throwaway container: `docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 sh -c 'apt-get install -y dnsutils && dig +noall +answer MX iana.org; dig +noall +answer A iana.org'`. Output: `iana.org. 4502 IN MX 10 pechora7.icann.org.` (plus three more MX RRs) versus `iana.org. 1615 IN A 192.0.43.8` and nothing else. The A query returned no mail-routing data of any kind, which directly refutes o2. o3 is not also correct: the stem's failure is inbound mail for this domain, and PTR checks concern the sending mail server's own address; its 'why' states this truthfully. o4 is refuted by RFC 1035 section 4.1.3, where TTL is only the cache lifetime of a record. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A reverse-lookup zone for 192.0.2.10 needs to be found. Where does that PTR record actually live, and who typically controls that zone?

options.text: At `10.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa`, in a zone usually delegated to whoever owns the address block, not to whoever owns the domain name the address happens to be used for.
options.why: PTR records live in the reverse in-addr.arpa hierarchy, keyed by address, and control of that zone follows address-block ownership rather than domain-name ownership.

options.text: In the same forward zone as the domain's A record, since PTR and A records for the same host are always stored together in one place.
options.why: PTR records live in the separate in-addr.arpa reverse hierarchy, keyed by address, not alongside the forward A record in the domain's own zone.

options.text: At `192.0.2.10.in-addr.arpa`, written in the same forward order as the original address, in a zone controlled by whoever owns the domain name.
options.why: The in-addr.arpa naming reverses the address octets, so the reverse name is `10.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa`, not the forward-ordered form, and control follows the address block, not the domain.

options.text: PTR records do not have a fixed location at all; a resolver locates them dynamically by querying every authoritative server it knows about in sequence, stopping at the first one that answers.
options.why: PTR records have a well-defined location, the reverse in-addr.arpa hierarchy for the address in question, not an ad hoc search across arbitrary servers.
