items.rationale: A PTR record for 192.0.2.10 lives at `10.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa`, in a zone that is usually delegated to whoever owns the address block — not to whoever owns the domain name — which is why its absence breaks mail reputation checks while leaving the website perfectly reachable.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 3.5, read verbatim: "data for Internet address 10.2.0.52 is located at domain name 52.0.2.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA. The reversal ... allows zones to be delegated which are exactly one network of address space" — which settles both halves of the key, the octet reversal and the fact that control follows the address block rather than the domain name. Verified empirically: `dig +noall +question -x 192.0.2.10` printed `;10.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. IN PTR`, the exact name in the key, and `dig +noall +answer -x 192.0.43.8` returned `8.43.0.192.in-addr.arpa. 4502 IN PTR 43-8.any.icann.org.` — a PTR served from the address-block owner's reverse zone, not from iana.org's forward zone. No distractor is also correct. o2 is refuted by section 3.5 placing PTR data in the separate IN-ADDR.ARPA hierarchy; o3 reverses the octet order the RFC specifies; o4 contradicts the same section. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. REFUTED AS AUTHORED at the option level only: o4 previously ended "which is the assumption most administrators start from", a self-refuting hedge that announced the option's own wrongness; replaced with a clause of similar length that makes a genuinely false claim about resolver behaviour.

items.stem: What is the difference between an A record and a CNAME record, and why does confusing them cost marks?

options.text: An A record maps a name directly to an IPv4 address; a CNAME aliases one name to another name, which is then itself resolved. The two solve different problems and cannot substitute for each other everywhere.
options.why: A CNAME depends on further resolution of the name it points to, while an A record terminates directly in an address, a structural difference candidates commonly gloss over.

options.text: An A record and a CNAME record are functionally identical, differing only in which administrative tool is conventionally used to create each one.
options.why: They are structurally different: an A record resolves directly to an address, while a CNAME resolves to another name that must itself then be resolved.

options.text: An A record is used only for IPv6 addresses, while a CNAME is used only for IPv4 addresses, making them address-family-specific alternatives.
options.why: AAAA, not A, is the IPv6 address record; A is IPv4, and CNAME has no address-family restriction at all since it aliases names, not addresses.

options.text: An A record can only be queried with `nslookup`, while a CNAME can only be queried with `dig`, because the two record types are carried in different wire formats that only the tool originally written for each one can decode.
options.why: Both record types can be queried by any of the DNS query tools; the distinction between them is structural, about what each record resolves to, not about tool compatibility.

items.rationale: A maps a name to an IPv4 address directly, terminating the lookup; CNAME aliases one name to another name, which must then itself be resolved — the A-versus-CNAME distinction is a commonly tested, commonly missed structural difference.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 3.4.1 (A RDATA is a 32-bit Internet address) and RFC 1034 section 3.6.2 ("A CNAME RR identifies its owner name as an alias, and specifies the corresponding canonical name in the RDATA section", with the resolver then restarting the query at the canonical name), so an A terminates in an address while a CNAME requires further resolution. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by that structural difference; o3 is refuted by RFC 3596 section 2.1, which assigns IPv6 addresses to AAAA rather than A; o4 is refuted by RFC 1035 section 4, where every RR type shares one wire format and any query tool can request any QTYPE — confirmed empirically, since the same `dig` binary returned A, MX, PTR and CNAME answers in this pass. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. REFUTED AS AUTHORED at the option level only: o4 previously ended "an assumption that holds until it does not", a self-refuting hedge; replaced with a similar-length clause that states a real falsehood about wire formats. Length balance: after the self-refuting tail was removed, o4 fell short enough that the key became the longest option, so o4's replacement clause was extended to restore the previous balance.

items.stem: A TLS certificate must be issued for a server, and the certificate authority requires an unambiguous, absolute name rather than whatever short label the host happens to answer to locally. Which kind of name is required, and why does it matter here specifically?

options.text: A fully qualified domain name is required, because it locates the host absolutely within the DNS hierarchy, unlike a bare hostname, which is only meaningful relative to a search domain that varies by context.
options.why: Configuration that must work everywhere — TLS certificates, mail routing, cluster membership — uses FQDNs for exactly this reason: an unqualified name depends on local context to resolve at all.

options.text: A bare hostname is sufficient, since certificate authorities are defined to resolve any short label the same way regardless of where the request originates.
options.why: A bare hostname is only meaningful relative to a local search domain; a certificate authority has no such local context, which is exactly why an FQDN is required.

options.text: Either name works identically for this purpose, since `hostname -f` and a plain hostname always resolve to the exact same value on every system.
options.why: `hostname -f` resolves a qualified name that can differ from the plain hostname depending on `/etc/hosts` or DNS; the two are not guaranteed to be identical.

options.text: The transient hostname set by DHCP is required, since it is the only name type systemd considers valid for external services such as certificate issuance.
options.why: The transient hostname is a runtime label, not a DNS-hierarchy name; it is unrelated to whether a name is fully qualified, which is what certificate issuance actually requires.

items.rationale: A hostname is only meaningful relative to a search domain, so the same short label can succeed on one host and fail on another; an FQDN locates the host absolutely within the DNS hierarchy, which is exactly why configuration that must work everywhere — TLS certificates, mail routing, cluster membership — uses FQDNs.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 8499 section 2, read verbatim: "The need for the term 'fully-qualified domain name' comes from the existence of partially qualified domain names, which are names where one or more of the last labels in the ordered list are omitted ... Such relative names are understood only by context." That is precisely the key's reason. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the same passage; o3 is refuted by hostname(1), which states that the FQDN "is the name that the resolver(3) returns for the host name" and that this depends on configuration such as /etc/hosts, so it need not equal the plain hostname; o4 is refuted by hostname(5) HOSTNAME SEMANTICS, where the transient hostname is a runtime value taken from network configuration and has no bearing on qualification. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: the concept cited only RFC 1034, which RFC 8499 itself notes does not define "host name" at all; man-hostname-1, man-hostname-5, man-hostnamectl-1 and rfc-8499-dns-terminology were registered and wired into sysadmin.networking.fqdn-and-hostname.

items.stem: `hostname -f` fails on a host that clearly has a hostname configured, since `hostname` alone prints a value. What does the failure actually mean?

options.text: It means nothing resolves the short name to a qualified one (usually a missing `/etc/hosts` line), not that the hostname itself is unset.
options.why: `hostname -f` depends on resolution succeeding, so its failure is a resolution problem, most often a missing hosts entry, and not evidence that the hostname configuration is absent.

options.text: It means the hostname configuration has been wiped and must be reconfigured from scratch using `hostnamectl set-hostname`.
options.why: A plain `hostname` succeeding proves the hostname configuration exists; the `-f` failure is about resolving a qualified form, not about the base configuration being missing.

options.text: It means the host is not running systemd, since `hostname -f` is a systemd-only flag unavailable on non-systemd distributions.
options.why: `hostname -f` is a flag of the `hostname` command itself, not a systemd-specific feature; `hostnamectl` is the systemd-specific tool, and its absence is a different matter entirely.

options.text: It means DHCP failed to issue an address to this host, since `hostname -f` is defined to depend on a successful DHCP lease being present across virtually every environment of this kind.
options.why: `hostname -f` depends on name resolution, not on DHCP addressing; a host can have a perfectly good DHCP-issued address while `hostname -f` still fails to resolve a qualified name.

items.rationale: `hostname -f` asks for the FQDN, which is resolved rather than merely read, and therefore depends on `/etc/hosts` or DNS returning a qualified name; its failure means nothing resolves the short name to a qualified one, usually a missing hosts entry, not that the hostname is unset.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against hostname(1), THE FQDN section, read verbatim: "The FQDN of the system is the name that the resolver(3) returns for the host name ... Therefore it depends on the configuration (usually in /etc/host.conf) how you can change it. If hosts is the first lookup method, you can change the FQDN in /etc/hosts." A failing `hostname -f` is therefore a resolution failure, and the /etc/hosts line is the usual missing piece. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the same page, where plain `hostname` prints the value from gethostname(2) — so its success proves the configuration exists; o3 is refuted by the hostname(1) SYNOPSIS, which lists `-f, --fqdn, --long` as a flag of hostname(1) from net-tools, entirely separate from hostnamectl(1); o4 is refuted because nothing in hostname(1) makes the FQDN depend on a DHCP lease. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: RFC 1034 documents no command-line tool, so man-hostname-1 was registered and wired into the concept.

items.stem: On a systemd system, `hostnamectl` distinguishes a static, a transient and a pretty hostname. What is the difference between the static and the transient one?

options.text: The static hostname is persisted in `/etc/hostname` and survives reboots; the transient one is a runtime value, typically from a DHCP lease, and is used only when no static hostname is set.
options.why: These are genuinely different sources of truth: one is a file-backed, administrator-set value, and the other is set dynamically at runtime from network configuration, which systemd falls back to only when the static hostname is absent.

options.text: The static hostname is set by DHCP on every boot, while the transient hostname is the one an administrator writes permanently to `/etc/hostname`, a pattern that holds across most deployments encountered.
options.why: This reverses the actual roles: the static hostname is the one persisted in `/etc/hostname`, and the transient one is what the kernel or DHCP may set at runtime.

options.text: The static hostname is a free-form, human-readable label, while the transient hostname is the strict, machine-parsable form used in DNS lookups.
options.why: The free-form, human-readable label is the pretty hostname, a third distinct category from either the static or the transient one described here.

options.text: The static hostname only applies to IPv4-configured hosts, while the transient hostname only applies to hosts configured for IPv6.
options.why: Neither the static nor the transient hostname is tied to a specific IP address family; the distinction is about persistence and source, not about IPv4 versus IPv6.

items.rationale: `hostnamectl` distinguishes the static hostname, persisted in `/etc/hostname`, from the transient one, set by the kernel and possibly by DHCP, and from the pretty one, a free-form label — three genuinely different sources of the same general concept.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The key originally read "the transient one is set by the kernel, and possibly by DHCP, and may not persist the same way", which misstates the mechanism and omits the priority rule. hostname(5), HOSTNAME SEMANTICS, read verbatim: "the 'static' hostname specified by /etc/hostname ... Otherwise, a transient hostname may be set during runtime, for example based on information in a DHCP lease ... systemd-hostnamed.service(8) gives higher priority to the static hostname, so the transient hostname will only be used if the static hostname is not configured." The key was rewritten to that wording and re-checked: it now matches the manual clause for clause. Rewritten without a trailing em-dash clause, so the file's key/distractor em-dash gap is not widened. No distractor is also correct: o2 reverses the two roles, refuted by the same section; o3 describes the pretty hostname, which hostnamectl(1) defines as the third, free-form name ("Lennart's Laptop"); o4's address-family claim appears nowhere in hostname(5) or hostnamectl(1). Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Length balance: the rewritten key was trimmed so that it is not the longest option, which it briefly became after the first rewrite.

items.stem: A name written as `web01.lab` has a dot in it. Does that dot alone make it an FQDN?

options.text: No: a name with a dot is not automatically fully qualified; `web01.lab` is qualified only if `lab` is a real domain in the hierarchy being queried.
options.why: A dot alone does not confer full qualification; what matters is whether the suffix names a genuine position in the DNS hierarchy being resolved against.

options.text: Yes — the presence of any dot in a name is what defines it as fully qualified, regardless of what follows the dot.
options.why: A dot alone is not sufficient; the suffix after the dot must correspond to a real domain in the hierarchy being queried for the name to actually be fully qualified.

options.text: No, but only because a trailing dot at the very end of the whole name is required in addition to the one already present after `web01`.
options.why: A trailing dot representing the root zone is strict DNS notation for a fully qualified name, but the core issue here is whether `lab` is a genuine domain, not merely whether a trailing dot is present.

options.text: Yes, but only when the name is used inside `/etc/hosts` rather than in a DNS query, since `/etc/hosts` treats any dotted name as fully qualified.
options.why: `/etc/hosts` does not redefine what counts as fully qualified; qualification depends on the DNS hierarchy, not on which file or mechanism happens to be resolving the name.

items.rationale: A name with a dot in it is not automatically an FQDN — `web01.lab` is qualified only if `lab` is a real domain in the hierarchy you are querying, and because the resolver appends search domains to unqualified names, a successful `ping web01` proves nothing portable about the name.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 8499 section 2, which defines a partially qualified domain name as one "where one or more of the last labels in the ordered list are omitted" and notes that names written relative to the root "are still called fully qualified". Qualification therefore turns on whether the written suffix reaches the root of the hierarchy being queried, not on the presence of a dot — so `web01.lab` is fully qualified only if `lab` is a real domain there. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the same definition; o3 is wrong in its "only because", though its 'why' correctly notes that strict notation writes the root as a trailing dot (RFC 8499: "such a name would be written 'www.example.net.' (note the terminating dot)"); o4 is refuted because hosts(5) resolution does not redefine DNS qualification. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A service must move to a new address next week with minimal disruption. What should be changed first, and when, relative to the actual move?

options.text: The record's TTL should be lowered well before the change, so resolvers hold the old answer for a shorter time once the change actually lands.
options.why: Planning a migration means lowering the TTL before the change, not during it, since a TTL that is only lowered at the moment of the change has not yet propagated and does nothing to shorten the transition.

options.text: The record's TTL should be raised right before the change, since a higher TTL is what makes a new answer propagate to every resolver faster.
options.why: A higher TTL makes resolvers cache an answer longer, which slows propagation of a later change, not speeds it; lowering the TTL in advance is what shortens the transition.

options.text: Nothing about DNS needs to change beforehand; flushing every resolver's cache at the moment of the move achieves the same effect as lowering the TTL in advance.
options.why: Flushing a local cache does nothing to the caches held by every other resolver on the internet; you cannot force other people's resolvers to forget an answer, which is exactly why lowering the TTL in advance is necessary instead.

options.text: The A record should be deleted entirely first, then recreated with the new address once the actual move has completed.
options.why: Deleting the record first would cause resolution failures during the gap, which is the opposite of minimising disruption; lowering the TTL in advance is the standard, non-disruptive preparation instead.

items.rationale: TTL explains why a DNS change is not visible everywhere at once, and planning a migration means lowering the TTL before the change, not during it, so that resolvers are already holding a short-lived cached answer by the time the actual change lands.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 4.1.3, which defines TTL as "the time interval (in seconds) that the resource record may be cached before it should be discarded". Because a resolver may hold the old answer for the whole of the previously published TTL, a reduction only takes effect for caches that fetch the record after the change, which is why it must precede the move. Demonstrated empirically in this pass: a local unbound resolver returned example.com A with TTL 300, then 270, then 240 over one minute, i.e. it was still serving the answer it had already cached and would have kept doing so for the full original interval regardless of any later edit. No distractor is also correct: o2 inverts the effect of TTL; o3 is refuted because a cache flush reaches only the resolver you control, while RFC 1035 places the caching decision in every resolver that holds the record; o4 would produce an outage rather than a shortened transition. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: Repeated `dig` queries against the same resolver show a record's TTL falling from 300 to 240 to 180 across successive requests a minute apart. Is this evidence of a misconfiguration?

options.text: No. A caching resolver returns the remaining lifetime of the cached record on each answer, so a falling TTL across repeated queries is the expected countdown, not an error.
options.why: A recursive resolver caches a record and returns it with the remaining TTL on each subsequent answer, so watching the number count down across repeated queries is exactly the expected behaviour.

options.text: Yes — a correctly configured authoritative server should always show a falling TTL exactly like this on every repeated query it answers, a pattern that holds across most deployments encountered.
options.why: An authoritative server returns the full configured TTL every time, not a falling countdown; the falling pattern specifically indicates the queries hit a caching resolver, not the authoritative server.

options.text: Yes, and it indicates the zone's SOA parameters have been misconfigured to force an artificially short negative-caching interval.
options.why: SOA parameters govern negative caching for answers that do not exist; a falling TTL on a normal positive answer from a caching resolver is unrelated to SOA configuration at all.

options.text: No, but only because the resolver being queried must actually be the authoritative server rather than a caching, recursive one.
options.why: A falling TTL specifically indicates a caching resolver rather than the authoritative server; the authoritative server would show the full configured value on every query instead.

items.rationale: A recursive resolver caches a record and, on each subsequent answer, returns it with the remaining TTL, counting down — repeated queries against a caching resolver showing a falling number are expected, while a query sent to the authoritative server shows the full configured value every time.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed by direct experiment plus RFC 2308. Experiment: in `docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04` I installed unbound and dnsutils, started unbound with a minimal config (interface 127.0.0.1, access-control 127.0.0.0/8 allow), and ran `dig +noall +answer @127.0.0.1 A example.com` three times at 30-second intervals. Output: `example.com. 300 IN A ...`, then `example.com. 270 IN A ...`, then `example.com. 240 IN A ...` — a countdown of exactly the elapsed time. For contrast, `dig +noall +answer @a.iana-servers.net A example.com` run twice returned `300` both times. RFC 2308 section 6 states the general rule for cached data: a server answering from cache adds the record "with the TTL decremented by the amount of time it was stored in the cache", and notes this applies "[a]s with all answers coming from the cache". So the observed pattern is expected, not a misconfiguration. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the authoritative control above, which showed no countdown; o3 is refuted by RFC 2308 sections 5 and 6, where SOA parameters govern negative answers, not a positive cached A record; o4 inverts which server type counts down. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-2308-negative-caching added, since RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 define the TTL but do not state the decrement-on-serve rule.

items.stem: A name that did not exist yesterday was created this morning, but a branch office still gets NXDOMAIN when looking it up. The zone is confirmed correct at the authoritative server. What explains the branch office's result?

options.text: Negative answers are cached too, governed by the zone's SOA parameters, so the branch office's resolver may still hold a cached NXDOMAIN from before the name existed.
options.why: A name queried before it existed can stay NXDOMAIN in a resolver's cache after it is created, because negative caching follows the same TTL-governed mechanism positive answers do.

options.text: NXDOMAIN answers are never cached under any circumstances, so the branch office's resolver must instead be pointed at an entirely different, wrong nameserver.
options.why: Negative answers are cached too, governed by the zone's SOA parameters, which is exactly the mechanism that explains a stale NXDOMAIN persisting after the name is created.

options.text: The branch office's `/etc/hosts` file must contain a stale entry actively overriding DNS with an incorrect result for this specific name.
options.why: An `/etc/hosts` override would need a prior entry for a name that did not previously exist, which is unlikely here; negative DNS caching is the ordinary, sufficient explanation.

options.text: The branch office is using a different record type than the rest of the organisation, which is why its query returns NXDOMAIN while others succeed.
options.why: Record type choice does not explain a stale result across offices; a cached negative answer governed by TTL is the direct, sufficient explanation for this pattern.

items.rationale: Negative answers are cached too, governed by the zone's SOA parameters, so a name queried before it existed can stay NXDOMAIN in a resolver's cache after it is actually created — the branch office's report needs no fix beyond waiting out that cached negative answer's TTL.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2308 section 5, read verbatim: "Like normal answers negative answers have a time to live (TTL) ... This is done by including the SOA record from the zone in the authority section of the reply. When the authoritative server creates this record its TTL is taken from the minimum of the SOA.MINIMUM field and SOA's TTL. This TTL decrements in a similar manner to a normal cached answer." RFC 1034 section 4.3.4 says the same thing in its original, optional form. Verified empirically: `dig +noall +authority @127.0.0.1 A nosuchname-t57d.example.com` against the local unbound instance returned `example.com. 1800 IN SOA elliott.ns.cloudflare.com. dns.cloudflare.com. 2411783310 10000 2400 604800 1800` — the SOA carried in the authority section with the 1800-second negative-cache lifetime, exactly the mechanism the key names. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted head-on by RFC 2308 section 3, which makes negative caching non-optional for resolvers; o3 and o4 both propose explanations the scenario does not need and that do not produce a stale NXDOMAIN after the name is created. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: Is lowering a record's TTL ahead of a planned change a free safety margin, or does it have a cost?

options.text: It has a real cost: a low TTL raises query volume against the authoritative servers, since resolvers must re-ask far more often, so it is a deliberate trade rather than a free margin.
options.why: A low TTL raises query volume and is a cost, not a free safety margin, which is why it is applied deliberately and temporarily around a planned change rather than left low permanently.

options.text: It is entirely free — lowering a TTL has no effect on anything except how quickly resolvers pick up the eventual new answer, since resolvers re-query on a fixed internal schedule that the record's TTL value does not influence.
options.why: A lower TTL means resolvers cache the answer for less time and must re-query more often, which raises load on the authoritative servers; it is not a cost-free change.

options.text: It has a cost, but only in the form of a one-time fee charged by the domain registrar each time a TTL value is changed.
options.why: Changing a TTL is not a billable, one-time registrar event; the actual cost is ongoing increased query load against the authoritative servers while the lower value is in effect.

options.text: It is free as long as the change is made using `dig` rather than through the zone's own administrative interface.
options.why: Which tool is used to inspect or change a TTL has no bearing on the cost of a lower TTL; the cost is the increased query volume against authoritative servers regardless of tooling.

items.rationale: A low TTL raises query volume and is a cost, not a free safety margin — resolvers cache the answer for less time and must re-ask more often, which is exactly why it has to be lowered deliberately in advance rather than left permanently low.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 1035 section 4.1.3 together with RFC 1034 section 4.3.4's stated rationale for caching: the TTL bounds how long a resolver may reuse a cached answer, so shortening it necessarily increases how often resolvers return to the authoritative servers. RFC 2308's abstract makes the same load argument in the negative direction — "[a] large proportion of DNS traffic on the Internet could be eliminated if all resolvers implemented negative caching" — which is the same trade seen from the other side. The mechanism is visible in the unbound experiment recorded on item .02: the resolver served the cached answer without re-querying until the TTL ran out, so a smaller TTL means more upstream queries per unit time. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by the same passages; o3 invents a registrar fee that appears in no source; o4 confuses the tool used to inspect a value with the value's effect. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. REFUTED AS AUTHORED at the option level only: o2 previously ended "which is the assumption most administrators start from as a matter of routine operational practice", a self-refuting hedge announcing its own wrongness; replaced with a similar-length clause asserting a genuinely false mechanism.

items.stem: A new employee's laptop cannot get online. It shows no IP address at all. A separate report says a colleague's laptop has an address and can ping the gateway, but web pages by name fail while an IP address typed directly still works. Which service is implicated in each case?

options.text: The first case implicates DHCP, since no address means the addressing exchange failed; the second implicates DNS, since an address that works while names do not is DNS's signature, not DHCP's.
options.why: DHCP hands out addresses and configuration; DNS answers questions about names — the two failure signatures are opposite and distinct, which is exactly why conflating them is the classic error.

options.text: Both cases implicate DHCP, since DHCP is responsible for issuing addresses and also for resolving the names that web pages depend on.
options.why: DHCP hands out addressing configuration only; it does not resolve names at all, and does not create DNS records by itself, so the second case is not a DHCP problem.

options.text: Both cases implicate DNS, since a missing IP address is treated as ultimately a naming failure at a lower layer.
options.why: A completely missing IP address is an addressing failure, which is DHCP's job to provide; DNS has no role in whether a host receives an address at all.

options.text: The first case implicates DNS, since a missing address is read as evidence the hostname could not be resolved during boot; the second implicates DHCP, since a missing default route is read as evidence the address lease itself never completed.
options.why: A missing IP address entirely is an addressing failure — DHCP's job — not a name-resolution failure, and the second case, addresses working while names fail, is squarely DNS.

items.rationale: DHCP hands out addresses and configuration; DNS answers questions about names — a machine with no address needs DHCP, and a machine with an address that cannot resolve a name needs DNS, and conflating the two is the classic error this competency tests.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2131 section 1, which scopes DHCP to "passing configuration information to hosts" and describes automatic, dynamic and manual allocation of an IP address, and RFC 1034 section 2.1, which scopes the DNS to mapping names to resources. The two failure signatures in the stem map one-to-one onto those two scopes. No distractor is also correct: o2 fails because nothing in RFC 2131 gives DHCP any name-resolution role; o3 fails because RFC 2131 makes address allocation DHCP's function; o4 inverts both halves. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact — in particular o2's "does not create DNS records by itself" is true of the protocol as specified, DDNS being a separate server-side integration rather than part of RFC 2131. Citation fixed at concept level: the concept cited only RFC 2131, and this item turns equally on the DNS half, so rfc-1034-dns-concepts was added to sysadmin.networking.dhcp.

items.stem: A DHCP server on one subnet must serve clients on a physically separate subnet, and DHCP discovery is a broadcast that does not cross routers. What component makes this work, and what does it do?

options.text: A relay agent placed on the clients' subnet, which forwards the broadcast DISCOVER on to the DHCP server at a configured address, normally by unicast, and relays the reply back.
options.why: Since broadcasts do not cross routers, serving a subnet whose DHCP server sits elsewhere requires a relay agent on that subnet to forward the request onward to a configured server address and to hand the reply back to the client.

options.text: Nothing extra is needed, since routers are defined to always forward the first four bytes of any broadcast packet regardless of protocol.
options.why: Routers do not selectively forward parts of a broadcast packet; broadcasts simply do not cross a router at all without a relay agent to convert them to unicast.

options.text: A DHCP reservation configured on the server, which is what allows a single broadcast to be forwarded across a router boundary to remote clients as a matter of routine operational practice.
options.why: A DHCP reservation binds one MAC to one fixed address; it has no bearing on whether a broadcast crosses a router, which is the relay agent's job entirely.

options.text: A static default route added to the clients' subnet, which redirects the broadcast DISCOVER message toward the remote DHCP server directly.
options.why: A static route affects unicast forwarding of known destinations; it does not enable a broadcast, which by definition has no single destination, to cross a router at all.

items.rationale: Because the client has no address yet, the first DHCP messages are broadcasts, and since broadcasts do not cross routers, serving a subnet whose DHCP server sits elsewhere requires a relay agent on that subnet to forward the requests as unicast to the remote server.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The key originally said the relay "forwards the broadcast DISCOVER to the remote server as a unicast message", which overstates the specification. RFC 2131 section 2 defines a relay agent as "an Internet host or router that passes DHCP messages between DHCP clients and DHCP servers" and defers the behaviour to RFC 951 and RFC 1542. RFC 1542 section 4.1.1 says the relaying destination "MUST be configurable" and, in its DISCUSSION, that "[t]he network manager may wish the relaying destination to be an IP unicast, multicast, broadcast, or some combination" — so unicast is the normal deployment, not a protocol requirement. The key was rewritten to "at a configured destination address, normally by unicast" and re-checked against RFC 1542 section 4.1.1; the reply path is covered by RFC 2131 section 4.1, "[i]f the 'giaddr' field in a DHCP message from a client is non-zero, the server sends any return messages to the 'DHCP server' port on the BOOTP relay agent whose address appears in 'giaddr'". Neither the old nor the new key carries a trailing em-dash clause. No distractor is also correct: o2's partial-broadcast forwarding appears in no source; o3 is refuted by dhcpd.conf(5), where a reservation binds a client identity to an address and says nothing about broadcast propagation; o4 is refuted because a broadcast has no unicast destination for a route to select. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-1542-bootp-clarifications added to sysadmin.networking.dhcp, since RFC 2131 explicitly points elsewhere for relay behaviour. Length balance: the rewritten key was trimmed so it is not the longest option.

items.stem: A laptop comes up with an address in the 169.254.0.0/16 range and no internet access. A colleague calls this "a bad DHCP lease." Is that accurate?

options.text: No, the laptop received no lease at all; it self-configured a link-local address because no DHCP server answered its broadcast DISCOVER.
options.why: A client showing a 169.254 address has not been given a bad lease; it has received no lease at all and self-configured, which is a distinct and more specific diagnosis.

options.text: Yes — a 169.254 address is exactly what a DHCP server issues when its address pool is temporarily exhausted of usable leases.
options.why: A 169.254 address is self-assigned by the client, not issued by any DHCP server; pool exhaustion would instead produce a straightforward lease failure with no address issued at all.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to renew the lease immediately using the DHCP client's renewal command, since the address is simply near expiry and the client is still bound to a lease the server granted earlier.
options.why: There is no lease to renew, since none was ever granted; the address is self-assigned specifically because DISCOVER went unanswered, not because an existing lease is expiring.

options.text: No, but only because 169.254.0.0/16 is actually RFC 1918 private address space rather than link-local space.
options.why: 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (APIPA) space, a separate reservation from the three RFC 1918 private ranges, not one of them.

items.rationale: DHCP hands out addresses and configuration; it does not by itself make an address permanent, and a client showing a 169.254 address has not been given a bad lease — it has received no lease at all and self-configured after no DHCP server answered.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 3927. Its abstract states that address configuration information "may not always be available" and describes "how a host may automatically configure an interface with an IPv4 address within the 169.254/16 prefix"; section 1.1 adds that this "is especially valuable in environments where no other configuration mechanism is available". The address is therefore self-assigned by the client, not issued by any server, which is exactly the key's distinction. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted because RFC 2131 has no message or option by which a server hands out a 169.254 address, and RFC 3927 assigns the prefix to host self-configuration; o3 is refuted because there is no lease in the first place; o4 is refuted by RFC 3927 section 1.6, read verbatim: "Administrators wishing to configure their own local addresses ... should use one of the existing private address prefixes [RFC1918], not the 169.254/16 prefix" — the two are separate reservations. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact. REFUTED AS AUTHORED at the option level only: o3 previously ended "an assumption that holds until it does not", a self-refuting hedge; replaced with a similar-length clause that asserts a real falsehood. Citation fixed at concept level: rfc-3927-ipv4-link-local wired into sysadmin.networking.dhcp, since RFC 2131 never mentions 169.254/16 (checked by searching the full RFC text).

items.stem: Name the four messages of the DHCP exchange in order, and the two UDP ports involved.

options.text: DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK, using UDP port 67 for the server and port 68 for the client.
options.why: This is the DORA sequence: the client broadcasts DISCOVER, a server replies OFFER, the client broadcasts REQUEST naming the accepted offer, and the server confirms with ACK.

options.text: REQUEST, DISCOVER, ACK, OFFER — using UDP port 68 for the server and port 67 for the client.
options.why: This has both the message order and the port assignment reversed: DISCOVER comes before REQUEST, and the server uses port 67, the client port 68.

options.text: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, FIN — the same four-step exchange used to establish and later close a TCP connection.
options.why: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK and FIN are TCP handshake and teardown flags, an entirely different exchange from DHCP's DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK sequence.

options.text: DISCOVER, REQUEST, OFFER, ACK — using UDP port 53 for the server and port 68 for the client.
options.why: REQUEST and OFFER are swapped in order, and port 53 is DNS's port, not DHCP's; the DHCP server uses port 67.

items.rationale: The exchange is conventionally called DORA: the client broadcasts DISCOVER; a server replies with OFFER; the client broadcasts REQUEST naming the offer it accepts; the server confirms with ACK, over UDP port 67 for the server and port 68 for the client.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2131 section 3.1, which walks the exchange in order — "[t]he client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER message on its local physical subnet", each server "may respond with a DHCPOFFER", the client then sends DHCPREQUEST, and the server answers DHCPACK — and against RFC 2131 section 4.1 for the ports, read verbatim: "DHCP messages from a client to a server are sent to the 'DHCP server' port (67), and DHCP messages from a server to a client are sent to the 'DHCP client' port (68)." No distractor is also correct: o2 reverses both the order and the ports; o3 lists TCP flags, which belong to RFC 9293 and not to DHCP at all; o4 both swaps OFFER and REQUEST and substitutes port 53, which RFC 1035 section 4.2 assigns to DNS. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A machine has been powered off for far longer than its DHCP lease duration. When it powers back on, what should be expected?

options.text: It may receive a different address than before, since the previous lease will have expired and the address may have been reassigned to another client in the meantime.
options.why: The lease timer is why a "dynamic" address can look stable for weeks and then change after an outage — a machine off longer than its lease may come back with a different address.

options.text: It is guaranteed to receive the exact same address as before, since a DHCP server always reserves an expired lease's address permanently for its original holder under the great majority of ordinary configurations.
options.why: A lease is a time-bounded allocation, not a permanent reservation; once it expires, the address is free to be handed to a different client, so the same address is not guaranteed.

options.text: It will fail to obtain any address at all, since a DHCP server never issues a fresh lease to a client whose previous one has expired.
options.why: An expired lease simply means the client starts again from DISCOVER; a DHCP server issues a fresh lease to any requesting client, expired-lease history notwithstanding.

options.text: It will self-assign a 169.254 link-local address automatically, since that is the defined behaviour whenever a lease has expired for any reason.
options.why: Self-assignment to link-local space happens when no DHCP server answers at all, not simply because a previous lease expired while the server remains available.

items.rationale: A lease is a time-bounded allocation the client must renew to keep, which is exactly why a machine switched off longer than its lease may come back to find its old address already reassigned, requiring a fresh DISCOVER to obtain a new one.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2131 section 4.3.1, read verbatim: "In some environments it will be necessary to reassign network addresses due to exhaustion of available addresses. In such environments, the allocation mechanism will reuse addresses whose lease has expired." RFC 2131 section 4.4.5 covers the client side: "[i]f the client is given a new network address, it MUST NOT continue using the previous network address". The key's hedged "may receive a different address" matches the RFC exactly, which says reuse happens where addresses are scarce rather than always. No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted by section 2, where a lease is "a finite lease, allowing for serial reassignment of network addresses to different clients"; o3 is refuted by section 4.4.1, where a client with no valid lease simply restarts at DHCPDISCOVER and is served normally; o4 is refuted by RFC 3927, which ties 169.254/16 self-configuration to no configuration mechanism being available, not to an expired lease with a reachable server. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: At roughly what point in a lease does a client first attempt to renew, and how, and what happens if that first attempt fails?

options.text: At T1, about half the lease duration, the client tries to renew directly with the server that granted it, by unicast; if that fails, at T2 it broadcasts a renewal request any server may answer.
options.why: The ACK that grants a lease states its duration and two timers, T1 and T2, giving the client an orderly escalation from a targeted unicast renewal to a broader broadcast rebinding attempt.

options.text: At T2, about seven-eighths of the lease duration, the client tries to renew by broadcast first, only falling back to unicast to the original server if that fails.
options.why: The order is reversed: the client first tries unicast renewal to the original server at T1, and only broadcasts more broadly at the later point, T2, if that attempt fails.

options.text: Exactly at lease expiry, with no earlier renewal attempt made at all, since the client is defined to wait until the very last possible moment.
options.why: The client attempts renewal well before expiry, at T1 (about half the lease) and again at T2 (about seven-eighths), not only at the moment of expiry itself.

options.text: Immediately after the lease is granted, with the client re-requesting the same address again right away as a confirmation step.
options.why: There is no immediate re-request right after a lease is granted; the first renewal attempt happens later, at T1, roughly half the lease duration in.

items.rationale: At T1, by default half the lease time, the client tries to renew directly with the server that granted it, by unicast; if that fails, at T2, seven-eighths of the lease time, it enters rebinding and broadcasts a renewal request that any server may answer, and if the lease expires with no answer it must start again from DISCOVER.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2131 section 4.4.5, read verbatim: "T1 is the time at which the client enters the RENEWING state and attempts to contact the server that originally issued the client's network address. T2 is the time at which the client enters the REBINDING state and attempts to contact any server"; "[a]t time T1 the client moves to RENEWING state and sends (via unicast) a DHCPREQUEST message to the server"; "[i]f no DHCPACK arrives before time T2, the client moves to REBINDING state and sends (via broadcast) a DHCPREQUEST message"; and "T1 defaults to (0.5 * duration_of_lease). T2 defaults to (0.875 * duration_of_lease)." All four elements of the key — timing, unicast, escalation, broadcast — are in that one section. No distractor is also correct: o2 states the 7/8 figure correctly but reverses unicast and broadcast against the section above; o3 is refuted by the existence of T1 and T2 before expiry; o4 is refuted because the state machine goes from DHCPACK to BOUND with no immediate re-request. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A hypervisor host needs a predictable address without visiting the machine to configure it by hand, and the team wants every address kept in one authoritative place rather than scattered across host configurations. Which addressing choice fits, and how does it differ from a plain static address?

options.text: A DHCP reservation fits. The client stays an ordinary DHCP client while the server binds its MAC to a fixed address, keeping every address centrally managed rather than configured by hand on the host.
options.why: A reservation gives a device a predictable address without visiting it, and keeps every address in one authoritative place, the DHCP server, instead of scattering hand-written configurations across machines.

options.text: A plain static address fits equally well, since a static address and a reservation both live on the DHCP server and behave identically in every respect as a matter of routine operational practice, regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved.
options.why: A static address is held by the host itself, not the server, and a static host does not depend on the DHCP server being reachable at boot the way a reservation-based client does.

options.text: Neither fits; only a purely dynamic lease from the general pool satisfies the requirement for centrally managed addressing without visiting the host.
options.why: A purely dynamic lease from the general pool gives no guarantee of address stability at all, which fails the requirement for a predictable address.

options.text: A reservation fits, but it requires the host to be manually configured with a static IP address in addition to being registered on the server.
options.why: A reservation requires no extra host-side configuration at all; the client is configured for DHCP like any other client, and the stability comes entirely from the server side.

items.rationale: A DHCP reservation binds a specific MAC address to a fixed IP on the server side, giving a device like a hypervisor a stable, centrally managed address without visiting it or configuring it by hand — the client is configured for DHCP like any other client, and the stability comes entirely from the server.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 2131 section 1, read verbatim: "In 'manual allocation', a client's IP address is assigned by the network administrator, and DHCP is used simply to convey the assigned address to the client" — the client remains an ordinary DHCP client while the assignment lives on the server. dhcpd.conf(5) supplies the MAC-keyed mechanism: "[h]ost declarations are matched to actual DHCP or BOOTP clients by matching the dhcp-client-identifier option specified in the host declaration to the one supplied by the client, or, if the host declaration or the client does not provide a dhcp-client-identifier option, by matching the hardware parameter in the host declaration to the network hardware address supplied by the client." No distractor is also correct: o2 is refuted because a static address is held by the host, so it satisfies neither the central-management nor the no-visit requirement; o3 is refuted because a general-pool lease is explicitly a time-bounded allocation subject to reuse (RFC 2131 section 1); o4 is refuted because manual allocation requires no host-side address configuration at all. Every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: A DHCP server is unreachable when two brand-new machines boot onto the network for the first time. One is configured by hand with a static address; the other has a DHCP reservation waiting for it on the server. What is the difference in outcome?

options.text: The statically configured machine comes up regardless of the server; the reservation-based one gets nothing, because it is still a DHCP client with no lease of its own to fall back on.
options.why: A reservation is not a static address: the client is still a DHCP client, so on a first boot with the server unreachable it has no remembered lease to reuse and comes up with no address, whereas a statically configured host comes up regardless.

options.text: Both machines come up identically, since a reservation is functionally indistinguishable from a static address once it has been configured on the server, which pushes the address into the client's own persistent configuration.
options.why: A reservation still requires a successful DHCP exchange at boot; unlike a static address held by the host itself, it fails to come up if the server is unreachable.

options.text: Neither machine comes up, since any DHCP server outage is defined to block every host on the network from initialising its networking at all.
options.why: A statically configured host does not depend on DHCP at all, so a DHCP server outage has no bearing on whether it comes up; only the reservation-based client is affected.

options.text: The reservation-based machine comes up regardless of the server, since a reservation is cached locally on the client the first time it is granted.
options.why: A reservation is a server-side binding and nothing about it is stored on the client. A DHCP client may reuse a previously granted, still-unexpired lease when no server answers, but a machine booting for the first time has no such lease to reuse.

items.rationale: A reservation is not a static address. The client is still a DHCP client, so on a first boot with the server unreachable it has no lease at all, while a statically configured host comes up without needing the server.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED — this item had two defensible answers. The original stem said only "[a] DHCP server is briefly unreachable at boot time" and the key asserted flatly that the reservation-based machine "gets nothing". RFC 2131 section 3.2 contradicts that for a client that already holds a lease: "[i]f the client receives neither a DHCPACK or a DHCPNAK message after employing the retransmission algorithm, the client MAY choose to use the previously allocated network address and configuration parameters for the remainder of the unexpired lease." Under the original stem, distractor o4's headline claim — that the reservation-based machine comes up anyway — was therefore defensible for any reboot inside the lease period, even though its stated reason was wrong. Repair: the stem now fixes the scenario as a first boot of brand-new machines, so no remembered lease exists; the key now says "with no lease of its own to fall back on"; and o4's 'why' was rewritten to state the real nuance (a client caches a lease, never a reservation) rather than the false blanket claim that nothing survives a failed exchange. Re-checked after rewrite: the key follows from RFC 2131 section 1's manual allocation, where "DHCP is used simply to convey the assigned address to the client", so the client must complete an exchange; o2 is refuted because nothing is pushed into the client's persistent configuration; o3 is refuted because a statically configured host never consults DHCP; o4 is refuted on a first boot. No em-dash clause was added to the key. Also repaired o2's self-refuting tail "an assumption that holds until it does not", replacing it with a similar-length clause that makes a genuinely false claim.

items.stem: A printer's network card fails and is replaced, which changes the device's MAC address. Its DHCP reservation, keyed to the old MAC, is left unchanged. What happens the next time the printer requests an address?

options.text: The reservation silently no longer applies, since it is keyed on the MAC address; the printer receives an ordinary address from the general pool instead of its reserved one.
options.why: A reservation is keyed on the MAC address, so replacing a failed network card — or a virtual machine getting a regenerated MAC — silently breaks the binding without any error being raised.

options.text: The reservation automatically follows the printer to its new MAC address, since DHCP servers are defined to track devices by hostname rather than by MAC in the overwhelming majority of real deployments.
options.why: A reservation is bound to a MAC address specifically, not a hostname; nothing about the binding automatically updates to follow a device to a new MAC.

options.text: The printer fails to obtain any address at all, since a DHCP server refuses to serve any device whose MAC does not match an existing reservation.
options.why: A DHCP server does not refuse unreserved devices outright; the printer simply receives an ordinary address from the general dynamic pool instead of its now-mismatched reservation.

options.text: The reservation is automatically deleted and replaced with a static address configuration pushed to the printer over the network by the server.
options.why: DHCP servers do not push static configuration to a device; the reservation simply stops matching, and the printer falls back to receiving an ordinary dynamic lease instead.

items.rationale: A reservation is keyed on the MAC address, so replacing a failed network card, or a virtual machine getting a regenerated MAC, silently breaks the binding — the device simply receives an ordinary address from the dynamic pool instead, with no error raised.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against dhcpd.conf(5), host statement section, read verbatim: "Host declarations are matched to actual DHCP or BOOTP clients by matching the dhcp-client-identifier option specified in the host declaration to the one supplied by the client, or, if the host declaration or the client does not provide a dhcp-client-identifier option, by matching the hardware parameter in the host declaration to the network hardware address supplied by the client." A replaced NIC changes that hardware address, so the declaration stops matching and the client is served from the ordinary pool per RFC 2131 section 4.3.1. o2 is refuted head-on by the same manual page: "only the dhcp-client-identifier option and the hardware address can be used to match a host declaration ... it is not possible to match a host declaration to a host-name option". o3 is refuted because dhcpd.conf(5) only ignores clients where `deny booting` is set, not by default; o4 is refuted because DHCP has no mechanism for pushing a static configuration onto a device. No distractor is also correct and every distractor 'why' states a true fact.

items.stem: An address inside a Kea DHCP server's dynamic pool is already leased to one host when an administrator adds a reservation for that same address to a different host. What does the server do?

options.text: It cannot hand the address over at once: it parks the newly reserved host on another pool address, and reclaims the reserved one by NAKing the original holder when it next renews.
options.why: Reservations and lease data are stored separately, so a reservation added over a live lease is resolved over time rather than instantly, with the reserved host parked on another address until the old lease has been taken back.

options.text: It deletes the existing lease immediately — a reservation always outranks an active dynamic lease, so the reserved host is given its reserved address on the spot.
options.why: Removing the lease outright does not solve the problem: the reserved host would find the address still in use by the original holder and send a DHCPDECLINE, which is why the server hands it a different address in the meantime.

options.text: It refuses the reservation outright at configuration load time, because an address that falls inside a dynamic pool's active range cannot be reserved for a specific client at all.
options.why: In-pool and out-of-pool reservations use identical syntax and are handled uniformly; a reservation may name any address belonging to the subnet, including one that lies inside a dynamic pool.

options.text: It assigns the reserved address to both hosts at once — each client's own duplicate-address detection then settles the conflict between them.
options.why: The server never deliberately double-assigns an address; it resolves the conflict itself, holding the reserved address back until the original holder's lease has been taken away with a DHCPNAK.

items.rationale: Reservations and leases are stored separately, so reserving an address that is already leased to a different client creates a conflict the server resolves over time: the reserved host is parked on another pool address, and the original holder is NAKed at its next renewal.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED and rewritten. The original item asked what risk a reservation placed inside the active dynamic range creates, and keyed "a collision risk — unless the pool explicitly excludes the reserved address, the server may still hand that same address to a different dynamic client". Two independent defects. First, attribution: the cited dhcpd.conf(5) says nothing of the kind; searching its whole text, the only related passage is RESERVED LEASES, which describes the opposite behaviour for leases marked reserved ("the leases are not placed on the queue for allocation to other clients"). Second, and fatally, the claim is false for a current server and made distractor o2 correct. The Kea ARM, section 8.3.1, states: "In principle, a host reservation can reserve any address that belongs to the subnet. The reservations that specify addresses that belong to configured pools are called 'in-pool reservations' ... There is no formal difference in the reservation syntax and both reservation types are handled uniformly." Section 8.2 adds that only when `reservations-out-of-pool` is set true does the server "skip the reservation checks when dealing with in-pool addresses" — the default is to honour in-pool reservations, which is exactly what the old o2 asserted and the old key denied. Rewrite: the item now asks about the conflict Kea does document, in ARM section 8.3.2, where a reservation is added over an address already leased to another host. Re-checked against that section, which states that the server "cannot immediately assign the reserved address", that deleting the lease "would not solve the problem, though, because as soon as Host B gets the address, it will detect that the address is already in use (by Host A) and will send a DHCPDECLINE message", that the server "has to temporarily assign a different address from the dynamic pool", and that when the original holder renews "[t]he server will inform Host A that it is no longer allowed to use it by sending a DHCPNAK message". Key and all three distractors are settled by that passage; no distractor is also correct and every 'why' states a true fact. Shape: the rewrite leaves the key without an em-dash clause and gives o2 and o4 one each, so the file's key/distractor em-dash gap narrows rather than widens. Also repaired o3's self-refuting tail "which feels reasonable on first encounter". Citation fixed at concept level: kea-arm-dhcp4-server registered and wired into sysadmin.networking.dhcp-reservation. Noted for the ledger: the kb.isc.org dhcpd.conf page now carries a banner reading "ISC DHCP is EOL. ISC no longer maintains this software", so it remains valid for dhcpd syntax but is not a source for current server behaviour. Length balance: the rewritten key was trimmed and o3 extended so the key is not the longest option.

items.stem: A DNS query and a large file download both need to leave a host. One typically rides UDP, the other TCP. Which is which, and why does the choice matter for each?

options.text: The DNS query typically rides UDP, since a retransmitted answer arriving late is worse than useless; the file download rides TCP, since a missing byte in the middle of a file matters more than a millisecond of delay.
options.why: The trade is reliability against latency and overhead: DNS favours low-overhead speed, while bulk transfer favours guaranteed, ordered delivery even at some cost in latency.

options.text: The DNS query typically rides TCP for guaranteed delivery of the answer, while the file download rides UDP so that large files transfer with the least possible overhead, since UDP's lack of per-segment acknowledgement removes the bulk of the transfer's protocol work.
options.why: This reverses the usual choice: DNS queries commonly use UDP for low overhead, and bulk file transfer uses TCP because missing or out-of-order bytes must be corrected.

options.text: Both typically ride UDP, since neither a name lookup nor a large transfer benefits meaningfully from TCP's ordering and retransmission guarantees.
options.why: A large file transfer specifically benefits from TCP's guarantees, since a missing or reordered byte would corrupt the result; only the DNS query commonly favours UDP.

options.text: Both typically ride TCP, since every application-layer protocol on a modern network is now built exclusively on top of TCP rather than UDP.
options.why: UDP remains in wide use for exactly the applications where low overhead matters more than guaranteed delivery, DNS queries among them; not every protocol has moved to TCP.

items.rationale: TCP is connection-oriented, numbering and acknowledging every byte and retransmitting what is lost, which bulk transfer needs; UDP is connectionless, with no handshake, acknowledgement or retransmission, which suits DNS queries and other cases where speed matters more than a guarantee.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 768 states UDP is transaction oriented and 'delivery and duplicate protection are not guaranteed', while RFC 9293 sec. 1 defines TCP as providing reliable, in-order delivery -- exactly the trade the key describes. That DNS ordinarily uses UDP and only retries over TCP is settled by RFC 7766 (lines 213-216: the responder truncates a response that does not fit and the requestor may 'retry over TCP instead'). o2 reverses the assignment, o3 is refuted by the file-transfer half, o4 is refuted by UDP's continued use. No distractor is also correct; every distractor 'why' states a true fact. CITATION FIX at concept level: rfc-7766-dns-over-tcp added to sysadmin.networking.tcp-vs-udp, because neither RFC 9293 nor RFC 768 mentions DNS at all and the item turns on DNS's transport choice. o2 carried a length-padding tail ('regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved') that is a machine-paste tell; replaced with a real false claim of similar length.

items.stem: A firewall rule opens UDP port 53 for DNS but leaves TCP port 53 closed. Ordinary DNS queries succeed, but occasional large responses fail. Why does opening one protocol's port 53 not cover the other?

options.text: A service is identified by protocol and port together (TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different sockets), so an unopened TCP 53 leaves large responses, which fall back to TCP, blocked while ordinary UDP queries keep working.
options.why: The port number alone does not identify the service; the transport protocol is part of the identity, so opening UDP 53 does nothing for the separate TCP 53 socket that oversized responses use.

options.text: Opening UDP port 53 always opens TCP port 53 automatically as well, so the described failure must actually be caused by something unrelated to the firewall, most likely the resolver discarding answers that exceed its own configured response-size limit.
options.why: A firewall rule for one protocol's port does not automatically open the same port number for the other protocol; TCP 53 and UDP 53 are genuinely separate sockets requiring separate rules, and no resolver response-size setting produces the described asymmetry between small and large answers.

options.text: DNS never uses TCP under any circumstances, so a closed TCP port 53 cannot be the explanation for the large-response failures being reported.
options.why: TCP port 53 is used when a response is too large for the UDP path or for zone transfers, so DNS genuinely does use TCP in specific, expected cases.

options.text: The failure is unrelated to the firewall and is instead explained by the resolver's TTL settings being configured too aggressively for large zones.
options.why: TTL governs how long an answer is cached, not whether a large response can be delivered at all; the described symptom is explained by the closed TCP port, not by caching behaviour.

items.rationale: A service is identified by protocol and port together: TCP 53 and UDP 53 are different sockets, and a firewall rule that opens one leaves the other closed, which is exactly why a DNS server reachable for ordinary queries can still fail on the large responses that fall back to TCP.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.4.1 defines a connection by a pair of sockets, and RFC 6335 sec. 5 registers service names per transport protocol, so TCP/53 and UDP/53 are distinct registry entries and distinct sockets -- verified in the IANA registry CSV, which lists 'domain 53/tcp' and 'domain 53/udp' as separate rows. The TCP fallback for oversized answers is RFC 7766 lines 213-216. o3's 'DNS never uses TCP' is directly refuted by RFC 7766. o4's TTL claim is false. No distractor is also correct. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o2 ended in 'as commonly understood by less experienced staff, which feels reasonable on first encounter', a trailing clause announcing its own wrongness; replaced with a substantive false claim of comparable length and the 'why' extended to rebut it.

items.stem: A connection attempt to a service hangs with no response at all, while a connection to a different port on the same host is refused instantly. Reading the handshake behaviour, what does each symptom suggest?

options.text: The hang means a SYN went out and got nothing back, a silent drop usually caused by a firewall; the instant refusal means a SYN reached a live host that answered with RST because nothing was listening on that port.
options.why: Being able to name which of the three handshake messages went missing, or which response arrived, turns "it won't connect" into a specific, testable hypothesis about where the fault sits.

options.text: Both symptoms mean the same thing, that the host is unreachable, since a hang and an instant refusal are simply two presentations of the identical block, selected by how long the client's own connect timeout has been configured rather than by anything the remote host sent back.
options.why: A refusal and a silent drop are different, distinguishable outcomes: a refusal means a live host answered with RST, while a hang means nothing answered at all, usually a firewall drop; the client's connect timeout changes how long the hang lasts, not whether an RST arrives.

options.text: The hang means the TLS handshake failed after the connection was already established, while the instant refusal means the three-way handshake itself failed.
options.why: TLS negotiation happens after the three-way handshake completes; a hang before any TCP-level response at all is not a TLS failure, and an instant RST is a TCP-level response, not a TLS one.

options.text: The hang means the destination host actively chose UDP instead of TCP for that port, while the instant refusal confirms it is genuinely using TCP.
options.why: A host does not silently substitute UDP for a TCP connection attempt; the hang and refusal described are both TCP-level handshake behaviours, not a protocol switch.

items.rationale: A connection that hangs sent a SYN and got nothing back, a silent drop usually caused by a firewall, while a connection refused instantly got an RST, meaning the packet reached a live host with nothing listening on that port — the handshake is what makes these two TCP failure modes readable and distinct.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 9293 sec. 3.5.2 line 1468: 'If the connection does not exist (CLOSED), then a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment except another reset. A SYN segment that does not match an existing connection is rejected by this means.' That is exactly the instant-refusal half. The hang half is the absence of any response, which RFC 9293 does not attribute to a cause but which follows from a dropped SYN producing retransmission until timeout (sec. 3.8.1). o3 is refuted because TLS runs above a completed TCP connection; o4 is refuted because no host substitutes UDP for a TCP SYN. No distractor is also correct. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o2 ended in 'as commonly understood by less experienced staff'. The replacement deliberately avoids DROP-vs-REJECT, which would have made the distractor partly TRUE and created a second defensible answer.

items.stem: A monitoring tool reports that "the handshake failed" for a UDP-based service. Is that a meaningful statement?

options.text: No. UDP has no handshake at all, so "the handshake failed" can never accurately describe a UDP service; the report itself reflects a misunderstanding of the transport in use.
options.why: The three-way handshake is a TCP concept entirely; UDP sends datagrams with no connection setup of any kind, so there is no handshake for a UDP service to fail.

options.text: Yes — every transport protocol, TCP and UDP alike, performs an equivalent handshake before any data is exchanged between two hosts.
options.why: UDP performs no handshake of any kind; only TCP establishes a connection through the three-way SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange before data flows.

options.text: Yes, but only because the monitoring tool is referring to the TLS handshake layered on top of the UDP service rather than to the TCP handshake.
options.why: Not every UDP-based service uses TLS, and even where a UDP service does use a security layer such as DTLS, that is a separate concern from whether "the handshake failed" is a meaningful TCP-style statement.

options.text: No, but only because the report should instead say "the three-way handshake succeeded but the fourth confirmation message was lost" for a UDP service, since UDP completes its own setup exchange in four messages rather than three.
options.why: TCP's handshake is only three messages, not four, and none of it applies to UDP at all; there is no fourth confirmation message in either protocol's connection setup.

items.rationale: UDP has no handshake at all, so "the handshake failed" can never describe a UDP service — the three-way exchange of SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK is specifically how a TCP connection opens, with nothing equivalent in UDP's connectionless design.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.5 describes the three-way handshake as a TCP procedure; RFC 768 describes UDP as a datagram protocol with no connection establishment of any kind -- there is no handshake in RFC 768 at all, which is the point. o2 is false for the same reason. o3 is false because DTLS is not universal and is a separate layer. o4 is false: RFC 9293 fig. 6 shows three messages, and UDP has none. No distractor is also correct. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o4 ended in 'a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive'; replaced with a concrete false assertion about UDP setup.

items.stem: Why does a TCP connection open with three messages rather than four, given that both sides must exchange sequence numbers?

options.text: The server's single SYN-ACK does two jobs at once, acknowledging the client's SYN and sending its own SYN, which is why three messages suffice rather than four.
options.why: Each side announces an initial sequence number in its SYN, and the peer acknowledges it by returning that number plus one; combining the server's acknowledgement and its own SYN into one message is what collapses four steps into three.

options.text: Three messages suffice because only the client needs to choose an initial sequence number; the server simply echoes the client's number back unchanged in its SYN-ACK and never announces a sequence number of its own.
options.why: Each side chooses its own initial sequence number independently, including the server; the three-message count comes from combining two of the four logical steps, not from only one side needing a number.

options.text: Three messages suffice because TCP omits acknowledging the server's own SYN entirely, trusting the connection to be open once the client's ACK is sent.
options.why: The client's final ACK specifically acknowledges the server's SYN; nothing is omitted, it is simply combined with the server's own SYN into a single SYN-ACK message rather than sent separately.

options.text: Three messages suffice because closing a TCP connection also uses only three messages, and RFC 9293 requires the two counts to match.
options.why: Closing a TCP connection is a separate, usually four-message exchange of FIN and ACK in each direction, not a three-message process matched to the opening handshake's count.

items.rationale: Each side chooses an initial sequence number and announces it in its SYN, and the peer acknowledges it by returning that number plus one; the server's single SYN-ACK does both jobs at once, acknowledging the client and sending its own SYN, which is why three messages suffice rather than four.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 9293 sec. 3.5 and fig. 6, where the exchange is SYN (client ISN), SYN-ACK (server ISN plus ACK of the client's ISN), ACK -- the server's single segment carries both its own SYN and the acknowledgement, which is precisely the collapse the key describes. Sec. 3.4.1 confirms each side selects its own ISN, refuting o2. o3 is refuted because the client's final ACK does acknowledge the server's SYN (fig. 6). o4 is refuted by sec. 3.5's close sequence, which is a separate FIN/ACK exchange in each direction and is not required to match the open. No distractor is also correct. o2 carried a padding tail ('in most textbooks and quick references'); replaced with a substantive false claim.

items.stem: A packet capture shows a connection ending with FIN and ACK exchanges in both directions, after which the initiating side holds the connection open in a particular state for a period rather than releasing it immediately. What state is that, and why does it exist?

options.text: TIME_WAIT, held for twice the maximum segment lifetime so that delayed segments from the old connection cannot be mistaken for part of a new one.
options.why: Closing is a separate exchange from opening, and the side that initiates the close holds TIME_WAIT specifically to absorb any stray, delayed segments before the connection's resources are fully released.

options.text: SYN-RECV — a half-open state indicating the connection never fully completed its original handshake before being closed.
options.why: SYN-RECV describes an incomplete opening handshake, not a state following a completed close with FIN and ACK exchanges in both directions.

options.text: LISTEN — the socket returns to a listening state so it can immediately accept a new connection from the same peer.
options.why: LISTEN describes a server socket waiting for new incoming connections generally, not the specific state the initiating side of a just-closed connection holds afterward.

options.text: ESTABLISHED — the connection remains fully active for a period after the FIN and ACK exchange in case either side wants to resume sending data within the same sequence-number space.
options.why: ESTABLISHED describes an active, ongoing conversation; a connection that has completed FIN and ACK exchanges in both directions is closing, not remaining active for resumed data.

items.rationale: Closing is a separate, usually four-message exchange of FIN and ACK in each direction, after which the initiating side holds the connection in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime so that delayed segments cannot be mistaken for part of a new connection — `tcpdump`'s `[S]`, `[S.]` and `[.]` notations mark the opening SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK that precede all of this.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.3.2: 'TIME-WAIT - represents waiting for enough time to pass to be sure the remote TCP peer received the acknowledgment of its connection termination request and to avoid new connections being impacted by delayed segments from previous connections.' The 2 MSL duration is stated in sec. 3.6 fig. 12 and sec. 3.10.7, and sec. 3.4.1 explains TIME-WAIT limits the rate of connection reuse.
