EMPIRICAL: in a Docker ubuntu:24.04 container, a Python listener on 127.0.0.1:7777 with a client connect then client close gave 'ss -tan sport = :7777 or dport = :7777' output of LISTEN 127.0.0.1:7777, FIN-WAIT-2 on the closing side and CLOSE-WAIT on the peer, confirming the close is a separate four-message exchange and that the closing side does not return to LISTEN or stay ESTABLISHED. o2 (SYN-RECV), o3 (LISTEN) and o4 (ESTABLISHED) are each refuted by the sec. 3.3.2 state definitions. No distractor is also correct. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o4 ended in 'which is why the assumption spreads so easily'.

items.stem: A thousand clients connect to the same web server on port 443 at once. How does the server distinguish one client's conversation from another's, given they all target the identical port?

options.text: By the full four-tuple (source address, source port, destination address, destination port), since each client's own address and ephemeral source port make its connection unique even though the destination port is shared.
options.why: A connection is identified by the pair of sockets, and it is the client side of that pair, a different source address and ephemeral port for each client, that keeps a shared destination port unambiguous.

options.text: By destination port alone, since port 443 is defined to be unique per connection and the server simply opens a fresh port 443 instance for each new client.
options.why: The server does not open a new destination port per client; the port stays 443 for every connection, and it is the client-side address and port that make each connection distinct.

options.text: By MAC address alone, since every client's hardware address is preserved end to end and is what the server actually uses to distinguish one conversation from another.
options.why: MAC addresses are rewritten at every router and never reach the server intact from a remote client; the server identifies connections by IP address and port, not by MAC.

options.text: By TTL value alone, since each client's operating system sets a sufficiently distinct starting TTL for the server to use as a unique per-connection identifier.
options.why: TTL is a hop-count field that decrements at every router and is not designed or reliable as a connection identifier; the four-tuple of addresses and ports is what actually distinguishes connections.

items.rationale: A connection is identified by the pair of sockets: source address, source port, destination address, destination port — the four-part identity is why thousands of clients can reach the same server port simultaneously without ambiguity, since each client contributes a distinct address and ephemeral source port.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.4.1: 'A connection is defined by a pair of sockets', and its glossary (sec. 4) defines a connection as 'a logical communication path identified by a pair of sockets', each socket being an address/port pair -- i.e. the four-tuple the key names. EMPIRICAL: in a Docker ubuntu:24.04 container, 'ss -tan' during a live loopback connection showed the pair 127.0.0.1:47566 <-> 127.0.0.1:7777 alongside the LISTEN row for 127.0.0.1:7777, demonstrating that the shared destination port is disambiguated by the client's ephemeral source port. o2 is refuted because the listening port is not re-instantiated per client. o3 is true only about MAC rewriting, which is what its 'why' says -- the option's own claim (server distinguishes by MAC) is false. o4's TTL claim is false. No distractor is also correct; all distractor 'why' texts state true facts. No self-refuting padding in this item.

items.stem: `ss -tulpn` shows a process listening at `127.0.0.1:8080` and another at `0.0.0.0:9090`. A remote client can reach the second but not the first. Why?

options.text: The Local Address column decides it: `127.0.0.1` accepts only from the same machine, while `0.0.0.0` accepts on every address the host holds, including from remote clients.
options.why: The bind address in the Local Address column is exactly what determines whether a listener accepts connections from other hosts or only from itself; the port number alone does not decide reachability.

options.text: The port numbers decide it — 9090 is inherently reachable from remote hosts while 8080 is inherently restricted to local connections regardless of the bind address shown, because the kernel reserves the 8000-8999 band for loopback traffic.
options.why: No port number is inherently local-only or inherently remote-reachable; reachability is governed by the bind address in the Local Address column, not by which port number is chosen.

options.text: The process names decide it, since `ss -tulpn` restricts remote reachability based on which named process owns each socket rather than on the bound address.
options.why: `ss -tulpn`'s `-p` column reports which process owns a socket for diagnostic purposes; it does not itself restrict or grant reachability, which is governed by the bind address instead.

options.text: Whether `-n` was used decides it, since numeric output is what actually enables remote clients to reach a listening socket in the first place.
options.why: `-n` only affects whether ports are displayed numerically rather than as translated service names; it has no effect at all on which addresses a socket is actually reachable from.

items.rationale: Binding to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 is the single most common cause of "the service is running but nothing can connect," and it is invisible unless you read the Local Address column rather than just the port — 127.0.0.1 accepts only from the same machine, while 0.0.0.0 accepts on every address the host holds.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. ip(7) states: 'When INADDR_ANY is specified in the bind call, the socket will be bound to all local interfaces', and its address list gives 'INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) means any address for socket binding' and 127.0.0.1 as the loopback address that 'always refers to the local host via the loopback device'. That settles the 127.0.0.1-versus-0.0.0.0 distinction the key turns on. ss(8) confirms the distractors' mechanics: '-n, --numeric: Do not try to resolve service names' (so o4 is false) and '-p, --processes: Show processes using sockets' (a diagnostic column, so o3 is false). o2 is false: no port band is inherently local. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: man-ip-7 added to sysadmin.networking.ports-and-sockets -- ss(8) reports the Local Address column but does not define what binding to 0.0.0.0 versus 127.0.0.1 means, which is ip(7)'s territory. o2 carried a padding tail ('in every configuration seen in practice'); replaced with a substantive false claim. IP(7) RE-CHECK 2026-08-19 (documentation split): ip(7) was re-fetched and now contains 0 occurrences of "/proc/sys/net" and 0 of "ip_local_port_range" -- that table has moved to the kernel ip-sysctl document, which ip(7) SEE ALSO now points at ("The kernel source file Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst"). Every sentence THIS item attributes to ip(7) was re-verified present verbatim in the live page, so the citation is retained rather than swapped: "When INADDR_ANY is specified in the bind call, the socket will be bound to all local interfaces", "INADDR_LOOPBACK (127.0.0.1) always refers to the local host via the loopback device" and "INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) means any address for socket binding".

items.stem: An unprivileged process tries to bind port 80 directly and fails with a permission error, though the port is not in use by anything else. Why?

options.text: Ports below 1024 require privilege to bind on Linux, so a non-root process cannot simply listen on 80 regardless of whether the port is otherwise free.
options.why: The permission requirement applies to the well-known range below 1024 specifically, independent of whether the port happens to be free — it is a privilege check, not a conflict check.

options.text: The port must actually be in use by something else already, since binding failures below 1024 are always caused by an existing conflicting listener rather than by a privilege check.
options.why: The scenario states the port is not in use; the failure is a privilege requirement specific to ports below 1024, not evidence of an undetected conflicting listener.

options.text: The process must be trying to bind the wrong address family, since binding failures on low-numbered ports are typically an IPv4-versus-IPv6 mismatch rather than a privilege issue.
options.why: An address-family mismatch produces a different kind of error, not specifically a permission error; the described failure is the well-documented privilege requirement for ports below 1024.

options.text: A firewall rule must be blocking the bind attempt, since firewalls are what typically prevent an unprivileged process from binding a low-numbered port on Linux.
options.why: A firewall filters traffic in transit; it does not prevent a local process from binding a socket at all, which is a kernel-level privilege check unrelated to firewall policy.

items.rationale: Ports below 1024 require privilege to bind on Linux, which is why a non-root process cannot simply listen on 80 — the port is not "opened by the operating system," it is open because a privileged process bound it and is listening, independent of whether the port would otherwise be free.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. capabilities(7): 'CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE — Bind a socket to Internet domain privileged ports (port numbers less than 1024).' The kernel ip-sysctl documentation adds 'Privileged ports require root or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in order to bind to them.' EMPIRICAL: 'docker run --rm --sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=1024 ubuntu:24.04' then binding as user nobody gave 'PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied' for port 80 and 'BOUND' for port 8080. (The --sysctl flag was needed because Docker's own default sets ip_unprivileged_port_start=0, which is a container override, not the kernel default.) o2 is refuted by the stem's own statement that the port is free plus the fact that this is a privilege check. o3 and o4 are false; a firewall filters traffic, it does not gate bind(2). No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: man-capabilities-7 and kernel-ip-sysctl added -- neither RFC 9293 nor RFC 6335 documents Linux's privileged-port rule, which was an attribution failure.

items.stem: Where does a client's own source port typically come from when it initiates a connection, and does the administrator normally choose it?

options.text: The kernel picks an unused source port automatically from a configured ephemeral range (on Linux, from `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range`, 32768 to 60999 by default), without the administrator choosing it per connection.
options.why: The client side of a connection needs a locally unique port, and the kernel handles this automatically from its configured local port range rather than requiring manual selection.

options.text: The administrator manually assigns a fixed source port for every outbound connection a client makes, matching the destination port being contacted so that both ends of the connection use the identical port number.
options.why: Source ports are picked automatically by the kernel for outbound connections; manually assigning a fixed source port per connection is neither the default nor the ordinary practice.

options.text: The source port always matches the destination port, so a connection to port 443 automatically uses source port 443 as well on the client side.
options.why: The client's source port is an arbitrary ephemeral value chosen by the kernel, unrelated to the destination port; source and destination ports are not required to match.

options.text: DHCP assigns the source port to the client alongside its IP address, gateway and DNS servers as part of the same lease.
options.why: DHCP assigns addressing configuration only — address, mask, gateway, DNS servers; it has no role in choosing a source port, which the kernel selects per connection instead.

items.rationale: A client's kernel picks an unused source port automatically — on Linux from the range in `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range`, 32768 to 60999 by default — and connects to the server's address and port, with no manual per-connection selection required.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, including the exact numbers. Kernel ip-sysctl documentation, ip_local_port_range: 'Defines the local port range that is used by TCP and UDP to choose the local port... The default values are 32768 and 60999 respectively.' ip(7) confirms the automatic behaviour: 'When connect(2) is called on an unbound socket, the socket is automatically bound to a random free port'. EMPIRICAL: 'cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range' in ubuntu:24.04 returned '32768\t60999', and an observed outbound connection used source port 47566. o2, o3 and o4 are each false; DHCP assigns addressing only. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: kernel-ip-sysctl added. NOTE ON A SOURCE THAT NO LONGER CARRIES THE CLAIM: man7.org's ip(7) no longer documents any /proc/sys/net/ipv4 file -- a grep of the fetched page for '/proc/sys/net' returns nothing and only 'IP_LOCAL_PORT_RANGE(2const)', a socket option, is cross-referenced. ip(7) is therefore not a valid citation for the 32768-60999 default; the kernel documentation is. IP(7) RE-CHECK 2026-08-19 (documentation split): ip(7) was re-fetched and now contains 0 occurrences of "/proc/sys/net" and 0 of "ip_local_port_range" -- that table has moved to the kernel ip-sysctl document, which ip(7) SEE ALSO now points at ("The kernel source file Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst"). Every sentence THIS item attributes to ip(7) was re-verified present verbatim in the live page, so the citation is retained rather than swapped: "When connect(2) is called on an unbound socket, the socket is automatically bound to a random free port". The 32768-60999 range was already sourced to the kernel ip-sysctl document, which is where it still lives, so the split costs this item nothing.

items.stem: A study note lists 3306 (MySQL) and 5432 (PostgreSQL) as "well-known ports" alongside 22 and 443. Using the strict IANA range definitions, is that labelling correct?

options.text: No. Strictly, only 0-1023 is the well-known range; 3306 and 5432 both sit above 1023 in the 1024-49151 registered range, so they are registered ports, not well-known ones, however familiar they are.
options.why: The terminology trap is exactly this: 3306, 3389 and 5432 sit above 1023, so they are registered ports, not well-known ones, regardless of how commonly they are used.

options.text: Yes — any port number that is commonly recognised and consistently used for one particular service, like MySQL or PostgreSQL, qualifies as well-known by that usage alone.
options.why: Common recognition and consistent use do not define the well-known range; that range is strictly 0-1023 by IANA definition, and 3306 and 5432 fall outside it in the registered range.

options.text: No, but only because 3306 and 5432 are actually dynamic or ephemeral ports, in the 49152-65535 range, rather than registered ones.
options.why: 3306 and 5432 fall in the 1024-49151 registered range, well below the 49152-65535 dynamic range; the correct correction is registered, not dynamic.

options.text: Yes, but only for 3306, since 5432 alone falls below 1024 and genuinely belongs in the well-known range while 3306 does not.
options.why: Neither 3306 nor 5432 falls below 1024; both are above it, in the registered range, so neither one genuinely belongs in the well-known range.

items.rationale: Strictly, IANA calls only 0-1023 the well-known or system range; 1024-49151 are registered ports and 49152-65535 are the dynamic or private range — 3306, 3389 and 5432 sit above 1023, so they are registered ports, not well-known ones, however familiar they are.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 6335 sec. 6: 'the System Ports, also known as the Well Known Ports, from 0-1023 (assigned by IANA); the User Ports, also known as the Registered Ports, from 1024-49151 (assigned by IANA); the Dynamic Ports, also known as the Private or Ephemeral Ports, from 49152-65535 (never assigned)'. The IANA registry CSV lists 'mysql 3306/tcp' and 'postgresql 5432/tcp', both inside 1024-49151, so both are registered, not well-known. o2 is refuted because the range is numeric, not reputational. o3 is refuted because 3306 and 5432 are below 49152. o4 is refuted because 5432 is above 1023. No distractor is also correct; all distractor 'why' texts are true. Minor note, not a defect: the key's 'why' mentions 3389, which does not appear in the stem; it is a true statement (3389/tcp ms-wbt-server is likewise registered) so it misleads nobody.

items.stem: Match the well-known port numbers to their conventional services: 22, 25, 53, 80, 143, 443.

options.text: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS, each the conventional assignment recognised in the well-known range.
options.why: These are exactly the conventional service-to-port assignments an administrator is expected to recognise on sight in the well-known 0-1023 range.

options.text: 22 HTTP, 25 SSH, 53 SMTP, 80 DNS, 143 HTTPS, 443 IMAP — each service shifted one position down the list from its actual conventional port.
options.why: Every pairing here is shifted one position off from the actual conventional assignment; 22 is SSH, not HTTP, and the pattern continues that way down the list.

options.text: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 143 IMAP, 443 MySQL — matching the first five correctly but naming a registered-range service for the last one.
options.why: 443 is conventionally HTTPS, not MySQL; MySQL's conventional assignment is 3306, a registered port entirely outside this list.

options.text: 22 SSH, 25 DNS, 53 SMTP, 80 HTTP, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS — swapping the conventional assignments of 25 and 53 relative to their actual services.
options.why: 25 is conventionally SMTP and 53 is conventionally DNS; this pairing has those two specifically swapped relative to their correct assignments.

items.rationale: The conventional well-known assignments worth memorising include 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 143 IMAP and 443 HTTPS, all within the 0-1023 well-known range, with `ss -tulpn` remaining the only authoritative statement about what a given host is actually listening on.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the IANA Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry CSV, filtered on TCP: 'ssh 22/tcp The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol', 'smtp 25/tcp Simple Mail Transfer', 'domain 53/tcp Domain Name Server', 'http 80/tcp World Wide Web HTTP', 'imap 143/tcp Internet Message Access Protocol', 'https 443/tcp http protocol over TLS/SSL'. All six sit in 0-1023, which RFC 6335 sec. 6 defines as the well-known range, so the key's framing is accurate rather than merely conventional. o2 shifts every pairing, o3 substitutes MySQL for 443 (mysql is 3306/tcp in the registry), o4 swaps 25 and 53. No distractor is also correct; all distractor 'why' texts are true. No self-refuting padding.

items.stem: A security review finds SSH answering on port 2222 on one server instead of port 22. A reviewer argues this cannot really be SSH, since SSH "is" port 22. Is that reasoning sound?

options.text: No, nothing forces a service onto its conventional port; SSH can genuinely run on 2222, and a port number is evidence about intent, never proof of protocol.
options.why: A port number is a convention, not an enforced binding between protocol and number; running SSH on a nonstandard port is a common, deliberate practice, and `ss -tulpn` combined with actually probing the service is what confirms what is really there.

options.text: Yes — a service can only ever run on its officially registered port number, so anything answering on 2222 must be a different protocol entirely.
options.why: No enforcement mechanism binds a protocol to its conventional port number; SSH, like many services, can be configured to listen on any port an administrator chooses.

options.text: No, but only because 2222 is itself a second officially registered port for SSH alongside 22, so both numbers are equally valid by definition.
options.why: 2222 is not a second registered assignment for SSH; it is simply a commonly chosen nonstandard port, not an alternate official one.

options.text: Yes, but only because a well-known port and its service are bound together specifically by the operating system's kernel, unlike a registered port such as this one.
options.why: The kernel does not bind any port number to a specific protocol or service at all; a well-known port carries only a lower binding privilege requirement, not a protocol-enforcement mechanism.

items.rationale: Nothing forces a service onto its conventional port — SSH on 2222 is still SSH — so a port number is evidence about intent, never proof of protocol; `ss -tulpn` shows only which of the conventional assignments a host is actually listening on, not a guarantee about what protocol answers there.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 6335 governs the registry, not host behaviour: sec. 7.2 assigns port numbers to service names but nothing in the document binds a running process to its assigned number, and Linux enforces only the privilege boundary at 1024 (capabilities(7), CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE), never a protocol identity -- which settles o4. o3 is checked directly and refuted: the IANA registry lists 2222/tcp as 'EtherNet/IP-1 (EtherNet/IP I/O)', not as a second SSH assignment. o2 is refuted by the same absence of any enforcement mechanism. No distractor is also correct. No self-refuting padding.

items.stem: A client's outbound connection uses source port 51000. Does that number fall inside IANA's dynamic/private range, 49152-65535?

options.text: Yes, it does, but note that Linux's default ephemeral range, 32768 to 60999, overlaps the registered range rather than matching IANA's dynamic range exactly, so a source port can also land below 49152 in the registered band.
options.why: 51000 does fall in IANA's 49152-65535 dynamic range, but the more testable fact is that Linux's actual default ephemeral range often produces source ports below 49152, inside the registered band, contrary to a naive reading of the IANA ranges alone.

options.text: No — client source ports are always assigned somewhere within the well-known 0-1023 range regardless of what Linux's ephemeral range configuration says.
options.why: Client source ports are ephemeral values from a much higher range; the well-known 0-1023 range is for service ports requiring privilege to bind, not for a client's outbound source port.

options.text: No — 51000 falls in the registered range, 1024-49151, since IANA defines that range to extend up to the top of the operating system's default ephemeral window, 60999 on Linux, rather than stopping at the nominal 49151 boundary printed in older tables.
options.why: The registered range is defined as 1024-49151 by IANA; 51000 is numerically above that boundary and falls in the 49152-65535 dynamic range as stated, not inside the registered one.

options.text: The question is unanswerable, since IANA does not actually define a fixed numeric boundary for where the dynamic or private port range begins.
options.why: IANA does define a fixed boundary, 49152, for the start of the dynamic/private range; the boundary is well defined even though Linux's actual default ephemeral range does not align with it exactly.

items.rationale: Linux's default ephemeral range, 32768 to 60999, overlaps the registered range rather than matching IANA's 49152-65535 dynamic range, so a client's source port frequently lands on a number the registry has assigned to something else — a source port of 51000 does sit in IANA's dynamic band, but many others in practice will not.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on both halves. RFC 6335 sec. 6 puts 49152-65535 in the Dynamic/Private range, so 51000 is inside it. The second, subtler half is confirmed by the kernel ip-sysctl documentation: ip_local_port_range 'default values are 32768 and 60999 respectively', which straddles 49152. EMPIRICAL: 'cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range' returned '32768\t60999' in ubuntu:24.04, and an actual outbound loopback connection observed under 'ss -tan' used source port 47566 -- below 49152, inside IANA's registered band, exactly as the key claims. o2 is false, o3 is false (49151 is the registered ceiling), o4 is false (RFC 6335 does fix the boundary). No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: kernel-ip-sysctl added to sysadmin.networking.well-known-ports; RFC 6335 and the IANA registry say nothing about Linux's ephemeral range and the key's whole point depends on it. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o3 ended in 'in the overwhelming majority of real deployments, a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive'.

items.stem: Two questions arrive about the same server: "is the service even running?" and "is anyone actually using it right now?" Which `ss` invocation answers each?

options.text: The two are mutually exclusive views of the same table: `ss -tulpn` answers whether it is running, by showing the LISTEN socket, while `ss -t state established` answers who is using it, by showing active ESTAB connections.
options.why: "Is the service running and accepting connections" is answered by the presence of a LISTEN socket, while "is anyone actually using it" is answered by established connections, and combining `-l` with a state filter is not meaningful because they select opposite things.

options.text: `ss -tulpn` alone answers both questions simultaneously, since its `-l` flag is defined to include every established connection alongside the listening sockets.
options.why: `-l` restricts output to listening sockets specifically and deliberately excludes established connections, so `ss -tulpn` alone cannot answer who is currently connected.

options.text: `ss -t state established` alone answers both questions, since a service with any established connections is thereby proven to also be listening.
options.why: A service can have zero established connections while still listening perfectly well; established connections alone do not confirm a listener is present, only that some past connections succeeded.

options.text: Neither command answers either question; only reading application logs directly can determine whether a service is running or in use.
options.why: `ss -tulpn` and `ss -t state established` are specifically designed to answer these two questions from the socket table directly, without needing to consult application logs at all.

items.rationale: `ss -tulpn` shows listening sockets, answering whether a service is running and accepting connections, while `ss -t state established` filters to TCP connections in the ESTAB state, answering who is actually using it — a service can be listening with zero clients, or have established connections while its listener is misconfigured elsewhere.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. ss(8) OPTIONS: '-l, --listening: Display only listening sockets (these are omitted by default)' and '-a, --all: Display both listening and non-listening (for TCP this means established connections) sockets'; its STATE-FILTER section lists 'established' as a valid identifier and defines 'connected' as 'all the states except for listening and closed', which is the documentary basis for the key's claim that the two views are mutually exclusive. EMPIRICAL: in ubuntu:24.04, 'ss -tanl' on a listener showed only the LISTEN row, while 'ss -tan' during a live connection showed LISTEN plus two ESTAB rows -- the -l view genuinely excludes the established ones. o2 is directly refuted by the '-l' text. o3 is refuted because a listener with zero clients still shows LISTEN. o4 is false. No distractor is also correct; every distractor 'why' is true. No self-refuting padding.

items.stem: A UDP-based service shows a socket in the ESTAB state under `ss`. A colleague treats this as proof a negotiated connection with a remote peer exists, the same as it would for TCP. Is that a safe reading?

options.text: No. A UDP socket showing ESTAB only records that its application called `connect()` to fix a default peer locally; unlike TCP, it involved no handshake and proves nothing about the far end.
options.why: That ESTAB is only a local socket property — a default destination the kernel records — not a negotiated connection, which is the key difference from TCP's ESTAB state.

options.text: Yes — ESTAB means exactly the same thing for UDP as it does for TCP: a fully negotiated, bidirectionally confirmed connection with the remote peer.
options.why: UDP has no handshake to negotiate anything with a peer; a UDP socket's ESTAB state is purely a local record of a fixed default destination, not a confirmed remote conversation.

options.text: No, but only because UDP sockets are never permitted to display ESTAB at all, so the tool output itself must be misreporting the socket's actual state.
options.why: A UDP socket whose application has called `connect()` to a single peer genuinely does show ESTAB; the output is not a misreport, it is simply a different, weaker meaning than TCP's ESTAB carries.

options.text: Yes, but only if the socket is also shown holding a LISTEN state at the same time, which together would confirm a genuine remote conversation.
options.why: LISTEN and ESTAB are mutually exclusive states in `ss` output for a given socket entry, not something that can be shown together to reinforce one another.

items.rationale: A UDP socket bound with no fixed peer shows UNCONN; one whose application has called `connect()` to a single peer shows ESTAB, but that ESTAB is only a local socket property, a default destination the kernel records, not a negotiated connection — unlike TCP it involved no handshake and proves nothing about the far end.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed EMPIRICALLY as well as by documentation. In a Docker ubuntu:24.04 container: one UDP socket bound to 127.0.0.1:9999 and a second bound to 127.0.0.1:9998 that called connect() to 127.0.0.1:9999; 'ss -uan' then printed 'ESTAB 0 0 127.0.0.1:9998 127.0.0.1:9999' and 'UNCONN 0 0 127.0.0.1:9999 0.0.0.0:*'. No packet was ever sent, so the ESTAB is purely the local effect of connect(), exactly as the key states. ip(7) supplies the mechanism: connect(2) on a UDP socket fixes the default peer. RFC 768 defines no handshake at all, so nothing was negotiated. o2 is refuted by that absence. o3 is refuted by the observed ESTAB row itself. o4 is refuted by ss(8)'s STATE-FILTER, where 'connected' is defined as all states except listening and closed, making LISTEN and ESTAB disjoint. No distractor is also correct. No self-refuting padding. ATTRIBUTION FIX 2026-08-19: the reasoning credited ip(7) with the UDP default-peer mechanism. ip(7) was re-fetched (17.5 KB of text) and contains 0 occurrences of "default peer" -- it documents only that connect(2) auto-binds a free local port. connect(2) is the page that states it, and is now cited: "If the socket sockfd is of type SOCK_DGRAM, then addr is the address to which datagrams are sent by default, and the only address from which datagrams are received." The empirical ESTAB observation and the RFC 768 no-handshake point are unaffected.

items.stem: `ss -tulpn` shows a service in the LISTEN state at `127.0.0.1:8080`, and a load balancer reports the connection refused rather than timing out. What does the refusal, as opposed to a timeout, tell you?

options.text: The refusal tells you the load balancer's SYN reached a host with nothing listening on that specific address; the service is up but bound to loopback only, so it answers with RST when addressed from elsewhere.
options.why: A listening socket bound to 127.0.0.1 shows up in `ss -tulpn` exactly like one bound to 0.0.0.0, so a service that "is listening" can still be unreachable from every other host, producing exactly this refusal pattern.

options.text: The refusal tells you the packet never reached the server at all, which would instead be the expected behaviour if a firewall were silently dropping the traffic, since a refusal and a timeout are produced by the same rule and differ only in how quickly the client gives up waiting.
options.why: A refusal specifically means a packet reached a live host that answered with RST; a silent firewall drop produces a timeout instead, the opposite symptom from what is described here.

options.text: The refusal tells you the service crashed between the LISTEN check and the load balancer's connection attempt, which is the only explanation for an instant RST.
options.why: A crashed service would also close its listening socket, but the scenario shows a working LISTEN entry; the far more direct explanation, consistent with both facts, is the loopback-only bind address.

options.text: The refusal tells you DNS resolved the load balancer to the wrong address, which is a name-resolution failure rather than a connection-level one.
options.why: The scenario describes a TCP-level refusal after reaching a host, not a resolution failure; DNS is a separate layer entirely from the reachability described here.

items.rationale: A listening socket bound to 127.0.0.1 shows up in `ss -tulpn` exactly like one bound to 0.0.0.0, so a service that 'is listening' can still be unreachable from every other host — from the server itself the handshake completes, but from elsewhere the SYN reaches a host with nothing listening on that address and is answered with RST, reported as refused rather than timed out.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.5.2: 'If the connection does not exist (CLOSED), then a reset is sent in response to any incoming segment except another reset. A SYN segment that does not match an existing connection is rejected by this means.' A listener bound to 127.0.0.1 does not exist as a connection endpoint for a segment arriving on an external address, so the RST is exactly what the key predicts. ip(7) supplies the binding semantics: 127.0.0.1 'always refers to the local host via the loopback device', while INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) 'means any address for socket binding'. o2 is refuted by the same RFC text: a drop produces no response at all, hence a timeout. o3 is refuted by the surviving LISTEN entry. o4 is a different layer. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: man-ip-7 added; ss(8) shows the Local Address column but does not define loopback-versus-any binding. o2 carried a padding tail ('as a matter of routine operational practice, regardless of which distribution or vendor is involved'); replaced with a substantive false claim, deliberately not the DROP-versus-REJECT distinction, which is true and would have made the distractor defensible. IP(7) RE-CHECK 2026-08-19 (documentation split): ip(7) was re-fetched and now contains 0 occurrences of "/proc/sys/net" and 0 of "ip_local_port_range" -- that table has moved to the kernel ip-sysctl document, which ip(7) SEE ALSO now points at ("The kernel source file Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst"). Every sentence THIS item attributes to ip(7) was re-verified present verbatim in the live page, so the citation is retained rather than swapped: "INADDR_LOOPBACK (127.0.0.1) always refers to the local host via the loopback device" and "INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) means any address for socket binding".

items.stem: A `ss` state column shows CLOSE-WAIT for a connection. What does that state typically indicate, and is it usually a network problem?

options.text: It typically indicates the peer closed the connection but the local application has not yet closed its end, usually an application bug rather than a network problem.
options.why: CLOSE-WAIT specifically means the far side has finished and sent FIN, but the local process has not called close() on its own socket, which is an application-level oversight rather than a network fault.

options.text: It typically indicates a firewall dropped the connection's traffic mid-stream, which is why the local side is shown waiting to close.
options.why: CLOSE-WAIT is not caused by a firewall drop; it reflects that the peer has already closed cleanly and the local application simply has not finished closing its own end yet.

options.text: It typically indicates the connection is still in the process of being established and has not yet completed its three-way handshake.
options.why: A connection still establishing shows SYN-SENT or SYN-RECV, not CLOSE-WAIT, which specifically applies after the peer has already sent FIN on an established connection.

options.text: It typically indicates high packet loss on the path, since a poor connection is what most commonly forces a socket into the CLOSE-WAIT state while the kernel retries the lost segments.
options.why: Packet loss is not what produces CLOSE-WAIT; that state follows a legitimately received FIN from the peer combined with the local application not yet closing its own socket.

items.rationale: Between LISTEN and ESTAB lie transient states worth recognising, including CLOSE-WAIT, where the peer closed but the local application has not, which usually indicates an application bug rather than a network one — distinct from a large but normal number of TIME-WAIT entries on a busy server, which is not a leak.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9293 sec. 3.3.2 defines 'CLOSE-WAIT - represents waiting for a connection termination request from the local user', i.e. the peer's FIN has been received and acknowledged and the local application has not yet called close() -- an application-level omission, which is the key's exact claim. EMPIRICAL: in ubuntu:24.04, a Python server accepted a loopback connection and the client called close() without the server closing; 'ss -tan sport = :7777 or dport = :7777' then showed 'FIN-WAIT-2' on the client side and 'CLOSE-WAIT 1 0 127.0.0.1:7777 127.0.0.1:47566' on the server side, with no packet loss and no firewall involved. That single observation refutes o2 and o4 directly. o3 is refuted by sec. 3.3.2's SYN-SENT and SYN-RECEIVED definitions. No distractor is also correct. SELF-REFUTING DISTRACTOR REPAIRED: o4 ended in 'an assumption that holds until it does not'.

items.stem: A request to an internal API returns HTTP 502. A junior engineer treats this as the API server itself reporting an error. Is that the right way to read a 502?

options.text: No: 502 is a gateway or proxy reporting a bad or missing answer from the server behind it, not the origin server answering for itself; the investigation should look at the proxy and what lies behind it.
options.why: Knowing that 502 and 504 are by definition a gateway or proxy reporting a problem with the server behind it, rather than that server answering for itself, redirects an investigation immediately toward the right component.

options.text: Yes — any 5xx status code is generated exclusively by the origin application server itself, regardless of whether a proxy or load balancer sits in front of it, because an intermediary is required to pass an upstream status code through untouched.
options.why: 502 specifically originates from a gateway or proxy reporting trouble with the server behind it; the origin application server did not necessarily generate this particular response at all.

options.text: No, but only because 502 actually indicates a client-side error, the same category of problem a 4xx status code represents, mislabeled under the 5xx range.
options.why: 502 falls squarely in the 5xx range, meaning the server side is blamed, not the client; it is not a mislabeled 4xx-style client error.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is always to clear the client's browser cache, since 502 responses are commonly caused by stale cached content on the requesting side.
options.why: A 502 is generated by a gateway reporting a problem with an upstream server; clearing a client-side cache addresses a different class of issue entirely and would not resolve this.

items.rationale: The status code is the fastest classifier available: 2xx succeeded, 3xx redirected, 4xx blamed the client, 5xx blamed the server — and specifically, 502 and 504 are by definition a gateway or proxy reporting a bad or missing answer from the server behind it, not that server answering for itself.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim. RFC 9110 sec. 15.6.3: 'The 502 (Bad Gateway) status code indicates that the server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an inbound server it accessed while attempting to fulfill the request.' The key's aside about 504 is likewise correct (sec. 15.6.5, Gateway Timeout, same gateway framing). o2 is refuted by that same sentence -- the response is generated by the intermediary. o3 is refuted by sec. 15.6, 'The 5xx (Server Error) class of status code indicates that the server is aware that it has erred', which is a server-side, not client-side, classification. o4 is false. No distractor is also correct. o2 carried a padding tail ('by default on most systems administrators encounter'); replaced with a substantive false claim.

items.stem: `curl -I https://example.com` is run to confirm a site responds, and it returns `301` with no body shown. A colleague reports the site is down. Is that conclusion supported?

options.text: No — 301 is a redirect, not a failure; without `-L`, `curl` stops there by design, and the site is answering exactly as configured.
options.why: Reading a 301 as a failure is a documented trap: it is a redirect, and the server responded correctly — `curl -L` would follow it to see the final destination.

options.text: Yes — any status code other than exactly 200 returned by `curl -I` is defined to indicate the site is unreachable or malfunctioning.
options.why: A 3xx status is a normal, successful classification of response, a redirect, not evidence of unreachability; only certain other ranges, like 5xx, indicate a server-side problem.

options.text: No, but only because `curl -I` is fundamentally the wrong tool to use here, and `wget` would have returned a success status instead for the identical request.
options.why: `wget` against the same URL would show the same redirect behaviour; the issue is not tool choice but correctly interpreting a 3xx status as a redirect rather than a failure.

options.text: Yes, since a HEAD request, which `curl -I` issues, is defined to always fail with a 301 status regardless of how the server is actually configured.
options.why: A HEAD request does not inherently produce a 301; the server's own redirect configuration is what causes this particular status, and many HEAD requests return 200 without issue.

items.rationale: `curl -I` issues a HEAD request and reports the status line the server returns; reading a 301 as a failure is a documented trap, since it is a redirect and, without `-L`, curl stops there by design rather than following it.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on both halves. RFC 9110 sec. 15.4.2: 'The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI' -- a redirect, not a failure. curl(1) supplies the tool half, which RFC 9110 cannot: '-I, --head: Fetch the headers only' and '-L, --location: If the server reports that the requested page has moved to a different location (indicated with a Location: header and a 3XX response code), this option makes curl redo the request to the new place'. Since -L is opt-in, curl stopping at the 301 is by design, as the key says. o2 is refuted by sec. 15.4. o3 is false; wget follows the same server-side redirect. o4 is false; curl(1) documents HEAD as an ordinary method with no inherent status. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: curl-manpage added to sysadmin.networking.http-and-https, because the item's operative claim is about curl's default redirect behaviour, which RFC 9110 does not and could not document -- a straightforward attribution failure.

items.stem: A site returns HTTP 200 for a request, but the page shown is an internal error message rather than the expected content. An automated monitor reports the site as healthy based on the status code alone. What is being missed?

options.text: A 200 response proves the server answered, not that the answer is correct — an error page returned with status 200 is a common misconfiguration that status-code-only monitoring misses entirely.
options.why: The status code classifies the type of response, but nothing about a 200 guarantees the body is the intended content; a server can return an error page while still reporting success at the protocol level.

options.text: Nothing is being missed — a 200 status code is defined to guarantee the response body is correct and matches what the client expected to receive.
options.why: A 200 status guarantees only that the server successfully processed and returned a response; it says nothing about whether the body content is the intended, correct content.

options.text: The monitor is missing the TLS certificate check, since an expired certificate would be the only explanation for an error page appearing under a 200 status, because a client presents a certificate failure as a 200 response carrying an error body.
options.why: A TLS certificate problem would typically prevent the connection from completing at all, or trigger a browser warning outside the HTTP response; it does not explain a 200-status page showing internal error content.

options.text: The monitor is missing the DNS TTL, since a low TTL is what causes a server to occasionally return its internal error page instead of the real content.
options.why: DNS TTL governs how long a resolved address is cached; it has no bearing on whether the server's application logic returns an error page under a 200 status.

items.rationale: A 200 response proves the server answered, not that the answer is correct — an error page returned with status 200 is a common misconfiguration that automated checks relying on the status code alone will miss, since nothing about a successful HTTP transaction guarantees the content is right.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. RFC 9110 sec. 15.3.1: 'The 200 (OK) status code indicates that the request has succeeded. The content sent in a 200 response depends on the request method' -- the specification ties 200 to the request having succeeded at the protocol level and says nothing about the content being semantically correct, which is precisely the gap the key names. o2 is refuted by that same text. o3 is refuted because a TLS failure aborts the connection during the handshake and never produces an HTTP status at all. o4 is refuted because DNS TTL governs address caching. No distractor is also correct. o3 carried a padding tail ('across virtually every environment of this kind'); replaced with a substantive false claim of similar length.

items.stem: Does HTTPS hide which host a client is talking to, given that the request and response bodies are encrypted?

options.text: No — the destination IP address is visible by definition, and the server name is normally sent in the clear in the TLS SNI extension, so HTTPS encrypts content but not the fact of which host is being contacted.
options.why: Encryption applies to the request and response content; the destination address and, typically, the SNI-carried server name remain visible on the wire, which is a commonly missed distinction.

options.text: Yes — HTTPS encrypts every part of the exchange, including the destination IP address and any server name information sent during connection setup, because the TLS handshake completes before any addressing or naming information is placed on the wire.
options.why: The destination IP address is necessarily visible for routing to work at all, and the server name is normally sent in the clear in the TLS SNI extension; neither is hidden by HTTPS.

options.text: No, but only because HTTPS hides the destination IP address specifically while leaving the server name fully visible in every case.
options.why: The destination IP address is inherently visible for routing, not specifically hidden by HTTPS; it is the server name, via SNI, that is normally visible in the clear, not concealed either.

options.text: Yes, but only for connections using TLS 1.3, since earlier TLS versions leave both the destination address and server name fully exposed.
options.why: The visibility of the destination address is a routing necessity independent of TLS version, and SNI is commonly sent in the clear across TLS versions in ordinary configurations.

items.rationale: HTTPS encrypts the request and response, but it does not hide which host is being talked to: the destination IP is visible by definition, and the server name is normally sent in the clear in the TLS SNI extension.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and the citation had to be corrected to reach it. RFC 8744 sec. 1: 'The SNI extension is carried in cleartext in the TLS ClientHello message', and sec. 1 further notes that as other monitoring is blocked 'monitoring focuses on the cleartext SNI' -- the exact claim the key makes. I searched the whole of RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, 338 KB) for a statement that SNI is unencrypted and found none stated that plainly, so I did not rest the item on it; RFC 8744 is a document devoted to the problem and states it directly. The destination-IP half follows from routing and is not in dispute. o2, o3 and o4 are each refuted by the same sentence plus the routing necessity; o4's TLS-1.3 caveat is wrong because ClientHello SNI is cleartext in TLS 1.3 too absent ECH. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: rfc-8744-sni-encryption added to sysadmin.networking.http-and-https; RFC 9110 is HTTP semantics and contains no TLS extension material, so the item was previously unsourced for its central claim. o2 carried a doubled padding tail; replaced with a substantive false claim.

items.stem: An administrator generates a key pair with `ssh-keygen` and then needs to enable key-based login to a remote server. Which file gets copied to the server, and with which command?

options.text: Only the public key file — using `ssh-copy-id`, which logs in with an existing method and appends the public key to the remote `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
options.why: Only the public half of the key pair ever leaves the client; `ssh-copy-id` is the tool designed to install it in the right place on the remote host.

options.text: The private key file — using `scp`, so that the server holds the same secret material the client uses to authenticate itself.
options.why: The private key must never leave the client; copying it to the server undermines the entire point of key-based authentication, and only the public key is meant to be shared.

options.text: Both the public and private key files — using `sftp`, so the server has a complete, matching copy of the client's key pair on file and can verify a login against either half of it.
options.why: The server needs only the public key to verify a login; sending the private key as well defeats the security model entirely, regardless of which transfer tool is used.

options.text: Neither key file — `ssh-copy-id` instead generates a brand-new key pair directly on the remote server during the copy process.
options.why: `ssh-copy-id` installs an existing local public key on the remote host; it does not generate a new key pair on the server as part of that process.

items.rationale: `ssh-keygen` generates a key pair, writing the private key to a file and the public key to a matching `.pub` file, and `ssh-copy-id` logs in using an existing method and appends that public key to the remote `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` — only the public half ever leaves the client.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against ssh-copy-id(1), which had to be added as a source: 'By default it adds the keys by appending them to the remote user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (creating the file, and directory, if necessary)', and under -i, 'If the filename does not end in .pub this is added' -- so even when an administrator points ssh-copy-id at a private key filename, the tool installs the .pub half. sshd(8) confirms the receiving side: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys 'Lists the public keys (ECDSA, Ed25519, RSA) that can be used for logging in as this user.' o2 and o3 are refuted by that: the server never needs, and must never hold, the private key. o4 is refuted by ssh-copy-id(1)'s description, which installs existing keys and never generates any. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: openssh-ssh-copy-id and openssh-sshd-8 added to sysadmin.networking.ssh -- ssh(1), the only man page previously cited, documents neither ssh-copy-id nor authorized_keys, which is the man-page attribution trap for this concept. o3 carried a padding tail ('under the great majority of ordinary configurations'); replaced with a substantive false claim.

items.stem: A user with correctly configured SSH keys is unexpectedly prompted for a password every time they connect, though the same key worked on another server. Their home directory on this server is world-writable. What is the likely cause?

options.text: SSH refuses key authentication silently if permissions are too open — `~/.ssh` should be 700 and `authorized_keys` 600, and a world-writable home directory alone can cause a fall back to password prompts.
options.why: This is a documented, specific behaviour: SSH silently declines key authentication under loose permissions rather than producing an obvious error, leading many administrators to suspect the key itself instead.

options.text: The public key was never actually copied to this server at all, since a working key on one server has no bearing on whether it was installed on another.
options.why: This is possible in general, but the scenario specifically flags a world-writable home directory, which is the documented, more likely cause of a silent fall back to password prompts.

options.text: The server's host key has changed since the last connection, which is what triggers SSH to silently fall back to password authentication instead of raising a warning.
options.why: A changed host key produces a loud, explicit warning about the change, not a silent fall back to password prompts; it is a separate class of event from the permission issue described.

options.text: The remote server is using the legacy SCP protocol instead of SFTP underneath, which is what causes key authentication to be silently skipped for logins.
options.why: Whether `scp` uses the legacy SCP protocol or SFTP underneath affects file transfer only, not interactive login authentication, which is governed separately by key and permission checks.

items.rationale: SSH refuses key authentication silently if permissions are too open: `~/.ssh` should be 700 and `authorized_keys` 600, and a world-writable home directory alone can cause a fall back to password prompts, which is a frequent and confusing source of 'permission denied' or unexpected password-prompt reports.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and the source that settles it is sshd(8), not ssh(1). sshd(8) FILES, on ~/.ssh/authorized_keys: 'If this file, the ~/.ssh directory, or the user's home directory are writable by other users, then the file could be modified or replaced by unauthorized users. In this case, sshd will not allow it to be used unless the StrictModes option has been set to "no".' That is precisely the key's claim, including that a world-writable HOME DIRECTORY alone is sufficient. The specific modes are also documented: for ~/.ssh/, 'the recommended permissions are read/write/execute for the user, and not accessible by others' (0700); for authorized_keys, 'the recommended permissions are read/write for the user, and not accessible by others' (0600). o2 is possible in the abstract but is not the scenario's flagged cause, and its 'why' says so honestly. o3 is refuted because a changed host key produces a loud WARNING banner, not a silent fallback. o4 is refuted because the SCP-versus-SFTP backend affects file transfer only. No distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX: openssh-sshd-8 added at concept level; ssh(1) is the client page and documents none of this.

items.stem: A user runs `scp -p 2222 report.tar.gz user@web01:/tmp/` against a host whose SSH daemon listens on port 2222. Rather than transferring, `scp` reports `stat local "2222": No such file or directory`. What is wrong, and what should they run instead?

options.text: `scp` spells the port flag with a capital `-P`, not lowercase `-p`; lowercase `-p` is a valid flag that preserves times and mode bits, so `2222` was parsed as a source filename. The corrected command is `scp -P 2222 report.tar.gz user@web01:/tmp/`.
options.why: `ssh` uses `-p` for a non-default port while `scp` uses `-P`; scp(1) says the capital is used "because -p is already reserved for preserving the times and mode bits of the file", which is why the lowercase form fails as a missing-file error rather than as an invalid flag.

options.text: The remote path is missing a second colon, and the corrected command needs `user@web01::/tmp/` with two colons before the destination path.
options.why: `scp`'s remote path syntax uses a single colon between the host and the path; the actual error here is the port flag's case, which pushed `2222` into the source-file list, not the number of colons used.

options.text: `scp` does not support a port option at all, and the fix is to first open an `ssh` session on port 2222 and then transfer the file manually from within that already-authenticated remote shell session.
options.why: `scp` does support specifying a nonstandard port; it simply uses the capital `-P` flag rather than lowercase `-p`, so a separate manual `ssh` session is not required.

options.text: The file name must be quoted in double quotes for `scp` to accept it, and the reported error is a misleading way of flagging that quoting problem, since `scp` reports an unquoted operand as a missing local file rather than naming the quoting fault itself.
options.why: Quoting only matters when a filename contains spaces or shell metacharacters, and `report.tar.gz` contains neither;

items.rationale: Using `-p` for scp is a frequent and confusing difference: `ssh` uses `-p PORT` for a non-default port, while `scp` spells the same option with a capital `-P`, and mixing the two up produces exactly this kind of unrecognised-option error.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED. The stem asserted that `scp -p 2222 report.tar.gz user@web01:/tmp/` 'gets an error about an unrecognised option'. That is false: scp(1) documents '-p   Preserves modification times, access times, and file mode bits from the source file', so `-p` is a VALID scp flag and `2222` is simply consumed as an extra source operand. EMPIRICAL, in a Docker ubuntu:24.04 container with openssh-client installed: `scp -p 2222 report.tar.gz user@web01:/tmp/` produced `scp: stat local "2222": No such file or directory`, whereas a genuinely invalid flag, `scp -Z 2222 ...`, produced `scp: unknown option -- Z` followed by the usage block. The item therefore taught a false diagnostic signature and its o4 'why' rested on the same false premise. FIXED: the stem now reports the real error, the key explains why lowercase `-p` is accepted rather than rejected, and o2's and o4's 'why' texts were rewritten to match. RE-VERIFIED after the rewrite against scp(1), which confirms '-P port ... Note that this option is written with a capital P, because -p is already reserved for preserving the times and mode bits of the file' -- the key is correct and no distractor is also correct. CITATION FIX at concept level: openssh-scp-man added; ssh(1) does not document scp's flags. o4 also carried a padding tail ('as a matter of routine operational practice').

items.stem: What is the practical difference between SFTP and FTPS, given that both names sound like secured variants of FTP?

options.text: SFTP rides SSH on port 22, as an SSH subsystem entirely unrelated to FTP or FTPS; FTPS is the original FTP protocol wrapped in TLS instead.
options.why: The two are genuinely different protocols despite the naming similarity: SFTP is an SSH subsystem, while FTPS is FTP itself carried inside a TLS session, with different ports and mechanisms.

options.text: SFTP and FTPS are two names for the exact same protocol, differing only in which vendor's client software happens to use which term.
options.why: They are structurally different protocols — SFTP is an SSH subsystem on port 22, FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS on FTP's own ports — not two names for identical technology.

options.text: SFTP is FTP wrapped in TLS, while FTPS is the SSH-based subsystem that rides on port 22 alongside ordinary SSH traffic.
options.why: This swaps the two definitions: SFTP is the SSH subsystem on port 22, and FTPS is the one that wraps FTP in TLS, not the other way around.

options.text: SFTP and FTPS differ only in that SFTP is used for uploads while FTPS is used exclusively for downloads, both otherwise sharing an identical underlying transport.
options.why: Neither protocol is restricted to uploads or downloads only; both support bidirectional transfer, and the actual difference is their underlying transport mechanism, SSH versus TLS-wrapped FTP.

items.rationale: SFTP and FTPS are different things despite the similar names: SFTP rides SSH on port 22, unrelated to FTP or FTPS, while FTPS is the original FTP protocol wrapped in TLS — a distinction worth holding onto given how often the two are assumed to be the same.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed. sftp(1) DESCRIPTION: 'sftp is a file transfer program, similar to ftp(1), which performs all operations over an encrypted ssh(1) transport. It may also use many features of ssh, such as public key authentication and compression.' sshd_config(5) documents 'Subsystem: Configures an external subsystem (e.g. file transfer daemon)', which is the mechanism by which sftp rides the SSH connection, and ssh(1)'s -s flag 'May be used to request invocation of a subsystem on the remote system'. The IANA registry gives 'ssh 22/tcp', so the port claim is an assignment, not a convention. FTPS is settled by RFC 4217, 'Securing FTP with TLS', and the IANA registry entry 'ftps 990/tcp' -- FTP itself carried inside TLS, on FTP's own ports, with no relationship to SSH. o2 is refuted by that structural difference, o3 swaps the two, o4 is false since both directions of transfer are supported by each. No distractor is also correct; every distractor 'why' is true. CITATION FIX at concept level: openssh-sftp-man and rfc-4217-ftp-over-tls added; ssh(1) alone documents neither sftp's subsystem model nor FTPS at all. No self-refuting padding in this item.

items.stem: A company wants to filter and log employee web access before it leaves the building, and separately wants to hide an internal application server behind a public hostname. Which kind of proxy fits each need?

options.text: A forward proxy fits filtering employee access, since it sits in front of clients and is configured by them; a reverse proxy fits hiding the internal server, since it sits in front of servers, invisible to clients.
options.why: The two directions solve opposite problems: filtering and policy enforcement on outbound client traffic is a forward-proxy job, while hiding and fronting an internal server is a reverse-proxy job.

options.text: A reverse proxy fits filtering employee access, since it is the type configured directly by the clients whose traffic needs to be filtered.
options.why: A forward proxy, not a reverse proxy, is the one configured by clients and positioned in front of them; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and is invisible to clients instead.

options.text: Both needs are met by the same forward proxy, since a forward proxy is capable of hiding an internal server from the public internet as well as filtering client traffic, because a proxy's position in the path rather than which party configures it is what decides its role.
options.why: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and is configured by them; hiding an internal server from the public internet is specifically a reverse-proxy job on the server side instead.

options.text: Neither need is met by a proxy at all; both require a VPN, since only a VPN is capable of filtering traffic or hiding an internal server from view.
options.why: A VPN provides an encrypted tunnel for network-level access; it does not filter and log web traffic or front an internal application the way a proxy specifically does.

items.rationale: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and is configured by them, which is why filtering employee web access, caching outbound requests and enforcing policy are forward-proxy jobs; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and is invisible to clients, which is why hiding an internal application server behind a public hostname is a reverse-proxy job.

verification.reasoning: Key checked against RFC 9110 §3.7 (fetched): a "proxy" is "a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client, usually via local configuration rules" and is used to "group an organization's HTTP requests through a common intermediary for the sake of security services" — the forward/filtering role; a "gateway (a.k.a. reverse proxy)" "acts as an origin server for the outbound connection" and is used "to encapsulate legacy or untrusted information services" — the server-fronting role. Both halves of the key are therefore directly sourced. o2 inverts client-chosen vs origin-facing and is false; o3 is false for the same reason; o4 is false because RFC 9110 attributes these roles to intermediaries, not to any tunnel/VPN. Each distractor why states a true fact. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on option shape only: o3 carried a self-refuting trailing clause ("as commonly understood by less experienced staff") that announced its own wrongness; replaced with a genuinely false causal clause of similar length, then re-checked — confirmed.

items.stem: A reverse proxy terminates TLS and forwards requests to a backend application over a private address. The backend's access logs show every request coming from the proxy's own IP address rather than the real client's. What explains this, and what fixes it?

options.text: Because a proxy terminates and re-issues the connection, the backend sees the proxy as its client; a forwarded header, added by the proxy, is what recovers the original client address for logging or access control.
options.why: This is a documented trap: because a proxy terminates and re-issues the connection, the backend logs show the proxy's address, which quietly breaks IP-based access control written before the proxy was introduced, unless a forwarded header preserves the original client address.

options.text: The backend's own network interface must be misconfigured, since a correctly working reverse proxy is defined to always preserve the original client's IP address in every log entry automatically, so no header configuration is needed on the proxy itself.
options.why: A working reverse proxy does not automatically preserve the original client address in logs; this requires a specific forwarded header to be added, not a fix on the backend's interface.

options.text: This only happens because the reverse proxy is also functioning as a load balancer, and load balancers are what specifically cause this address-masking behaviour.
options.why: The address-masking behaviour follows from being any kind of intermediary that terminates and re-issues the connection, a proxy trait, not specifically from also load-balancing across backends.

options.text: The fix is to switch from a reverse proxy to a forward proxy, since only a forward proxy is capable of preserving the original client's address in backend logs.
options.why: Switching proxy direction does not solve this; a forwarded header, not a change from reverse to forward proxy, is the standard fix that recovers the original client address for the backend.

items.rationale: A reverse proxy is reached because DNS resolves the public name to it, and it forwards to a backend on a private address; because a proxy terminates and re-issues the connection, the backend sees the proxy as its client unless a forwarded header preserves the original address.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: the item cited only RFC 9110, which defines the gateway/reverse-proxy role but says nothing about recovering the original client address. RFC 7239 §1 (fetched) states it directly: "these proxies make the requests appear as if they originated from the proxy's IP address", causing "a loss of information" whose main uses are "diagnostics, access control, and abuse management", and that IP-list access control "will not work if a proxy is used"; §4 defines the Forwarded header field that discloses the original information. Citation fixed at concept level (rfc-7239-forwarded added to sysadmin.networking.proxy) rather than weakening the content; re-checked — confirmed. o2 is false (RFC 7239 exists precisely because preservation is not automatic); o3 is false because the address masking follows from terminating and re-issuing the connection, which RFC 9110 §3.7 attributes to gateways generally, not to load balancing; o4 is false because direction of the proxy is irrelevant to the Forwarded header. Distractor whys all state true facts. Also repaired a self-refuting trailing clause on o2 ("a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive").

items.stem: A reverse proxy is added in front of a single backend application server. Later, a second backend is added for capacity, and the proxy begins distributing requests across both, health-checking each. Has the device's function changed, and how should it now be described?

options.text: Yes — it is now acting as a load balancer as well, since it distributes across several backends and health-checks them, which is a change of purpose, not merely of position.
options.why: A reverse proxy is not a load balancer merely by existing; it becomes one specifically when it distributes across several backends and health-checks them, exactly as described here.

options.text: No — it remains simply a reverse proxy throughout, since a reverse proxy is defined to always distribute traffic across multiple backends regardless of how many are configured.
options.why: A reverse proxy in front of a single backend is not inherently distributing anything; the distribution and health-checking behaviour is specifically what defines a load balancer once a second backend is added.

options.text: Yes — it has become a forward proxy, since adding a second backend changes which side of the connection, client or server, the device is now serving.
options.why: The device still sits in front of the servers, serving the service owner's side, exactly as before; adding a backend does not flip it to serving the client side, which is what would make it a forward proxy.

options.text: No, and it also cannot be described as a load balancer, since only a dedicated hardware appliance, not a software reverse proxy, is permitted to hold that label.
options.why: Load balancing is a functional description, not a hardware requirement; a software reverse proxy that distributes across health-checked backends is genuinely acting as a load balancer.

items.rationale: A reverse proxy is not a load balancer merely by existing — it becomes one when it distributes across several backends and health-checks them, which is exactly the change described: the same box now performs a different function, a change of purpose rather than of physical position.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED: the key read "it has become a load balancer", an exclusive rename that conflicts with the cited source — RFC 9110 §3.7 says gateways (reverse proxies) are used "to enable partitioning or load balancing of HTTP services across multiple machines", and nginx's load-balancing guide (fetched) says "Reverse proxy implementation in nginx includes load balancing". A reader could then defend o2. Key rewritten to "it is now acting as a load balancer as well", which the sources support without making o2 defensible (o2's stated reason, that a reverse proxy is "defined to always distribute traffic across multiple backends", is false: nginx documents a single-server upstream and RFC 9110 does not require multiplicity). Distribution-plus-health-checking as the load-balancing function is documented by nginx (round-robin/least_conn/ip_hash plus in-band passive health checks with max_fails/fail_timeout) and by the HAProxy Starter Guide §3.3.4-3.3.5. o3 is false: the device still fronts the servers, so it is not a forward proxy. o4 is false: HAProxy is software and the guide describes it as a load balancer throughout. Re-checked — confirmed.

items.stem: The word "proxy," used without qualification, is ambiguous between forward and reverse. How should a reader decide which one a scenario means?

options.text: By reading the direction from the scenario itself — "proxy" unqualified usually means forward proxy in a client context and reverse proxy in a server context, so the surrounding description decides it, not the bare word.
options.why: The direction has to be read from the scenario rather than the word alone, since the same unqualified term is conventionally used both ways depending on whose side of the exchange is being described.

options.text: By assuming "proxy" unqualified always means forward proxy, since that is the only sense the word carries in networking terminology regardless of context.
options.why: "Proxy" unqualified is genuinely ambiguous and commonly means reverse proxy in a server context; assuming it is always forward proxy will misread many scenarios.

options.text: By checking whether TLS is involved, since only a reverse proxy is ever capable of terminating TLS, making that the deciding factor in every scenario.
options.why: TLS termination alone does not decide the direction; a forward proxy can also be involved in TLS-related configurations, and the deciding factor is whose side is being served, not TLS presence.

options.text: By checking whether the device also performs load balancing, since only a reverse proxy is ever combined with load-balancing functionality in practice.
options.why: Whether load balancing is present does not itself decide forward versus reverse; the deciding factor is which side of the exchange, client or server, the device is described as serving.

items.rationale: "Proxy" unqualified usually means forward proxy in a client context and reverse proxy in a server context, so the direction has to be read from the scenario rather than the word — filtering employee web access is forward; terminating TLS in front of servers is reverse.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 9110 §3.7 (fetched), which is itself the evidence for the ambiguity: the specification reserves the bare word "proxy" for the client-chosen intermediary and calls the server-side one a "gateway (a.k.a. reverse proxy)", while ordinary operational writing uses "proxy" unqualified for both — so the scenario, not the bare word, decides. o2 is false for the same reason. o3 is false: RFC 9110 §3.7 describes TLS being established through a shared firewall proxy via a tunnel, so TLS involvement does not identify the direction; a forward proxy can also terminate TLS in an inspection deployment. o4 is false: RFC 9110 §3.7 attributes load balancing to gateways but nothing forbids a client-side intermediary from distributing across upstream proxies, and load balancing is not the deciding trait. All distractor whys state true facts. Note recorded as a limit: this item turns on conventional usage rather than a normative statement, which no primary source can settle outright; the RFC's own dual terminology is the strongest available evidence.

items.stem: A team needs a device that keeps a service available when any one of several backend servers fails, distributing load across all of them and removing failed ones from rotation automatically. Is a proxy, generically, defined to do this?

options.text: No — a proxy's defining trait is mediating a request on someone's behalf, and a single backend is entirely normal for it; it is a load balancer specifically that selects among several backends by a scheduling algorithm and health-checks them continuously.
options.why: The separating axis is intent rather than position: a load balancer exists to distribute work across many backends and survive their failure, while a proxy exists to stand in for one party in an exchange, which does not inherently require more than one backend.

options.text: Yes — every proxy, reverse or forward, is defined to distribute requests across multiple backends and health-check them as a core part of what a proxy fundamentally is.
options.why: A proxy commonly has just one backend behind it; distributing across several backends and health-checking them is what specifically defines a load balancer, not a proxy generically.

options.text: No, and neither is a load balancer, since removing a failed backend from rotation automatically requires a dedicated firewall device rather than either a proxy or a load balancer.
options.why: A firewall filters traffic by policy; it does not health-check backends or remove them from a rotation, which is specifically a load balancer's job, and it is exactly the device the team needs here.

options.text: Yes, but only for a forward proxy specifically; a reverse proxy by definition can never distribute traffic across more than one backend under any circumstances.
options.why: A reverse proxy commonly does distribute traffic across multiple backends once it takes on that role, which is exactly how it becomes a load balancer; the restriction described here does not hold.

items.rationale: A load balancer is the standard answer to both handling more traffic and surviving a server failure, distinguished from a proxy by intent: it selects a backend by a scheduling algorithm, health-checks each one continuously, and removes failing ones from rotation, which is not inherent to a proxy simply mediating on someone's behalf.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: RFC 9110 alone was cited, and it never defines a load balancer, a scheduling algorithm or a health check. Re-sourced to nginx's HTTP load-balancing guide (fetched), which documents the scheduling algorithms (round-robin default, least_conn, least_time, ip_hash, weights) and in-band passive health checks (max_fails/fail_timeout marking a failed server out of rotation and probing it back), and to the HAProxy Starter Guide §3.3.4-3.3.5 (fetched: "Only valid servers are used; the other ones are automatically evicted from load balancing farms", ten balancing algorithms). RFC 9110 §3.7 is retained because it supplies the proxy side of the contrast ("a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client") and notes that load balancing is something a gateway may do rather than something a proxy is. Key re-checked — confirmed. o2 is false: nginx documents an upstream group with one server and a proxy_pass to a single backend, so distribution is not constitutive of being a proxy. o3 is false: NIST SP 800-41r1 §2.1 places filtering, not backend rotation, in a firewall's remit. o4 is false: nginx's reverse-proxy implementation explicitly includes load balancing across several backends. All distractor whys state true facts.
