items.stem: An application keeps per-user session state in memory on whichever backend first served that user. Requests from the same user are then distributed evenly across every backend by the load balancer's default scheduling algorithm. What problem does this cause, and what feature addresses it?

options.text: Later requests may land on a backend without that user's session state, breaking the application; session affinity, or sticky sessions, pins a client to one backend to fix this, at the cost of even distribution.
options.why: Where an application keeps per-user state in memory, session affinity is exactly the mechanism designed to trade perfectly even load distribution for consistent routing back to the backend holding that state.

options.text: No problem is caused, since every backend behind a load balancer is defined to automatically share in-memory session state with every other backend by default.
options.why: Backends do not automatically share in-memory state with each other by default; a request landing on the wrong backend genuinely loses access to session state kept only in memory there.

options.text: The problem is caused by health checking, and the fix is to disable health checks so that every backend remains in rotation regardless of its actual state.
options.why: Health checking removes failing backends from rotation for availability reasons; disabling it does not address a session-state mismatch, and it would remove an unrelated safety mechanism.

options.text: The problem is caused by layer 4 balancing specifically, and the fix is to switch to layer 7 balancing, which is defined to always keep a user on one backend automatically across virtually every environment of this kind.
options.why: Neither layer 4 nor layer 7 balancing automatically pins a client to one backend by default; session affinity is a distinct, explicitly configured feature independent of which layer the balancer operates at.

items.rationale: Where an application keeps per-user state in memory, session affinity, or "sticky sessions," pins a client to one backend, at the cost of even distribution — without it, a scheduling algorithm distributing requests evenly across backends will eventually route a returning user to a backend that never saw their session.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the HAProxy Starter Guide §3.3.3 (fetched): "Layer 7 load balancers also face another challenge known as stickiness or persistence ... they generally have to direct multiple subsequent requests or connections from a same origin ... to the same target. The best known example is the shopping cart ... the user must always be sent to the server which holds his shopping cart", solved by "memorizing the chosen target". nginx's guide (fetched) states the same trade-off from the other side: "with round-robin or least-connected load balancing, each subsequent client's request can be potentially distributed to a different server. There is no guarantee that the same client will be always directed to the same server", and ip_hash "ensures that the requests from the same client will always be directed to the same server" — i.e. affinity is bought with even distribution. Re-sourced from RFC 9110, which is silent on session affinity. o2 is false (no state sharing is implied by being behind a balancer; HAProxy notes stickiness state "may have to be replicated to other load balancers", i.e. it is not automatic). o3 is false: health checks address backend failure, not state placement. o4 is false: HAProxy documents stickiness as an explicitly configured mechanism, and content-awareness only makes it easier, never automatic. All distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: A single load balancer is placed in front of two backend servers to improve availability. A reviewer says this fully removes the single point of failure the two-server design was meant to avoid. Is that correct?

options.text: No — the load balancer is itself a single point of failure unless it is made redundant too; putting one in front of two servers moves the risk rather than removing it.
options.why: This is a specifically documented trap: a non-redundant load balancer simply relocates the single point of failure from the backend layer to the balancing layer rather than eliminating it.

options.text: Yes — a load balancer is defined to be inherently redundant by design, regardless of whether a second instance of it is deployed alongside the first.
options.why: A load balancer is not inherently redundant simply by being a load balancer; it must itself be made redundant, through a second instance or equivalent, to avoid being a single point of failure.

options.text: Yes, but only because health checking on the backends is what specifically eliminates the load balancer itself as a single point of failure.
options.why: Health checking monitors the backends the load balancer forwards to; it does nothing to protect against the load balancer itself failing, which remains a single point of failure without its own redundancy.

options.text: No, but only because the two backend servers themselves remain the single point of failure regardless of whether a load balancer is added in front of them, since two servers in one rotation still share a single failure domain.
options.why: Two backend servers behind a load balancer are specifically not a single point of failure for that layer; the unaddressed risk described is the non-redundant load balancer itself, not the backends.

items.rationale: A load balancer is a single point of failure unless it is itself redundant — putting one in front of two servers moves the risk rather than removing it, since the servers gained resilience at the cost of introducing a new, unprotected single point upstream of them.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against the HAProxy Starter Guide §3.3.4 "Basic features : High availability" (fetched), which treats the balancer node itself as something that must be made redundant: it lists the "ability to return a global failed status for a farm ... making it possible for an upstream component to choose a different LB node for a given service" and "Integrates well with standard VRRP daemon keepalived: HAProxy easily tells keepalived about its state and copes very well with floating virtual IP addresses". A floating VIP and a second LB node exist only because a single balancer is otherwise the failure point. Re-sourced from RFC 9110, which is silent on availability design. o2 is false: nothing in either vendor's documentation makes a balancer inherently redundant, which is why keepalived/VRRP is documented at all. o3 is false: the same section separates evicting failed backends from protecting the balancer node. o4 is false: two health-checked backends behind a balancer are exactly the layer the design already made redundant. All distractor whys state true facts. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on option shape: o4 carried a self-refuting trailing hedge ("a pattern that holds across most deployments encountered"); replaced with a genuinely false claim of similar length, then re-checked — confirmed. Recorded as a limit: no source says the words "single point of failure"; the conclusion is a direct reading of the redundancy machinery HAProxy documents for the balancer itself.

items.stem: What is the practical difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?

options.text: A layer 4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP by address and port without reading the payload; a layer 7 balancer parses HTTP and can route on hostname, path or header.
options.why: The two operate at genuinely different depths of inspection: layer 4 makes decisions from addressing information alone, while layer 7 understands the application protocol well enough to route on its content.

options.text: A layer 4 balancer parses HTTP and can route on hostname, path or header, while a layer 7 balancer forwards TCP or UDP by address and port without reading the payload.
options.why: This swaps the two definitions: parsing HTTP content for routing decisions is layer 7's job, and forwarding purely by address and port without reading the payload is layer 4's.

options.text: A layer 4 balancer only supports TCP, while a layer 7 balancer only supports UDP, matching the transport protocols named by their respective layer numbers.
options.why: A layer 4 balancer can forward both TCP and UDP by address and port; the distinguishing trait between the two levels is depth of payload inspection, not which single transport each is restricted to.

options.text: There is no real difference; "layer 4" and "layer 7" are marketing terms describing identical balancing behaviour under two different vendor naming conventions.
options.why: The two genuinely differ in what they inspect and can route on — address and port alone versus parsed HTTP content — not merely in vendor naming for identical behaviour.

items.rationale: A layer 4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP by address and port without reading the payload, while a layer 7 balancer parses HTTP and can route on hostname, path or header — the OSI layer number in each name describes how deep into the traffic the balancer looks before deciding where to send it.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against the HAProxy Starter Guide §3.3.2 (fetched). Layer 4: the technology that "acts at the packet level and processes packets more or less individually ... consider the session a packet belongs to and called layer4-LB or L4 ... but provides almost no content awareness". Layer 7: "acts on session contents. It requires that the input streams is reassembled and processed as a whole ... generally performed by proxies and they're often called layer 7 load balancers or L7", and §3.3.3 adds "In order to extract information such as a cookie, a host header field, a URL or whatever" — hostname, path and header routing exactly. Re-sourced from RFC 9110, which never uses the layer-4/layer-7 vocabulary. o2 is the swapped definition and is false. o3 is false: the guide describes L4 as packet-level for sessions generally, not TCP-only, and the distinguishing trait is content awareness rather than transport. o4 is false: the guide contrasts real behavioural differences, including that L7 requires stream reassembly and cannot always reach line rate. All distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: A remote worker connects to a VPN and is told they now behave, for addressing and routing purposes, as though attached to the private network directly. What does that description actually mean in practice?

options.text: It means a virtual interface appears on the client and routes are installed pointing some or all destinations through the encrypted tunnel, so private-network resources are reached as though the client were physically on that network.
options.why: The client authenticates to a VPN endpoint, gains a virtual interface, and has routes installed pointing traffic through the tunnel, which is the mechanism behind the "as though attached directly" description.

options.text: It means the client's own physical network interface is temporarily relocated to the private network's physical location for the duration of the connection, as if the network card itself changed sites.
options.why: Nothing physical relocates; the effect is produced entirely through a virtual interface and routing changes on the client, not any actual physical relocation of hardware.

options.text: It means DNS records for the private network are automatically republished to the public internet for the duration of the client's VPN session.
options.why: VPN access does not republish private DNS records publicly; it grants the connected client its own private routing and, typically, private-facing name resolution, without exposing anything to the wider internet.

options.text: It means the client's MAC address is reassigned to match one already registered on the private network's local switch infrastructure.
options.why: A VPN operates above the link layer, through routing over an encrypted tunnel; it does not reassign or spoof the client's MAC address to match anything on the remote network's switches.

items.rationale: Typically the client authenticates to a VPN endpoint, a virtual interface appears on the client, and routes are installed pointing some or all destinations through that interface — it is the routing table, not any physical change, that determines which traffic actually enters the tunnel.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against NIST SP 800-77r1 §8.2 (PDF fetched and searched in full, 166 pages): "The host obtains a new virtual interface configured with one or more IP addresses. Packets to and from this virtual interface use a transport protocol to encapsulate the packets securely to the remote endpoint of the VPN. The packets are then further routed, just like packets that arrived on a physical network interface." §6.5 adds that "Once the tunnel is established, routing is used to determine which packets to send over the IPsec connection", and §7 discusses split tunnelling, i.e. which destinations are routed into the tunnel. Virtual interface plus installed routes is therefore the documented mechanism behind the "as though attached directly" description. o2 is false: nothing physical moves; the document describes a virtual interface only. o3 is false: §6.10 discusses the DNS configuration needed for cross-network name resolution, which is private-side configuration, not publication of private records. o4 is false: the guide describes IPsec and transport-layer VPNs operating on IP packets above the link layer, with no MAC reassignment. All distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: A user reports the VPN client shows "Connected," yet an internal server is still unreachable. What is usually implicated first, given that the tunnel itself reports as up?

options.text: Routing or name resolution rather than the tunnel itself — in most implementations the tunnel is genuinely up, and that particular destination simply is not routed through it, which is why the routing table is checked first.
options.why: Because the routing table decides which traffic enters the tunnel, most "the VPN is connected but I still cannot reach the server" reports are generally routing or DNS problems rather than tunnel problems.

options.text: The tunnel's own encryption must be broken, since a report of unreachability after a successful connection message is always a cryptographic negotiation failure.
options.why: A successful 'Connected' status means the tunnel and its encryption negotiated successfully; the described unreachability is far more often a routing or split-tunnel configuration issue.

options.text: The VPN endpoint's own internet connection must be down, since a client-reported 'Connected' status is always unreliable and cannot be trusted on its own.
options.why: A "Connected" status from the client reflects a genuinely established tunnel in most implementations; the more common explanation for a specific unreachable destination is routing, not the endpoint's own connectivity.

options.text: The server's firewall must have blocked the VPN client's specific address, since that is the only plausible explanation once a tunnel reports as successfully connected, because a tunnel that reports up necessarily has every destination inside it already routed.
options.why: A firewall block is possible but is not the first or most usual explanation; routing or name resolution not sending that traffic through the tunnel at all is the more common, better-supported explanation.

items.rationale: Because the routing table decides which traffic enters the tunnel, most "the VPN is connected but I still cannot reach the server" reports are generally routing or DNS problems rather than tunnel problems — the tunnel is up and simply is not being used for that particular destination.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against NIST SP 800-77r1 §6.5 (fetched): routing, not the tunnel's own state, decides what enters the tunnel — "Once the tunnel is established, routing is used to determine which packets to send over the IPsec connection", and when "the routes into the IPsec devices on both ends do not match ... network connectivity will fail" even though the SA is up. §6.9/§6.10 add that "special DNS configuration is required if machines in one network need to be able to reach machines in the other network by DNS name", which sources the name-resolution half of the key. §7.2.6 on split tunnelling documents the same class of "connected but this destination is not carried" outcome. o2 is false: a completed IKE/TLS negotiation is what produces the Connected state, so encryption failure would prevent it, not follow it. o3 is false for the same reason. o4 is false: a firewall block is one of several possibilities, and the guide places routing and policy scope first. All distractor whys state true facts. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on option shape: o4 ended with a self-refuting hedge ("which many take as self-evident without checking further under typical operating conditions"); replaced with a genuinely false causal clause, then re-checked — confirmed.

items.stem: A branch office link is upgraded from 100 Mbit/s to 1 Gbit/s. Nightly bulk backups finish much faster, but an interactive ticketing application "feels exactly the same" to users. Why is that outcome expected rather than a sign the upgrade failed?

options.text: The ticketing application's responsiveness is dominated by latency, the per-request delay for many small requests, which capacity upgrades do not change; bulk backups are throughput-bound and benefit directly from more bandwidth.
options.why: A high-bandwidth link can still feel slow for an interactive workload dominated by many small requests, because that experience is governed by round-trip latency rather than by how much data the link can carry per second.

options.text: The upgrade genuinely failed for the interactive application, since any bandwidth increase is defined to proportionally reduce every kind of user-perceived delay equally.
options.why: An interactive workload dominated by small requests is bound by latency, not by bandwidth, so a bandwidth increase alone does not proportionally reduce its perceived delay.

options.text: The ticketing application must be using UDP rather than TCP, since only a UDP-based application would fail to benefit from additional link bandwidth.
options.why: Which transport protocol the application uses is unrelated to why capacity upgrades do not help a latency-bound workload; the explanation is the dominance of round-trip delay, not protocol choice.

options.text: The ticketing application's lack of improvement means DNS resolution, not the link itself, must be the actual bottleneck limiting its performance.
options.why: Nothing in the scenario points at DNS specifically; the described symptom, an interactive app unaffected by more bandwidth, is the textbook signature of latency dominance, not a naming problem.

items.rationale: A high-bandwidth link can still feel slow: an interactive session or a page load with many small requests is dominated by latency, not by capacity, so buying more bandwidth changes nothing for that kind of workload, while a bulk transfer is bounded by capacity and benefits directly.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 6349 (fetched), which treats capacity and delay as two independent path properties that must be measured separately: §1.2 defines "Round-Trip Time (RTT)" and Bottleneck Bandwidth (BB) as distinct baseline quantities and the Bandwidth-Delay Product as "the product of a data link's capacity (in bits per second) and its end-to-end delay (in seconds)", and §3.2 requires baselining "the inherent, non-congested" RTT separately from BB. Raising BB therefore leaves the RTT term untouched, which is precisely why a request-response workload governed by per-request round trips does not improve while a bulk transfer, whose achievable throughput RFC 6349 derives from BDP and window size, does. o2 is false for the same reason. o3 is false: RFC 6349 is a TCP framework and the latency dominance argument is independent of transport choice. o4 is false: nothing in the scenario implicates name resolution. All distractor whys state true facts. Recorded as a limit: RFC 6349 does not itself use the phrase "interactive application"; the key is an application of its RTT-vs-BB separation, not a quotation.

items.stem: Why does jitter, the variation in latency, matter more for voice traffic than the absolute value of latency itself?

options.text: Voice tolerates a steady delay reasonably well but not an unpredictable one, since variation in timing disrupts the playback rhythm listeners depend on.
options.why: A consistent, even high, delay can be adapted to, but unpredictable variation in that delay disrupts playback timing in a way a steady delay does not.

options.text: Voice traffic is unaffected by either latency or jitter, since audio codecs are defined to fully compensate for both automatically regardless of network conditions.
options.why: Voice traffic is genuinely sensitive to jitter; codecs do not fully compensate for unpredictable timing variation, which is exactly why jitter degrades call quality noticeably.

options.text: Jitter matters more because it is measured in a completely different unit than latency, making it inherently a larger and more significant number.
options.why: Jitter and latency are both measured in time, typically milliseconds; the reason jitter matters more for voice is about how playback timing is disrupted, not about differing units of measurement.

options.text: Jitter matters more only for UDP-based voice traffic, and TCP-based voice traffic is entirely unaffected by any timing variation between packets.
options.why: The sensitivity to jitter comes from the real-time playback nature of voice traffic, not specifically from the choice of UDP as transport; the concept is about timing disruption during playback.

items.rationale: Jitter — variation in latency rather than its absolute value — is typically what degrades voice and video, which tolerate a steady delay far better than an unpredictable one, since consistent timing can be adapted to while variable timing disrupts playback.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: RFC 6349 mentions jitter only in passing (§1, §5.1) and says nothing about why voice is sensitive to it. Re-sourced by adding RFC 5481 §3.2 (fetched), which is exactly on point: "Most isochronous applications (a.k.a. real-time applications) employ a buffer to smooth out delay variation encountered on the path from source to destination. The buffer must be big enough to accommodate the expected variation of delay, or packet loss will result. However, if the buffer is too large, then some of the desired spontaneity of communication will be lost and conversational dynamics will be affected." That is the key's claim in the source's own terms: a steady delay can be absorbed, an unpredictable one costs either loss or responsiveness. §1.1 also records that the phenomenon "some refer to ... as jitter (and the buffers that attempt to smooth the variations as de-jitter buffers)", tying the item's vocabulary to the RFC's. o2 is false: RFC 5481 §3.2 exists because compensation is bounded by buffer size, not automatic. o3 is false: §1.1 and §4 define delay variation in units of time, the same as delay. o4 is false: the mechanism is the playout buffer of a real-time stream, which RFC 5481 attributes to isochronous applications generally rather than to a transport. All distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: A service is confirmed running and correctly bound to 0.0.0.0, yet remote clients get connection refused instantly, while another service on a different host times out with no response at all. What does the difference between these two symptoms suggest about the cause?

options.text: The instant refusal suggests a REJECT-style response — something on the path answered; the silent timeout suggests a DROP-style policy — the packet vanished, which is the more classic 'firewall is blocking this' signature.
options.why: DROP gives the client a timeout while REJECT gives an immediate refusal, and that difference is diagnostic and worth more than the rule text itself when deciding where to look next.

options.text: Both symptoms indicate exactly the same underlying cause, since DROP and REJECT firewall policies are defined to always produce identical client-side behaviour.
options.why: DROP and REJECT are deliberately different behaviours precisely so the client-side symptom differs: one is silent, producing a timeout, and the other answers, producing an instant refusal.

options.text: The instant refusal proves no firewall is involved at all, since any device applying a firewall policy is defined to always produce a silent timeout rather than a refusal.
options.why: A firewall configured to REJECT rather than DROP produces an immediate refusal too, so an instant refusal does not by itself prove no firewall is involved on the path.

options.text: The timeout proves the destination host is completely powered off, since only a powered-off host is capable of producing a connection attempt that never receives any answer.
options.why: A silent timeout is also produced by a DROP firewall policy on a fully powered-on, reachable host; it does not by itself prove the destination is powered off.

items.rationale: A firewall that drops traffic and one that rejects it produce different symptoms: DROP gives the client a timeout, REJECT gives an immediate refusal — that difference is diagnostic and worth more than the rule text itself, and is the reason to look first at policy versus reachability differently for the two symptoms described.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: the only claim-bearing citation was `netfilter-documentation`, whose URL (https://www.netfilter.org/documentation/index.html) was fetched and contains a project navigation menu and a release-news list and no statement about DROP, REJECT or client-visible symptoms — a 200 OK with no content on the point at issue. Re-sourced to the pages that do state it: iptables(8) TARGETS (fetched) — "ACCEPT means to let the packet through.  DROP means to drop the packet on the floor" — and iptables-extensions(8) REJECT (fetched) — "This is used to send back an error packet in response to the matched packet: otherwise it is equivalent to DROP", with --reject-with selecting an ICMP unreachable type or tcp-reset. The netfilter index is kept as the concept's project landing page but is no longer load-bearing. Empirical check (docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04, iptables + netcat-openbsd + iproute2 installed): a listener was started with `nc -l -p 9001 -k`; then `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9003 -j DROP`, `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9004 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset` and `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9005 -j REJECT`. `ss -tuln` showed only `tcp LISTEN 0 1 0.0.0.0:9001`. Results of `nc -zv -w 3 127.0.0.1 <port>`: 9001 (open) "Connection to 127.0.0.1 9001 port [tcp/*] succeeded!"; 9002 (no listener, no rule) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9002 (tcp) failed: Connection refused"; 9003 (DROP) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9003 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress"; 9004 (REJECT tcp-reset) "Connection refused"; 9005 (REJECT, default icmp-port-unreachable) "Connection refused". DROP produced the timeout and both REJECT forms produced the instant refusal, exactly as the key states, so key re-checked — confirmed. o2 is false: the two targets are documented as different behaviours and measured as different symptoms. o3 is false: the REJECT rows above are firewall rules that produced an instant refusal. o4 is false: the DROP row above came from a fully powered-on host. All distractor whys state true facts. the netfilter documentation index (netfilter-documentation) returns 200 but its ~4.5 KB body is a navigation menu and release news, with 0 occurrences of "REJECT". Dropped. iptables(8) TARGETS re-fetched and re-verified: "ACCEPT means to let the packet through.  DROP means to drop the packet on the floor." iptables-extensions(8) REJECT re-fetched: "This is used to send back an error packet in response to the matched packet: otherwise it is equivalent to DROP". Nmap Port Scanning Basics added for the client-visible half the man pages do not state: a filtered port is one where "packet filtering prevents its probes from reaching the port ... filters that simply drop probes without responding are far more common", while a closed port "receives and responds to Nmap probe packets, but there is no application listening on it".

items.stem: A host with no inbound firewall rules configured at all can still browse the web without issue. A colleague argues this proves the firewall is not actually protecting anything. Is that the right conclusion?

options.text: No — a stateful firewall tracks connections, so a rule permitting outbound traffic implicitly permits the replies, which is exactly why a host with no inbound allows can still browse the web while remaining protected from unsolicited inbound connections.
options.why: The standard posture is default-deny inbound with explicit allows, and stateful inspection is why outbound-initiated traffic still works without any inbound rule needing to exist for the replies.

options.text: Yes — the ability to browse the web with no inbound rules proves the firewall is entirely inactive and providing no protection against inbound connections at all, since a firewall that permits any traffic in either direction has no default-deny policy left to apply.
options.why: Browsing the web working is expected stateful behaviour, not evidence the firewall is inactive; an unsolicited inbound connection attempt, unlike a reply to outbound traffic, would still be blocked by default-deny.

options.text: Yes, but only because web browsing specifically bypasses firewall inspection entirely as a documented protocol-level exception unique to HTTP and HTTPS.
options.why: Web traffic is not specially exempted from firewall inspection; the reason it works is ordinary stateful tracking of outbound-initiated connections, applicable to any protocol, not an HTTP-specific bypass.

options.text: No, but only because NAT, not the firewall, is what is actually permitting the return web traffic to reach the browsing host in this scenario.
options.why: NAT rewrites addresses and is commonly co-located with a firewall, but the mechanism permitting the reply traffic here specifically is stateful firewall inspection, not NAT's address translation itself.

items.rationale: A stateful firewall tracks connections, so a rule permitting outbound traffic implicitly permits the replies, which is why a host with no inbound allows can still browse the web — this is the standard default-deny-inbound posture working as intended, not evidence that no protection exists. `ufw status` and `firewall-cmd --list-all` are the commands that show this policy on Debian-family and Red Hat-family systems respectively.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution, for the same reason as firewall.01: the netfilter documentation index carries no statement about stateful inspection. Re-sourced to NIST SP 800-41r1 §2.1.2 (PDF fetched, 48 pages, searched in full) — "Stateful inspection improves on the functions of packet filters by tracking the state of connections ... If the firewall uses stateful inspection, it will first verify that the packet is part of an established connection" — to iptables-extensions(8) conntrack/state (fetched), which defines NEW, ESTABLISHED and RELATED, and to ufw(8) NOTES (fetched): "ufw is disabled with a default incoming policy of deny, a default forward policy of deny, and a default outgoing policy of allow, with stateful tracking for NEW connections for incoming and forwarded connections". That is default-deny inbound plus stateful replies, precisely the key. o2 is false. o3 is false: SP 800-41r1 §2.1 describes filtering applied by protocol and port with no HTTP exemption. o4 is false and is settled by SP 800-41r1 §4.1 — "The use of NAT should be considered a form of routing, not a type of firewall" — so the mechanism admitting the replies is conntrack, not translation. All distractor whys state true facts. Also repaired a self-refuting trailing clause on o2 ("which is the assumption most administrators start from as a matter of routine operational practice"). the netfilter documentation index (netfilter-documentation) returns 200 but its ~4.5 KB body is a navigation menu and release news, with 0 occurrences of "REJECT". Dropped. iptables-extensions(8) conntrack re-fetched and re-verified ("ESTABLISHED The packet is associated with a connection which has seen packets in both directions"), as was ufw(8) NOTES ("a default incoming policy of deny ... and a default outgoing policy of allow, with stateful tracking for NEW connections for incoming and forwarded connections").

items.stem: A restrictive network firewall sits in front of a host whose own local firewall is configured permissively, allowing everything. What is the effective policy actually governing traffic to that host?

options.text: The intersection of both — a host firewall protects only that host, so a permissive host firewall behind a restrictive network firewall means the effective policy is whatever the network firewall still allows through, regardless of the host's own permissiveness.
options.why: A host firewall protects only that host, so the effective policy in front of it is the intersection of both firewalls, whichever one — network or host — is more restrictive still governs what actually reaches the host.

options.text: The host's own permissive policy fully governs traffic, since a local firewall is defined to always take precedence over any upstream network firewall's rules.
options.why: A host firewall does not override an upstream network firewall; traffic must pass both, so the network firewall's restrictions still apply regardless of the host's own permissive local policy.

options.text: The network firewall's policy is irrelevant once traffic reaches the local network segment, leaving the host's own permissive rules as the sole effective policy from that point onward.
options.why: The network firewall governs traffic before it even reaches the host's segment; it remains fully relevant and combines with, rather than being superseded by, the host's own local policy.

options.text: Neither firewall's policy applies at all, since having two separate firewalls active on the same path is defined to disable both of them automatically.
options.why: Two firewalls on the same path do not disable each other; each continues to filter independently, and the combined, effective result is their intersection.

items.rationale: A host firewall protects only that host, so a permissive host firewall behind a restrictive network firewall — or the reverse — means the effective policy is the intersection of both, since traffic must pass whichever firewall is more restrictive at each point on the path.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: the only claim-bearing citation was `netfilter-documentation`, whose index page was fetched and contains only a project navigation menu and release news — no statement about firewall layering. Re-sourced to NIST SP 800-41r1 (PDF fetched, 48 pages, searched in full). §2.2.1 describes a host-based firewall as protecting the individual host it runs on and as an additional layer; §3.3 "Architecture with Multiple Layers of Firewalls" states it directly — "The use of multiple layers of firewalls is quite common to provide defense-in-depth. An example of this was mentioned in Section 2.2.1, where a host-based firewall creates a boundary just before the host it is installed upon and adds another set of firewall policies to the architecture of the network" — and warns against exactly the reasoning in the distractors: "the inner firewall's administrator assumes that the outer firewall is already preventing certain types of traffic". Traffic must clear both boundaries, so the effective policy is the more restrictive of the two: the key's "intersection" reading. o2 is false: §3.3 treats the layers as cumulative, never as one overriding the other. o3 is false: the outer firewall is at the network edge and filters before the packet reaches the host's boundary at all. o4 is false: §2.2.2 relies on both layers remaining active ("Should a personal firewall on a computer malfunction, be disabled, or be misconfigured, the firewall appliance can" still filter). All distractor whys state true facts. Recorded as a limit: SP 800-41r1 states the layering and defence-in-depth role but does not use the word "intersection"; that is the key's summary of cumulative filtering, not a quotation. the netfilter documentation index (netfilter-documentation) returns 200 but its ~4.5 KB body is a navigation menu and release news, with 0 occurrences of "REJECT". Dropped. The item now rests solely on NIST SP 800-41r1 2.2.1 and 3.3, which are what actually state firewall layering; no silent stand-in was added to pad the citation list.

items.stem: Is a NAT router with no filtering rules configured applying any security policy to the traffic it forwards?

options.text: No. NAT is not filtering; a NAT router with no rules applies no policy at all, even though it rewrites addresses as traffic crosses it.
options.why: Address rewriting and policy filtering are separate concerns; a NAT device performs the former by its nature, but it applies no policy of its own unless separate filtering rules are configured.

options.text: Yes — NAT itself is defined to apply a default-deny inbound policy automatically as an inherent part of the address-rewriting process it performs.
options.why: NAT's apparent inbound-blocking behaviour is a side effect of having no translation mapping for unsolicited traffic, not a deliberately applied filtering policy; a NAT router with no rules applies no policy at all.

options.text: Yes, but only for outbound traffic, since NAT is defined to inspect and filter every outbound packet's payload before permitting it to be translated and forwarded.
options.why: NAT does not inspect payload content for either direction; it only rewrites addresses and ports and forwards accordingly, applying no content-based policy to outbound traffic either.

options.text: No, but only because every NAT router is required to have at least one firewall rule configured by default before it is allowed to forward any traffic at all.
options.why: A NAT router is not required to have any filtering rule configured to function; it can forward and translate traffic perfectly well with zero rules present, applying no policy at all.

items.rationale: NAT is not filtering: a NAT router with no rules applies no policy at all, even though its address-rewriting side effect can make unsolicited inbound traffic appear blocked, which is a fundamentally different mechanism from a firewall's deliberate policy decisions.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed, and this is the strongest attribution in the group. NIST SP 800-41r1 (PDF fetched, searched in full) says it three times: §2.1 — "network address translation (NAT) is sometimes thought of as a firewall technology, but it is actually a routing technology"; §2.4 Summary of Recommendations — "The use of NAT should be considered a form of routing, not a type of firewall"; §3.2 "Firewalls Acting as Network Address Translators" — "Despite the popular misconception, NAT is not part of the security functionality of a firewall. The security benefit of NAT — preventing a host outside the firewall from initiating contact with a host behind NAT — can just as easily be achieved by a stateful firewall". The glossary entry likewise reads "Network Address Translation (NAT): A routing technology". Re-sourced from the contentless netfilter index. o2 is false by §2.4 directly, and its why correctly identifies the absence of a mapping as a side effect rather than a policy. o3 is false: NAT rewrites addresses and ports and does not inspect payloads (§3.2 describes source-port and destination-port mapping only). o4 is false: nothing requires a filtering rule for a NAT to forward. All distractor whys state true facts. the netfilter documentation index (netfilter-documentation) returns 200 but its ~4.5 KB body is a navigation menu and release news, with 0 occurrences of "REJECT". Dropped. The item now rests solely on NIST SP 800-41r1 2.1/2.4/3.2, which state the NAT-is-routing-not-filtering point three times; no silent stand-in was added.

items.stem: An administrator SSHed into an Ubuntu server runs `ufw enable` without first running `ufw allow 22/tcp`. What is the likely, serious consequence?

options.text: The administrator is likely locked out immediately, since enabling ufw applies default-deny inbound and the active SSH session's port was never explicitly allowed first.
options.why: Enabling ufw over an SSH session without allowing port 22 first is a documented, common mistake that locks the administrator out of the very session being used to make the change.

options.text: Nothing changes for the active session, since ufw is defined to always automatically allow the port the enabling command was itself issued over.
options.why: ufw does not automatically detect and allow the port a command was issued over; enabling it without an explicit rule for SSH is exactly what causes the lockout.

options.text: The command fails outright with an error and makes no change at all, since ufw refuses to enable itself while an active SSH session lacks an explicit allow rule, because it reads the current connection table before applying any policy.
options.why: ufw(8) documents a warning prompt when enabling under ssh, not a refusal, and ufw does not read the connection table at all; it flushes the chains and applies the default-deny policy, which is precisely what causes the lockout.

options.text: Only outbound traffic is affected, leaving the existing inbound SSH session completely unaffected regardless of any rules configured.
options.why: ufw's default-deny policy governs new inbound connections and can affect the existing session's continuity as well; assuming only outbound traffic is affected is exactly the wrong assumption that causes lockouts.

items.rationale: Enabling ufw over an SSH session without allowing 22 first is a documented mistake that locks the administrator out immediately, which is why `ufw allow 22/tcp` (or the equivalent for whatever port is in use) has to be run before, not after, enabling the firewall — the general form of the fix is simply `ufw allow` naming the needed port.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution: the concept cited only the netfilter documentation index and the firewalld documentation hub, neither of which documents ufw. Re-sourced to ufw(8) (Ubuntu noble manpage, fetched), which states the key outright in REMOTE MANAGEMENT: "When running ufw enable or starting ufw via its initscript, ufw will flush its chains. This is required so ufw can maintain a consistent state, but it may drop existing connections (eg ssh). ufw does support adding rules before enabling the firewall, so administrators can do: ufw allow proto tcp from any to any port 22 before running ufw enable", and in NOTES: "On installation, ufw is disabled with a default incoming policy of deny". The Ubuntu Server firewalls guide (fetched) confirms ufw as the default tool. o2 is false: the same section shows the remedy is an explicit rule the administrator must add, not detection by ufw. o3 is false: ufw(8) records a prompt ("By default, ufw will prompt when enabling the firewall while running under ssh"), which is a warning rather than a refusal, and no error-and-no-change path exists. o4 is false: the default deny policy is on the incoming direction, which is what the SSH session depends on. Distractor whys re-checked and rewritten where needed: o3s why previously said only that ufw does not refuse, which was true but did not name the prompt; it now does. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on option shape as well: o3 ended with the self-refuting hedge "under the great majority of ordinary configurations", replaced with a genuinely false mechanism claim; re-checked - confirmed.

items.stem: A rule is added with `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https`, but clients still cannot reach the service over HTTPS. What is missing?

options.text: `firewall-cmd --reload` — a `--permanent` change does not take effect until a reload, so the rule exists in the permanent configuration but not yet in the active runtime policy.
options.why: firewalld separates the runtime configuration from the permanent one, and firewall-cmd(1) states that --permanent changes are not effective immediately, only after a service restart, a reload, or a reboot; forgetting the reload is the most commonly failed practical detail in this topic.

options.text: Nothing is missing — a `--permanent` rule is defined to take effect in the running configuration the instant the command completes, without any further step.
options.why: A `--permanent` rule specifically does not take effect immediately; it is written to the permanent configuration only, requiring `firewall-cmd --reload` to activate it in the running policy.

options.text: The `--zone` flag must be added to the command, since firewalld rules added without an explicit zone are silently discarded rather than applied to any zone at all.
options.why: A rule added without an explicit `--zone` applies to the default zone rather than being discarded; the actual missing step here is reloading to activate the permanent configuration.

options.text: The service must also be explicitly restarted, since firewalld rules are defined to have no effect on any service until that service itself is restarted.
options.why: Restarting the HTTPS service itself has no bearing on whether firewalld's permanent rule has been reloaded into the active runtime configuration; the missing step is `--reload`, not a service restart.

items.rationale: `firewall-cmd` distinguishes the runtime configuration from the permanent one: a change without `--permanent` is lost at the next reload, and a `--permanent` change does not take effect until `firewall-cmd --reload`, so adding a rule with `--permanent` and expecting it active immediately is exactly the trap in this scenario.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED: the key text is correct but the keys why asserted that "a --permanent change is lost at the next reload if not saved", which is backwards and is contradicted by the cited tool. firewall-cmd(1) (fetched) says the opposite: --reload means "Current permanent configuration will become new runtime configuration, i.e. all runtime only changes done until reload are lost with reload if they have not been also in permanent configuration" - it is the runtime-only change that is lost, never the permanent one. Fedora Quick Docs (fetched) states the same: "Any changes made while firewalld is running will be lost when firewalld is restarted. When firewalld is restarted, the settings revert to their permanent values." The why has been rewritten to the sourced statement, Permanent Options in firewall-cmd(1): "--permanent ... These changes are not effective immediately, only after service restart/reload or system reboot." Key re-checked against that sentence - confirmed. o2 is false by the same sentence. o3 is false: firewall-cmd(1) Zone Options define a default zone that applies when --zone is omitted, so the rule is applied rather than discarded. o4 is false: firewalld rules take effect in the kernel independently of the served applications lifecycle. All remaining distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: `iptables -L` on a current distribution shows no rule for traffic that a colleague insists was configured natively in nftables. Does the absence of a rule in `iptables -L` prove no such rule exists?

options.text: No — on current distributions the `iptables` command is frequently a compatibility layer over nftables, so its output may not show rules created natively in nftables at all.
options.why: Because `iptables` is often an nftables compatibility front-end now, "the rule is not in `iptables -L`" is not proof that no rule exists; it may simply be invisible to that particular view.

options.text: Yes — `iptables -L` is defined to display every packet-filtering rule active on the system regardless of which underlying framework or tool originally created it.
options.why: `iptables -L` reflects rules visible through its own compatibility layer; a rule created natively in nftables may not appear there at all, so its absence is not conclusive proof of nothing existing.

options.text: No, but only because `iptables -L` specifically requires the `-v` flag to reveal any rules created by nftables, which are otherwise omitted from the default terse chain listing shown without it.
options.why: `-v` adds verbose output such as packet counters; it does not reveal nftables-native rules that `iptables -L` is simply not designed to display at all.

options.text: Yes, but only on distributions using ufw or firewalld as a front-end, since only those two tools are capable of hiding rules from `iptables -L` in this way.
options.why: The visibility gap comes from `iptables` itself acting as an nftables compatibility layer, independent of whether ufw or firewalld happen to be installed as additional front-ends.

items.rationale: On current distributions the `iptables` command is frequently a compatibility layer over nftables, the successor framework, so its output may not show rules created natively in nftables — "the rule is not in `iptables -L`" is not proof that no rule exists.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against iptables-nft(8)/xtables-nft (Ubuntu noble manpage, fetched): "xtables-nft are versions of iptables that use the nftables API ... These tools use the libxtables framework extensions and hook to the nf_tables kernel subsystem using the nft_compat module ... the main idea was to replace each legacy binary with a symlink to the xtables-nft program, for example: /sbin/iptables -> /usr/sbin/iptables-nft-multi ... The iptables version string will indicate whether the legacy API (get/setsockopt) or the new nf_tables api is used". Verified empirically rather than by inference, since the manpage does not spell out the visibility gap: docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iptables and nftables installed. `iptables -V` printed "iptables v1.8.10 (nf_tables)". After `nft add table inet t57f; nft add chain inet t57f input { type filter hook input priority 0 ; }; nft add rule inet t57f input tcp dport 9999 drop`, `nft list ruleset` showed the rule, while `iptables -L -n` printed the three built-in chains with no rules at all, and `iptables -L -n -v` likewise showed nothing. That confirms the key and simultaneously confirms o3s why: -v adds counters and does not reveal nft-native rules. o2 is false by the same experiment. o4 is false: the gap comes from iptables being an nftables front-end, and neither ufw nor firewalld was installed in the container that reproduced it. All distractor whys state true facts. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on option shape: o3 ended with the self-refuting phrase "deliberately hidden by default as a matter of routine operational practice", replaced with a genuinely false claim of similar length; re-checked - confirmed. the netfilter documentation index (netfilter-documentation) returns 200 but its ~4.5 KB body is a navigation menu and release news, with 0 occurrences of "REJECT". Dropped. iptables-nft(8) re-fetched and re-verified: "xtables-nft are versions of iptables that use the nftables API ... These tools use the libxtables framework extensions and hook to the nf_tables kernel subsystem using the nft_compat module."

items.stem: On Debian-family and Red Hat-family Linux distributions respectively, which firewall front-end is conventional, and what do both ultimately configure?

options.text: ufw is conventional on Debian-family systems and firewalld on Red Hat-family systems; both ultimately configure the kernel's netfilter packet-filtering framework.
options.why: This is the direct distribution-to-tool mapping the exam tests in the same style as package-manager questions, and both front-ends ultimately drive the same underlying kernel mechanism.

options.text: firewalld is conventional on Debian-family systems and ufw on Red Hat-family systems; both ultimately configure a completely separate framework from netfilter.
options.why: This reverses the conventional distribution mapping — ufw belongs to Debian-family systems and firewalld to Red Hat-family ones — and both, in fact, configure netfilter, not a separate framework.

options.text: ufw is conventional on Debian-family systems and firewalld on Red Hat-family systems, but each configures a distinct, independent kernel packet filter rather than a shared one.
options.why: Both front-ends ultimately configure the same kernel packet-filtering framework, netfilter; they are not independent, separately implemented filtering mechanisms underneath.

options.text: Neither tool is distribution-specific; both ufw and firewalld ship as equally standard defaults across every major Linux distribution family without exception.
options.why: ufw and firewalld are each associated with a specific distribution family by convention, Debian and Red Hat respectively, not shipped as equal defaults across every distribution.

items.rationale: `ufw` (Uncomplicated Firewall) is the simplified front-end shipped by the Debian family, and `firewalld` is the zone-based, dynamically managed front-end shipped by the Red Hat family — all of them, including raw `iptables`, ultimately configure netfilter in the kernel.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against distribution-vendor documentation rather than the two project hubs originally cited. Debian family: Ubuntu Server documentation (fetched) - "The default firewall configuration tool for Ubuntu is ufw" - and ufw(8), whose NAME line is "ufw - program for managing a netfilter firewall". Red Hat family: Fedora Quick Docs (fetched) - "All Fedora Editions install, configure and activate the firewall by default", that firewall being firewalld. Shared substrate: the Ubuntu guide states "The Linux kernel includes the netfilter subsystem, which is used to manipulate or decide the fate of network traffic headed into or through your server. All modern Linux firewall solutions use this system for packet filtering", and firewalld.conf(5) (fetched) shows FirewallBackend selecting "nftables (default), or iptables", both of which are netfilter subsystems. o2 is false on both halves. o3 is false by the Ubuntu guide sentence above. o4 is false by the two vendor statements, which are distribution-specific defaults. All distractor whys state true facts. Recorded as a limit: the Red Hat-family evidence is Fedora rather than RHEL, because docs.redhat.com was not used; Fedora is the same family and the same firewalld project, and the substitution is named here rather than glossed over.

items.stem: A monitoring check against a new service on port 8443 has been failing since deployment. `nc -zv api.example.com 8443` hangs for the full timeout with no response, while `nc -zv api.example.com 22` succeeds instantly. What does this pair of results indicate, and what is the correct next diagnostic step?

options.text: The 8443 timeout indicates a silent drop, port-specific since 22 works instantly; routing is ruled out, so the next step is checking the server's own bind address and then the firewall policy for port 8443 specifically.
options.why: A silent timeout is the signature of packet filtering rather than of a missing service: a closed port answers at once, so no answer at all means the probe or its reply was dropped. Because a different port on the same host answers instantly, routing and host reachability are already excluded, leaving a fault specific to 8443.

options.text: Both results indicate the exact same underlying cause, since a timeout and an instant success are treated as equally strong evidence of the identical routing problem.
options.why: A timeout and an instant success are opposite outcomes with different diagnostic meanings; treating them as equally indicating the same cause discards the most useful evidence in the report.

options.text: The 8443 timeout proves the entire host is unreachable, and the 22 success must therefore be a stale cached result rather than a genuine current connection.
options.why: A working connection on port 22 to the same host at the same time is genuine evidence of reachability, not a stale cache; the host is clearly reachable, and only port 8443 specifically is affected.

options.text: The correct next step is to read the firewall policy first, before checking anything about the server's own service configuration or bind address.
options.why: Reading firewall rules before checking the server's own listening state is how administrators spend an hour on a firewall that was never involved; the server's bind address should be checked first.

items.rationale: Timing the failure is the first diagnostic move: an instant refusal means the host is up and reachable, pointing at the service or its bind address, while a timeout means nothing answered at all — testing a known-open port like 22 alongside the failing one isolates whether the filtering is selective by port or a blanket problem, and `ss -tulpn` on the server itself is the complementary check from the listening side, before reading any firewall policy.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against Nmaps Port Scanning Basics chapter (fetched): filtered means "Nmap cannot determine whether the port is open because packet filtering prevents its probes from reaching the port. The filtering could be from a dedicated firewall device, router rules, or host-based firewall software ... filters that simply drop probes without responding are far more common", whereas closed means "accessible (it receives and responds to Nmap probe packets)". Empirical check (docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2, netcat-openbsd and iptables): listener started with `nc -l -p 9001 -k`; `ss -tuln` showed only `tcp LISTEN 0 1 0.0.0.0:9001`; rules added were `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9003 -j DROP`, `... --dport 9004 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset` and `... --dport 9005 -j REJECT`. `nc -zv -w 3 127.0.0.1 <port>` gave: 9001 "Connection to 127.0.0.1 9001 port [tcp/*] succeeded!"; 9002 (no listener, no rule) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9002 (tcp) failed: Connection refused"; 9003 (DROP) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9003 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress"; 9004 and 9005 (both REJECT forms) "Connection refused". The DROP row reproduces the 8443 symptom and the open row reproduces the 22 symptom on one host, which is exactly the pairing in the stem and shows routing is not implicated. ss(8) is retained because the recommended first step, reading the servers own listening state and bind address, is what `ss -tuln` shows - and in the container above it showed the listener bound on 0.0.0.0:9001 only. o2 is false: a timeout and an instant success are different observations with different meanings. o3 is false: the port 22 success is a live connection, not a cache. o4 is false as advice: the bind address is cheaper to check and is the more common fault, and reading firewall rules first is the documented time sink. All distractor whys state true facts. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on the keys why, which opened by contrasting "refused" with "timed out" although no refusal appears in the stem; rewritten to the observation the scenario actually contains, then re-checked - confirmed.

items.stem: A port scan reports a target port as "closed." A junior analyst reads this as "blocked by a firewall." Is that the correct reading?

options.text: No — closed is not blocked; it is a cooperative answer, an RST, from a working host with nothing listening on that port, which proves layer 3 reachability rather than a block.
options.why: "Closed" is not "blocked": a closed port is a cooperative answer from a working host, and it proves reachability, which is the opposite of what a silent, filtered block would indicate.

options.text: Yes — a port reported as closed always means a firewall somewhere on the path silently dropped the connection attempt without ever reaching the host.
options.why: A silently dropped connection attempt is reported as filtered, not closed; closed specifically means the host answered with an RST, proving the packet reached a live host.

options.text: No, but only because "closed" actually means the destination host does not exist at all, rather than that it exists but has nothing listening.
options.why: A closed port specifically means a live, existing host answered; a nonexistent host would more typically produce a routing failure or a timeout, not a cooperative RST response.

options.text: Yes, but only for UDP scans, since a UDP port reported closed is defined to always indicate a firewall block rather than an application-level absence of a listener, because UDP provides no way for a host to report an absent listener.
options.why: A closed UDP port is not a firewall signature: closed UDP ports usually answer with an ICMP port unreachable error, which is exactly how a scan reports them closed. The genuinely ambiguous UDP case is silence, which is reported as open or filtered rather than closed.

items.rationale: "Closed" is not "blocked": a closed port is a cooperative answer from a working host, and it proves layer 3 reachability — for TCP, a SYN to a closed port is answered with RST, an answer that arrives fast, unlike the silence a filtered port produces.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against Nmaps Port Scanning Basics (fetched): "A closed port is accessible (it receives and responds to Nmap probe packets), but there is no application listening on it. They can be helpful in showing that a host is up ... Because closed ports are reachable, it may be worth scanning later ... Administrators may want to consider blocking such ports with a firewall. Then they would appear in the filtered state" - closed and blocked are named as different states, and the source even describes the transition from one to the other. The RST detail in the key is sourced to the Port Scanning Techniques chapter (fetched): "A SYN/ACK indicates the port is listening (open), while a RST (reset) is indicative of a non-listener." Empirical check (docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2, netcat-openbsd and iptables): listener started with `nc -l -p 9001 -k`; `ss -tuln` showed only `tcp LISTEN 0 1 0.0.0.0:9001`; rules added were `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9003 -j DROP`, `... --dport 9004 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset` and `... --dport 9005 -j REJECT`. `nc -zv -w 3 127.0.0.1 <port>` gave: 9001 "Connection to 127.0.0.1 9001 port [tcp/*] succeeded!"; 9002 (no listener, no rule) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9002 (tcp) failed: Connection refused"; 9003 (DROP) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9003 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress"; 9004 and 9005 (both REJECT forms) "Connection refused". The 9002 row is a closed port answering with an instant refusal from a live host; the 9003 row is the filtered contrast. o2 is false: a silently dropped probe is reported filtered. o3 is false: closed requires a live responder. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o4: its why asserted that "a definitively closed reading is not the UDP case at all", which is false - Nmaps UDP scan section states "Closed ports ... usually send back an ICMP port unreachable error" and are classified closed on that basis, while it is open and filtered ports that "rarely send any response". o4s text and why were both rewritten so the option is wrong for a true stated reason, and o4 also carried the self-refuting tail "which is the assumption most administrators start from", which is gone. Re-checked - confirmed.

items.stem: A firewall configured to REJECT rather than DROP is in the path to a service. A scan against it comes back with an immediate refusal. Does that immediate refusal conclusively prove the destination host itself has nothing listening?

options.text: No, a REJECT rule answers on the destination host's behalf, so a firewall anywhere on the path can produce the refusal without the destination ever seeing the packet; an immediate refusal proves only that something on the path answered, not that the destination is up with nothing listening.
options.why: A REJECT firewall rule produces the same refused response a closed port would, but it can do so without the packet ever reaching the actual destination host, which is a documented subtlety worth holding onto.

options.text: Yes — an immediate refusal is always generated exclusively by the destination host itself and can never originate from an intermediate firewall or security appliance sitting somewhere on the path.
options.why: A REJECT rule on an intermediate firewall specifically can source the refusal on the destination's behalf, so an immediate refusal does not always originate from the destination host itself.

options.text: No, but only because REJECT rules are exclusively a UDP-scanning artefact and have no bearing whatsoever on TCP-based port scans, which always report closed ports as filtered instead.
options.why: REJECT rules apply to TCP scans as well as UDP ones; the described subtlety, the reply sourced on the destination's behalf, is not restricted to UDP scanning.

options.text: Yes, but only when the scan is run with `nc -zv` specifically, since other scanning tools are defined to correctly distinguish a REJECT rule from a genuinely closed port by inspecting the reply's source rather than just its type.
options.why: No standard scanning tool can reliably distinguish a REJECT rule's reply from a genuinely closed port's RST from outside the network; this is an inherent limitation of the technique, not specific to `nc -zv`.

items.rationale: A firewall configured to REJECT rather than DROP produces the refused response too, so an immediate refusal does not conclusively prove nothing is listening — it does prove something on the path answered, but a REJECT rule sources its reply from the original packet's destination address without the destination host itself ever seeing the packet.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED: the key claimed a REJECT rule "sources its RST or ICMP reply from the original packet's destination address". iptables-extensions(8) (fetched) documents only that REJECT "is used to send back an error packet in response to the matched packet: otherwise it is equivalent to DROP", with --reject-with selecting an ICMP unreachable type or tcp-reset; it says nothing about the source address of that reply, and for a forwarding firewall an ICMP error is normally sourced from the rejecting device rather than the original destination. The key has been narrowed to the claim the sources and the experiment support - that a REJECT rule answers on the destination's behalf, so the refusal proves only that something answered. Empirical check (docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04 with iproute2, netcat-openbsd and iptables): listener started with `nc -l -p 9001 -k`; `ss -tuln` showed only `tcp LISTEN 0 1 0.0.0.0:9001`; rules added were `iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9003 -j DROP`, `... --dport 9004 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset` and `... --dport 9005 -j REJECT`. `nc -zv -w 3 127.0.0.1 <port>` gave: 9001 "Connection to 127.0.0.1 9001 port [tcp/*] succeeded!"; 9002 (no listener, no rule) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9002 (tcp) failed: Connection refused"; 9003 (DROP) "nc: connect to 127.0.0.1 port 9003 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress"; 9004 and 9005 (both REJECT forms) "Connection refused". Ports 9004 (tcp-reset) and 9005 (default icmp-port-unreachable) both produced "Connection refused", indistinguishable at the client from the genuinely closed port 9002, which is the item's whole point. Nmap's Port Scanning Basics chapter supports the same reading from the scanner side: filtered ports "sometimes ... respond with ICMP error messages such as type 3 code 13 (destination unreachable: communication administratively prohibited)", i.e. a filter answering for a destination it is protecting. o2 is false by the experiment. o3 is false: the REJECT target is documented for the INPUT, FORWARD and OUTPUT chains and applies to TCP, with tcp-reset explicitly available. o4 is false: the ambiguity is in the reply itself, not in nc; the tcp-reset row above is byte-for-byte a normal RST. All distractor whys state true facts. Re-checked after the rewrite - confirmed.

items.stem: Why is a UDP port scan considered fundamentally unreliable compared to a TCP scan?

options.text: UDP has no handshake, so silence in response to a probe is ambiguous between an open port that simply chose not to reply and a port that is genuinely filtered.
options.why: TCP's SYN-ACK or RST gives a definitive answer either way, but UDP defeats that scheme entirely: with no handshake, silence cannot distinguish open from filtered.

options.text: UDP scans are unreliable only because `nc -zv` does not support the `-u` flag needed to test UDP ports at all on any current version.
options.why: `nc -zv` does support `-u` for testing UDP; the unreliability comes from UDP's lack of a handshake making silence ambiguous, not from a missing tool feature.

options.text: UDP scans are unreliable because UDP packets are always dropped by every firewall by default, making every UDP port appear closed regardless of its actual state.
options.why: Firewalls do not universally drop all UDP traffic by default; the unreliability is specifically about silence being ambiguous between an open, non-responding port and a genuinely filtered one.

options.text: UDP scans are unreliable only on IPv6 networks, since IPv4 UDP scanning is defined to always produce a definitive open, closed or filtered result.
options.why: The ambiguity in UDP scanning comes from UDP's connectionless design itself, applicable to both IPv4 and IPv6, not from any IPv6-specific limitation.

items.rationale: UDP has no handshake, so no response is ambiguous between an open port that simply does not reply and a filtered one — for TCP, a SYN to an open port gets SYN-ACK and a SYN to a closed port gets RST, both fast, definitive answers UDP has no equivalent of.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against Nmap. Port Scanning Basics (fetched) defines open|filtered as the state used "when it is unable to determine whether a port is open or filtered. This occurs for scan types in which open ports give no response. The lack of response could also mean that a packet filter dropped the probe or any response it elicited", and names UDP first among the scans that classify ports this way. Port Scanning Techniques (fetched) states the mechanism: "Open and filtered ports rarely send any response, leaving Nmap to time out and then conduct retransmissions", against TCP where "A SYN/ACK indicates the port is listening (open), while a RST (reset) is indicative of a non-listener" - a definitive answer either way. o2 is false: netcat-openbsd supports -u for UDP, and the unreliability is a protocol property. o3 is false: nothing makes firewalls drop all UDP by default, and the same chapter notes closed UDP ports usually return an ICMP port unreachable, so UDP ports are not uniformly reported closed either. o4 is false: the connectionless design is address-family independent. All distractor whys state true facts.

items.stem: A server does not respond to `ping`, and an operator immediately reports it as down. TCP services on the same host, tested separately, work perfectly. What does this combination actually show, and what should the operator have concluded first?

options.text: It shows ICMP is being filtered or the host is configured not to answer echo requests; the host is clearly up, so "ping fails, therefore the host is down" is the wrong conclusion.
options.why: A failed ping does not prove a host is down, because ICMP is very commonly blocked by policy while TCP services on the same host work perfectly — treating ping failure as proof of a dead host is a classic wrong conclusion.

options.text: It shows the host is genuinely down, since a working TCP connection to the same address without a working ping is a technical impossibility on any real network, because a TCP handshake cannot complete until the same host has already answered an ICMP echo request.
options.why: A host can be fully up and serving TCP connections while ICMP is filtered separately; the two are independent, and a working TCP connection alongside a failed ping is a common, expected combination.

options.text: It shows DNS is misconfigured for that host, since a failed ping combined with working TCP connections is defined to always indicate a name-resolution problem.
options.why: The scenario does not describe a naming issue at all; both the failed ping and the working TCP connections were tested against the same reachable host, which points at ICMP filtering, not DNS.

options.text: It shows the host's routing table is broken, since only a routing failure could explain ICMP failing while TCP traffic to the very same address succeeds.
options.why: A broken routing table would affect TCP traffic just as much as ICMP traffic to the same destination; the described split, ICMP failing while TCP succeeds, points at protocol-specific filtering, not routing.

items.rationale: `ping` is the cheapest reachability test available, but a failed ping does not prove a host is down: ICMP is very commonly blocked by policy while TCP services on the same host work perfectly, which is exactly why treating ping failure as proof of a dead host is a classic, examinable wrong conclusion.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution, plus one self-refuting distractor. (1) The key's load-bearing claim is that ICMP is commonly filtered while TCP works. RFC 792, the only cited source, defines ICMP message formats and says nothing about filtering policy - the exact 'plausible-but-silent citation' trap. Fixed at concept level by adding nmap-host-discovery, which states plainly: 'many hosts and firewalls now block these packets, rather than responding as required by RFC 1122. For this reason, ICMP-only scans are rarely reliable enough against unknown targets.' (2) o2 carried a self-refuting tail ('as commonly understood by less experienced staff') announcing its own wrongness; replaced with a real false claim (TCP handshake preceded by an ICMP echo) of greater length, which also narrows the key-is-longest gap. (3) No distractor is also correct: o3 (DNS) is excluded because the stem states TCP to the same host works, so the address resolved; o4 (routing) is excluded because a routing fault is destination-scoped, not protocol-scoped. Each distractor 'why' states a true fact. Empirical: on Ubuntu 24.04 in Docker, 'ping -c1 127.0.0.1' succeeded (64 bytes from 127.0.0.1 ... time=0.660 ms) while an ICMP-blocked host is the ordinary case per Nmap.

items.stem: Running `ping web01` produces "Name or service not known." A colleague starts checking cabling and switch ports. Is that the right first move given this particular error message?

options.text: No — this specific message means name resolution failed, not reachability; ping answers a name as well as an address, so this points straight at DNS or `/etc/hosts`, not at cabling or switching.
options.why: Ping answers a name as well as an address, so a ping that fails with "Name or service not known" is a DNS failure, not a reachability failure, a distinction the output states plainly and readers routinely skip.

options.text: Yes — "Name or service not known" is defined to always indicate a physical-layer fault, making cabling and switch ports the correct first thing to check, since ping reports resolver failures with a separate 'unknown host' message instead.
options.why: The message specifically reports a naming failure, not a physical-layer one; checking cabling and switches first skips past the actual, plainly stated cause.

options.text: No, but only because the correct first move is instead to check the default gateway configuration rather than name resolution at all.
options.why: The gateway matters for reaching off-subnet destinations by address, but this specific error message is about resolving a name, which points at DNS or `/etc/hosts`, not the gateway.

options.text: No, but only because the correct first move is instead to check the ARP cache for the target host's MAC address before anything else.
options.why: ARP resolves an already-known IP address to a MAC address on the local segment; a name-resolution failure happens before any address exists to resolve into a MAC at all.

items.rationale: Reading the failure text before anything else pays off here: "Name or service not known" is DNS, not reachability, and the message states this plainly, which is exactly the distinction readers routinely skip past on their way to checking cabling and switches.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED AS AUTHORED on attribution and one self-refuting distractor. RFC 792 does not document ping's CLI messages; man7-ping added at concept level. ping(8) takes a 'destination' that may be a name (the -n option is documented as 'Numeric output only. No attempt will be made to lookup symbolic names', which is only meaningful because names are otherwise resolved). Verified empirically on Ubuntu 24.04: 'ping -c1 web01' printed exactly 'ping: web01: Name or service not known', while 'ping -c1 127.0.0.1' succeeded - so the message is a resolver failure, not a reachability failure, confirming the key and refuting o2. o2's self-refuting tail ('a belief that persists because it sounds intuitive') was replaced with a genuinely false clause of similar length. o3 and o4 are wrong for the stated reasons: the gateway matters only once an address exists, and ARP operates on an already-resolved IP; both 'why' texts state true facts.

items.stem: A router along the path replies "Destination Host Unreachable" to a `ping`. Who generated that message, and what does it actually report?

options.text: A router along the path generated it, reporting that it could not deliver the packet; it is a third party's report, not the target host answering.
options.why: A router replying "Destination Host Unreachable" is not the target answering; it is a third party reporting that it could not deliver, an important distinction when localising a fault.

options.text: The target host itself generated it directly, confirming it received the ping but is deliberately refusing to answer it under its current configuration.
options.why: This specific message is generated by an intermediate router, not the target host; the target never received the packet at all in this scenario.

options.text: The originating host's own local DNS resolver generated it as a cached response to a previous, unrelated failed lookup for the same name.
options.why: A DNS resolver does not generate ICMP unreachable messages; this message is an ICMP-layer report from a router on the path, unrelated to name resolution or caching.

options.text: A firewall on the originating host itself generated it locally, before the ping packet had even left the machine attempting to send it.
